en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Khandha Vagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
1. Saṃyutta Nikāya: Khandha Saṃyutta 1.
Nakulapituvagga 1. Nakulapitu Sutta:
Commentary on the Discourse to Nakula’s Father
1. In the first chapter of the *Khandhaka*, "among the Bhaggas" means in the country of that name. "At Susumāragira" means at the city of Susumāragira.
It is said that while that city was being built, a crocodile (*susumāra*) let out a cry; therefore, they gave it the name "Susumāragira.
"In the Bhesakaḷā Grove" means in the forest that had acquired this name because it was inhabited by a female spirit (*yakkhinī*) named Bhesakaḷā. That very same...
It is called "Deer Park" (Migadāya) because it was given for the sake of providing safety to the herd of deer.
The Blessed One dwelt in that forest grove, depending upon that city in that district. "Nakulapitā" means the father of a boy named Nakula.
"Jiṇṇa" means worn out by old age. "Vuḍḍha" means advanced in years. "Mahallaka" means advanced in birth (aged). "Addhagata" means one who has reached the third stage of life (an octogenarian).
"Having reached old age" means having arrived at the final stage among those three stages of life.
"With a sick body" means with a diseased body. For this body, even if it is golden-hued, is indeed called "sick" in the sense of being constantly leaking [impurities].

Specifically, however, there are three types of sickness for it: the sickness of old age, the sickness of disease, and the sickness of death. Among these, although he—on account of his advanced age—...
"Like one afflicted by old age": here, his state of being afflicted by disease is intended in the sense of constant illness.
"Constantly distressed" means he is constantly ill, suffering from continuous disease.

"One who sees impermanence" means that because of that affliction, unable to come at every desired moment, he thinks, "I can see him only occasionally, not at all times. "Of those who are heart-pleasing" means of those who increase the mind's delight.

Indeed, through the power of skillfulness, the mind expands toward those things seen; these great elders, Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and others, are called "those who are to be cherished in mind" (*manobhāvanīya*).
"Let them instruct" means let them instruct again and again. For the initial statement is called "advice" (*ovāda*), while subsequent instruction is called "injunction" (*anusāsanī*).
Furthermore, a statement made when a matter has already arisen is called "advice," whereas one made before it has arisen is [called] "injunction" by way of its continuity.

Or it is called "instruction" (*anusāsanī*) because it is spoken according to the lineage. Furthermore, whether it is called "advice" (*ovāda*) or "instruction" (*anusāsanī*), they are identical in meaning;
there is only a difference in the phrasing.
It is "ailing" (*āturo*); for this [body] is indeed ailing, even though it possesses a golden complexion and the hue of *piyaṅgu*, in the sense that it is constantly oozing.
"Like one who is ill. "Become like an egg" means he has become weak like an egg.
Just as when one picks up a hen's egg or a peacock's egg and plays with it or strikes it as if it were a ball, it cannot withstand such treatment and breaks immediately;
even so, this body breaks if one stumbles over a thorn or a stump—it is like an egg.
"Become" means become as an egg. "Enveloped" means enveloped by a mere thin skin. For an egg is enveloped by a firm membrane;
thus, even if gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like settle upon it, they are unable to pierce the skin and cause the fluid to flow out.
But in this case [the human body], having pierced the skin, they do whatever they wish. Thus, by means of this subtle...
Enveloped in skin. What else [is there] than foolishness? What other meaning is there besides the state of being a fool? The meaning is that he is simply a fool.
"Therefore" means because this body is of such a nature, therefore.
"He approached him" means having gone to the presence of the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti), immediately thereafter [he approached] the Jewel of the General (Pariṇāyakaratana).

Like a royal official going to attend upon [his master], having gone to attend upon the Blessed One—the Wheel-turner of the True Dhamma—he then approached the Venerable Sāriputta, desiring to pay him honor.
"Vippasannāni" means perfectly clear. "Indriyāni" refers to the faculties, with the mind as the sixth. "Parisuddho" means...
"Flawless. "Pure" is a synonym for that very same quality. Indeed, it is called "pure" precisely because of its freedom from defilements, not because of its whiteness.
And it was by seeing this purity that he recognized the clarity of the faculties.
This, it is said, was the Elder’s wisdom of grasping the underlying method.
"How indeed might it not be so? means for what reason would it not be obtained? The meaning is that it certainly will be obtained. What does this illustrate?

It illustrates his state of being trusted by the Teacher. It is said that from the moment he first saw the Teacher, he acquired affection like that for a son, while the female lay follower acquired affection like that for a mother. Both of them addressed the Teacher as "my son. Even when he had passed to another existence...
For they had affection for one another. It is said that for five hundred births that laywoman was like the mother of the Tathāgata, and he, householder, was like the father.
Again, for five hundred births the laywoman was the chief queen and the layman was the chief minister; likewise, [for five hundred births] she was the junior queen and he the junior minister.
Thus, for fifteen hundred existences, the Teacher was nurtured by their very hands. For this very reason—
Those things which they could not have spoken in the presence of either their son or their father, they spoke while seated in the presence of the Teacher.

For this very reason, the Blessed One placed them in the foremost position, saying: "Bhikkhus, among my lay male disciples who are full of confidence, Nakulapitā the householder is the foremost; among my lay female disciples who are full of confidence, Nakulamātā the housewife is the foremost. Thus he ranked them as the best.
He established [this]. Thus, demonstrating this state of trustworthiness, he said, "How could it not be so? Regarding the phrase "anointed with the Deathless" (*amata-abhisitta*):
here, nothing else—neither jhāna, nor insight (*vipassanā*), nor the path (*magga*), nor the fruit (*phala*)—is to be understood as the "anointing with the Deathless.
Rather, it is the sweet teaching of the Dhamma itself that should be known as the "anointing with the Deathless. "Even from afar" means even from another kingdom or another province.
"An uninstructed worldling"—this has already been explained. Regarding the phrases "one who does not see the noble ones," and so forth:

they are called "noble ones" (*ariya*) because they are far removed from defilements (*ārakattā kilesehi*), because they do not proceed in what is not the right way (*anaye na iriyanato*), because they proceed in the right way (*aye iriyanato*), and because they are to be honored by the world together with its devas (*sadevakena ca lokena araṇīyato*).
Thus, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha are called noble ones. Or rather, it is the Buddhas alone who are the noble ones here, as it is said:
“Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is called ‘the Noble One.
Regarding the phrase “of true persons,” here it should be understood that Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Tathāgata are true persons (*sappurisa*).

For they are “true persons” because they are beautiful persons due to their possession of supramundane qualities. Alternatively, all these [categories] are stated in both ways; for Buddhas too are both noble ones (*ariya*) and true persons.
as well as paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Buddha. As it is said:
“He who is grateful and mindful of what has been done, wise, a good friend, and firm in devotion;”
“He performs his duty with care for one who is suffering;
such a person they call a true man.
By this much—namely, by the words “he has a virtuous friend and is firm in devotion”—the disciple of the Buddha is described, through his gratitude and other qualities.

"Paccekabuddhas and Buddhas. Now, one who is habitually not seeing those noble ones (ariya) and does not perform well in seeing them should be understood as "one who has not seen the noble ones" (ariyānaṃ adassāvī).
And he is of two kinds: one who has not seen with the eye, and one who has not seen with wisdom (ñāṇa).
Of these, it is the one who has not seen with wisdom who is intended here. For even if the noble ones have been seen with the fleshly eye or the divine eye, [they are still not seen by wisdom].
They are "not seen" by those eyes because they grasp only the mere color-form, not because they fall within the range of the noble state.
Even jackals, dogs, and the like see the Noble Ones with their eyes, yet these are not called "seers of the Noble Ones.
In this regard, there is this story: it is said that the attendant of an elder who had destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) and was an elder who had gone forth in old age lived on Mount Cittala.
One day, after walking for alms together with the Elder, he took the Elder’s bowl and robes and followed behind him.
As he was coming along, he asked the Elder: “Venerable sir, what are those called ‘noble ones’ (ariya) like? The Elder replied:
“In this case, even if some elderly man follows the noble ones, taking their bowl and robes and performing his duties and services, he still does not—”
“The Noble Ones know [this]; thus, friends, the Noble Ones are difficult to understand. Even when this was said, he did not yet understand.
Therefore, seeing with the eye is not true seeing; only seeing by means of knowledge is true seeing. As it has been said:
“Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this putrid body? He who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me. He who sees me…”
“Thus he sees the Dhamma. Therefore, even while seeing with the eye, one who does not see with wisdom the characteristics of impermanence and so forth as seen by the Noble Ones,
and who does not attain the Dhamma attained by the Noble Ones— because of not having seen the qualities that make one noble and the state of nobility—
is to be understood as “one who has not seen the Noble Ones.”
“Unskilled in the noble Dhamma” means unskilled in the noble Dhamma distinguished by the foundations of mindfulness and so forth. Regarding the phrase “undisciplined in the noble Dhamma,” it is said:
“Discipline is twofold, and each of these is fivefold;
Because of the absence of that [discipline], one is called undisciplined.”

For this discipline (vinaya) is twofold: the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) and the discipline of abandonment (pahāna-vinaya). And herein, each of these two types of discipline is further divided fivefold. For the discipline of restraint is fivefold:

the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), the restraint of mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), the restraint of knowledge (ñāṇa-saṃvara), the restraint of patience (khanti-saṃvara), and the restraint of energy (vīriya-saṃvara).
The discipline of abandonment is also [fivefold]: abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna),...
It is fivefold: abandonment by eradication, abandonment by subsiding, and abandonment by escape.

Therein, “He is endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha, fully endowed”—this is restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). “He guards the eye-faculty; he attains restraint over the eye-faculty”—this is restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*).
“Whatever streams there are in the world... (said the Blessed One, Ajita).
Mindfulness is their prevention;
I call it the restraint of the streams.
By means of wisdom, these are closed up.

This is the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*). “He is patient with cold and heat”—this is the restraint of patience (*khantisaṃvara*). “He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*)”—this is the restraint of energy (*vīriyasaṃvara*).

And all this restraint is called “restraint” (*saṃvara*) because it restrains those things that ought to be restrained and those things that ought to be disciplined, such as bodily misconduct; and it is called “discipline” (*vinaya*) because of its disciplining nature.
Thus, first of all, it should be understood that the discipline of restraint (saṃvaravinaya) is fivefold.

Likewise, among the insights (vipassanāñāṇa) such as the discernment of name-and-form (nāmarūpapariccheda), there is the abandoning of various unwholesome states by means of each respective insight-knowledge, because they stand as opposites to those states—just as darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp.
For example: by means of the analysis of name-and-form (nāmarūpavavatthāna)...

By means of the discernment of conditions, one abandons the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the views of no-cause or irregular cause; subsequently, by means of the overcoming of doubt, one abandons the state of indecisiveness;

by means of the comprehension of aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*), one abandons the grasping of "I" and "mine"; by means of the determination of what is and is not the path, one abandons the perception of a path where there is no path;
and by means of the vision of arising, one abandons the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*); and by means of the vision of passing away, one abandons the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

By seeing fear, there is the perception of fearlessness regarding what is fearful; by seeing danger, there is the perception of gratification; by the contemplation of disenchantment, there is the perception of delight;
by the knowledge of desire for liberation, there is the lack of desire for liberation. By the knowledge of equanimity, there is the lack of equanimity;
by conformity, there is the contrary state toward the stability of phenomena and Nibbāna; by the change-of-lineage, there is the grasping at the sign of formations.
This is called abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

Furthermore, that abandonment of various states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), which occurs through concentration— distinguished as access and absorption— by way of obstructing the process of existence,
just as the removal of moss from the surface of water by striking it with a pot, is called suppression-cessation (*vikkhambhanappahāna*).

The abandonment of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination— which occurs through the development of the four noble paths such that, within the continuum of one who possesses each respective path,
there is an absolute non-arising of those defilements described by the method beginning with "for the abandoning of views"—
is called abandonment by cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*). Furthermore, that which is the subsiding of the defilements at the moment of the fruition (*phala-kkhaṇa*)—
This is called abandoning by subsiding.
That which is Nibbāna—abandoned because it has escaped from all the conditioned—is called abandoning by escape.
And since all this abandoning is abandoning in the sense of relinquishing and discipline in the sense of subduing, therefore...

It is called "discipline by abandoning" (*pahānavinaya*). Alternatively, it is called "discipline by abandoning" because each respective discipline arises for one who has abandoned [the corresponding fault].
Thus, discipline by abandoning should be understood as being divided fivefold.
In this way, this discipline is twofold in brief, and tenfold when analyzed, due to the diversity of the restraints required for what is to be abandoned.
And because this [lack of training] does not exist for this uninstructed worldling due to its non-abandonment, it is therefore called "undisciplined" (*avinīta*) owing to its absence.
This same method applies here as well in the case of "one who has not seen the true persons, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of the true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the true persons.
For there is no difference in meaning between these [terms]. As it has been said:
“Those who are noble are the same as those who are true persons; those who are true persons are the same as those who are noble.
Whatever is the Dhamma of the noble ones is the same as the Dhamma of the true persons; whatever is the Dhamma of the true persons is the same as the Dhamma of the noble ones.

Those who are trained in the discipline of the noble ones are the same as those trained in the discipline of the true persons; those who are trained in the discipline of the true persons are the same as those trained in the discipline of the noble ones.”

These are the noble trainings. Whether one speaks of the noble one (*ariya*) or the true person (*sappurisa*), whether of the noble Dhamma or the true person’s Dhamma, whether of the noble training or the true person’s training—these are identical, one in meaning, one in purpose, equal, of the same category, and the very same thing.
“One regards form as self” means: here someone regards form as self, thinking, “Whatever is form, that is my self.”
"I am" and "that which I am is form"—thus one regards form and the self as non-dual.
Just as, for example, when an oil lamp is burning, one regards the flame and the color as non-dual—thinking, "That which is the flame is the color;
that which is the color is the flame"—even so, here someone regards form as the self... [and so on] ...regarding them as non-dual.
In this way, one views form as "self" through the vision of speculative views.
Or, regarding "the self as possessing form," having grasped the formless as "self," one regards it as possessing form, like a tree possessing shade.
Or, regarding "form in the self," having grasped the formless alone as "self," one regards form as being in the self, like fragrance in a flower. In form...
Or, taking the formless itself as "self," one regards that self within form, like a gem in a casket.
"One who dwells obsessed" means one who stands in the manner of obsession, in the manner of overcoming;
it refers to one who, having swallowed and finalized [the view] through craving and views such as "I am form, form is mine," becomes a grasper.
The meaning is as follows: "That form for him" refers to that very form apprehended by him. The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well.
In this context, the statement "he regards form as self" expresses the idea of pure form itself being the self. [Furthermore, there are:
"or a self possessed of form," "or form in the self," or "a self in form"; and likewise for "feeling as self," "perception," and "volitional formations."
In these seven instances, formless consciousness is described as the self: “one regards consciousness as the self.

Furthermore, by way of each of the four aggregates, the self is described as mixed with both form and the formless in twelve instances: “the self as possessing feeling,” “feeling in the self,” or “the self in feeling. In that context, “form as the self...”
“...or regards feeling... perception... volitional formations...
or consciousness as self”—in these five instances, the view of annihilationism is taught; in the remaining cases, it is the view of eternalism.
Thus, there are fifteen views of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*) and five views of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*) here; all of them are obstacles to the Path, not obstacles to heaven.
It should be understood that [these defilements] are to be abandoned by the first path.
Thus, householder, when it is said "the body is afflicted and the mind is afflicted," the body is indeed afflicted even for the Buddhas;
however, the mind accompanied by lust, hatred, and delusion is what is called "afflicted," and that is what is shown here. But it is not the case that [the Buddha] has an afflicted mind.
Here, the state of being unafflicted in mind through the absence of defilement is shown.
Thus, in this sutta, it is shown that the worldling is both afflicted in body and afflicted in mind; those whose taints are destroyed are afflicted in body but unafflicted in mind;

and the seven types of trainees (sekhas) should be understood as neither afflicted in mind nor unafflicted in mind. However, by cultivating [the path], they are indeed approaching the state of being unafflicted in mind.
“They resort to” means: first [is finished]. 2.
Commentary on the Devadaha Sutta.
Second: “Devadaha” means that kings are called *devas*; it is their auspicious lake (*maṅgaladaha*), or else that lake is self-arisen (*sayaṃjāta*).
Therefore, it was called “Devadaha. Not far from that place, a market town came to be known by the same name, Devadaha, according to its neuter grammatical gender.
“Bound for the western country” means those desiring to go to the region established in the western direction.
“Dwelling” refers to the three-month rains residence (*vassāvāsa*). “Having been asked” means having been invited. “Ask” means request permission. Why?
He has the elder informed. This is because they wish to remain with their burden.
For one who, even while living in the same monastery, does not go near [the elder] and departs without informing him when leaving, this is called "one without a burden" (*nibbhāra*).

One who, even while living in the same monastery, comes to see [the elder] and informs him when departing, this is called "one with a burden" (*sabhāra*). These monks also, the Blessed One said: "In this way..."
Wishing to make them his companions in the requisites of the path—thinking, "They shall increase in virtue and the other perfections"—he asks for permission.
"Wise" means endowed with the fourfold wisdom, such as proficiency in the elements (*dhātu*).
"Supportive" means one who supports by both kinds of support: material support and the support of the Dhamma. It is said that the Elder, unlike other bhikkhus, [acted thus].

Even before going out for alms in the morning, when all the other bhikkhus had already departed, he would wander throughout the entire monastic compound, sweeping the unswept places, discarding the rubbish that had not been thrown away, and putting back in their proper places the beds, stools, wooden articles, and earthenware that had been left poorly arranged.
For what reason? “Lest those belonging to other sects, having entered the monastery and seen this, should treat us with contempt.”
Then, having gone to the infirmary and comforted the sick, he asked, "What do you need?
Having taken those young novices who had whatever they required, he sought medicine for them either by means of the practice of alms-gathering or from a suitable place;
having given it to them, he said, "Attending the sick has been praised by the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas; go now."
"O virtuous men, be diligent! Having sent them off, he himself wanders for alms, performs his meal duties at the family of his supporters, and then returns to the monastery.
This, first of all, was his established practice regarding his fixed place of residence.
However, when the Blessed One was wandering on tour, [he would go out] thinking, "I am the foremost disciple," having put on sandals and taken up a parasol.

He does not go ahead of them. However, for those who are elderly, infirm, or very young, he has their vulnerable parts rubbed with oil, has his own bowl and robes taken by his young novices, and then takes them along—either that day or the next—and goes on his way.
For one day, he [took] that very venerable one...
Because they had arrived very late and failed to obtain a lodging, the Teacher saw them sitting in the robe-tent.

On the following day, he assembled the community of monks, related the story of the elephant, the horse, and the partridge, and established the training rule: "Lodgings must be assigned according to seniority. In this way, he assists them with material support.
When giving advice, he continues to advise even a hundred or a thousand times until that person is established in the fruit of stream-entry;

then, having released him, he advises another. By advising in this manner, those who have stood by his advice and attained arahantship exceed all calculation. In this way, he assists others through the support of the Dhamma.
Those bhikkhus replied, “He is neither our preceptor, nor our teacher, nor one with whom we have a personal bond of friendship.
What shall we do in his presence? Without remaining silent, they accepted the Teacher’s word, saying, “So be it, Bhante.
“At the *eḷagalāgumba*” means at a bower formed by creeping vines. It is said that this *eḷagalāgumba* grew in a place where water was constantly present.
It was born. Then, having constructed a pavilion there with four pillars, they placed that bush upon it, and it covered the pavilion.
Then, having built a foundation below it with bricks and scattered sand, they prepared a seat.
A cool breeze blew from the water toward the daytime resting place. The Elder sat down there. It is with reference to this that it is said: "in the eḷagalā bush."
"Nānāverajjagataṃ" means having gone to various kingdoms from the kingdom of one king. "Virajjaṃ" means another kingdom.
For just as there is a foreign land (videso) other than one's own country (sadeso), so too a kingdom other than the one in which one has lived is called "virajjaṃ";
that is what is meant by "verajjaṃ. "Khattiyapaṇḍitā" refers to wise kings such as Bimbisāra, the King of Kosala, and others. "Brāhmaṇapaṇḍitā" refers to...
The wise brahmins include Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and others. The wise householders include Cittasudatta and other wise laymen.
The wise recluses include Sabhiya, Pilindavaccha, and other wise wanderers. "Inquirers" (vīmaṃsaka) means those who seek the truth.
"What does he profess? (kiṃvādī) means what view does he state for himself; the meaning is, what is his doctrine? "What does he declare? (kimakkhāyī) refers to what he declares to his disciples.

Does he explain the instruction and admonition? "In accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammassa cānudhammam*) means a further explanation (*anubyākaraṇa*) of what was spoken by the Blessed One as an explanation (*byākaraṇa*).
"In accordance with the Dhamma" (*sahadhammiko*) means having a valid reason. "A discourse and counter-discourse" (*vādānuvādo*) means a counter-discourse to the discourse spoken by the Blessed One.

There is also a reading, "entering into the discourse" (*vādānupāto*); the meaning is entering into (*anupāto*), falling into (*anupatana*), or following (*anugamana*) the Teacher’s discourse. By this also, one has followed the discourse.
The discourse itself is thus illuminated.
In the phrases beginning with "one who has not overcome lust," the meaning should be understood by way of craving (*taṇhā*) alone. For craving is called "lust" (*rāga*) because of its coloring;
"desire" (*chanda*) because of its longing; "affection" (*pema*) in the sense of endearment; "thirst" (*pipāsā*) in the sense of a desire to drink; and "fever" (*pariḷāha*) in the sense of burning.
It is said. Why was the passage beginning with "And as for unwholesome states, friend... commenced?

It is to show the danger for one who is not free from lust for the five aggregates, and the benefit for one who is free from lust. In that context, "unafflicted" means free from suffering (*niddukkho*). "Untroubled" means free from distress (*nirupatāpo*).
"Without fever" means free from burning heat (*niddāho*). In this way, the meaning is to be understood in all instances. The second [section].

3. Commentary on the Hāliddikāni Sutta In the third [discourse], "In Avantī" means in the kingdom of Avantī, which is comprised of the southern region of Avantī. "At Kuraraghara" refers to a city of that name.
"On a precipice" means on a cliff on one side; it is said that one side of that mountain had been cut away and cast down.
It was as if [it were so]. There is also a reading “pavatte,” which means “in the place where the tenets of various sectarians prevail.
Thus the Elder dwelt on that mountain, depending upon that city in that kingdom.
“Hāliddikāni” is his name. Regarding the Māgaṇḍiya Question in the Aṭṭhakavagga: there is a question called the Māgaṇḍiya Question within the Aṭṭhakavagga; in that—
Regarding the question: "The form-element" (rūpadhātu) refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). "Bound by craving for the form-element" means bound by craving within the form-element.
"Consciousness" (viññāṇa) refers to kamma-consciousness. "One who wanders in a dwelling" (okasārī) means one who wanders in a home or wanders in attachment (ālayasārī).
But why is it not stated here, "The consciousness-element (viññāṇadhātu), householder"? It is for the purpose of dispelling confusion. [For] "dwelling" (oko)...
For in its actual meaning, "condition" (paccaya) is what is being spoken of;

and since a pre-arisen kamma-consciousness is a condition for a post-arisen kamma-consciousness as well as for a resultant consciousness, and a resultant consciousness is a condition for a subsequent resultant consciousness as well as for a kamma-consciousness, there might arise confusion as to which consciousness is meant here. To dispel that [confusion]:

Without including that [consciousness], the teaching was given as undivided. Furthermore, since the four stations of consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇaṭṭhiti*) were stated by way of their objects, consciousness itself was not included here in order to show those [stations].

"Approach and clinging" (*upaya-upādāna*): there are two types of approach, namely, the approach of craving (*taṇhūpaya*) and the approach of views (*diṭṭhūpaya*); and there are the four types of clinging, such as the clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
“Of the mind”: these are the mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies of unwholesome consciousness.

“Of the Tathāgata” means of the Perfectly Enlightened One. For although these have indeed been abandoned by all those whose taints are destroyed, it is said here with reference to the highest limit because the Teacher’s state of having destroyed the taints is most renowned in the world.
Regarding the phrase "in the consciousness-element": why is consciousness included here? It is for the purpose of showing the abandoning of the defilements (*kilesa*).
For the defilements are not abandoned only in the four aggregates; they are indeed abandoned in all five as well. Thus, it is included for the purpose of showing the abandoning of the defilements.
"In this way, householder, one is a wanderer without a home" means: in this way, by not wandering toward a home through karmic consciousness.
He is called "one who wanders homeless.
Regarding the phrase "the radiating and binding of the sign of form as a dwelling": form itself is the "sign" (*nimitta*) in the sense of being a condition for the defilements;

it is the "dwelling" (*niketa*) in the sense of being a place of residence consisting of the activity of taking an object. Thus, it is the "sign of form as a dwelling" (*rūpanimittaniketa*). "Radiating and binding" (*visāravinibandhā*) refers to both the spreading out and the fettering. By both [terms],...
For the state of pervasion and the state of bondage of the defilements have been described.

"Bondage to the diffusion in the abode of the sign of form" means bondage to the diffusion and bondage to the defilements that arise in the abode of the sign of form; thus, the meaning is: by both the diffusion of defilements and the bond of defilements arisen in the abode of the sign of form.
"One who wanders in the abode" (niketasārī) is said because it is a place of dwelling by way of making it an object.
It is called "home" (*sārī*). "Abandoned" means that those outflows of defilements which spread through and are bound to the sign of form and its abode have been abandoned.
But why, in this context, are the five aggregates called the "dwelling" (*okā*) and the six objects the "abode" (*niketa*)?

It is because of the relative strength or weakness of desire and lust (*chandarāga*). For although these [five aggregates] share the same status as objects in the sense of being a basis for attachment, the term "dwelling" refers specifically to the house where one constantly resides.
It is called a "home" (*niketa*) because it is a place where an appointment has been made, such as "Today we shall play at such-and-such a spot"—that is, a dwelling place like a garden and so forth.

Just as desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) are powerful toward a house filled with children, wife, wealth, and grain, so too are they toward the internal aggregates (*khandhas*). However, just as [desire] is weaker than that toward places such as gardens, so too is it toward external things.
Regarding the phrase "in the six objects": it should be understood that this teaching was given precisely because of the varying strength and weakness of desire and lust (*chandarāga*).

As for "being happy among those who are happy": when one's attendants are happy by way of obtaining wealth, grain, and so forth, one becomes happy with the happiness associated with the household, thinking, "Now I shall receive pleasant food," while experiencing the success achieved through them.

He conducts himself as if he were one of them. "Suffering with those who suffer" means that when suffering arises for them due to some cause, he himself becomes afflicted by a twofold suffering. "In matters of duty and service" means in those tasks designated as duties.
"He applies himself to them" means he personally undertakes the application and the necessity of performing those duties. "In sensual pleasures" means in sensual objects (*vatthu-kāma*).

"In this way, householder, one is 'empty of sensual pleasures' (kāmehi aritto): thus one is empty of the defilements of sensual pleasure (kilesakāmehi), being not void internally due to the presence of sensual pleasures.
The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood as 'empty' or 'void' because of their absence.

'Placing before oneself' (purakkharāno) means making the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) one's priority. Regarding the phrases 'one might be of such a form,' etc., [this refers to] long, short, dark, fair, and so forth."
Regarding forms, one aspires: "May I be of such a form. Regarding feelings such as pleasure, one aspires: "May I be of such a feeling.
Regarding perceptions such as the perception of blue, one aspires: "May I be of such a perception. Regarding volitional formations such as meritorious formations, one aspires:
"May I be of such a formation. Regarding consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness, one aspires: "May I be of such a consciousness."
"Apurakkharāno" means not placing the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) before oneself. "Sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ te":
your speech is unsuitable and unpolished, whereas mine is suitable, polished, and like a sweet drink. "Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ":
that which has been practiced by you for a long time and is well-mastered—all of that, upon encountering my argument, is overturned in an instant.
"Turned back, turned away. "The charge has been laid against you": the fault has been attributed to you by me.
"Go for the sake of clearing the charge": go and wander about, approaching various teachers and seeking further [evidence] for the sake of releasing yourself from this charge.
"Or unravel it, if you are able": then, if you yourself are capable, unravel it right here. This is the third.
4. Commentary on the Second Hāliddikāni Sutta.
In the fourth [sutta], regarding the "Questions of Sakka," this has already been stated in both the *Cūḷasakkapañha* and the *Mahāsakkapañha*.

"Liberated through the destruction of craving" means liberated by the liberation of the fruit which has as its object Nibbāna, the destruction of craving. "The ultimate goal" (*accantaniṭṭhā*) means the end...
"Having transcended the goal, they have reached the constant goal. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. This is the fourth [section]. 5.
Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta.
In the fifth [sutta], "Concentration": seeing those bhikkhus falling away from one-pointedness of mind, the Blessed One said, "One-pointedness of mind..."
Having understood, "For those who obtain it, this meditation subject will reach fulfillment," he said: "He delights" means he aspires.
"He welcomes" means that through that delight, he says, "Oh, how dear, desirable, lovely, and pleasing!
And even one who delights in speech, by giving rise to greed in dependence on that very object, is indeed said to welcome it.
"Abiding with attachment" means that having swallowed and digested it, one grasps it. "That delight in form" refers to that delight (nandī) which is characterized as a powerful longing for form.
"Grasping at that" means it is grasping (upādāna) in the sense of seizing. "Does not rejoice" means he does not long for it.
"Does not exult" means that by way of longing, he does not say, "It is desirable, it is lovely. [This is done] by means of the mind of insight (vipassanā-citta).
Even when making a verbal utterance with the mind that "it is impermanent, it is suffering," one does not yet truly affirm it. This is the fifth. 6.
Commentary on the Discourse on Seclusion (*Paṭisallāṇasutta-vaṇṇanā*):

Regarding the sixth discourse, "Seclusion," the Blessed One spoke this after seeing those bhikkhus falling away from physical seclusion. Having known, "If these [bhikkhus] obtain physical seclusion, their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) will reach fulfillment," he said this. This is the sixth.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on Agitation through Clinging (Upādāparitassanā-sutta) Seventh: "Agitation through clinging" (*upādāparitassanā*) means agitation arisen through grasping.

"Non-agitation through non-clinging" (*anupādāaparitassanā*) means the absence of agitation due to the absence of grasping. "The consciousness undergoes change and transformation along with the transformation of form" means: "My form has changed."
Or, in the manner beginning with "Alas, I had this, but now I have it no more," the kamma-consciousness follows upon the breakup of the form.
The "birth following upon change" arises from a consciousness that has change as its object, because it follows upon change.
"Agitation and the arising of states" refers to both the agitation of craving and the arising of unwholesome states.
"Citta" means wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta*). "They persist by taking hold" means they remain after having taken hold.
"With trepidation" means accompanied by trepidation. "With distress" means accompanied by distress and suffering. "With longing" means possessed of attachment.

"And by clinging he trembles" means that by grasping, he becomes one who is agitated. "Not following the transformation of form" refers to the kamma-consciousness of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
Since it does not exist, it is appropriate to say that there is no conformity with the differentiation of form.
This is the seventh. 8. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Agitation Due to Grasping (*Upādāparitassanā-sutta*).

In the eighth, the teaching is given by way of craving, conceit, and views. Thus, in these four discourses in succession, only the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) have been explained. This is the eighth.

9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Impermanence of the Three Times Regarding the ninth [discourse], "What then to say of the present?": there is no discussion whatsoever regarding the present; it is simply impermanent.
It is said that those monks, having observed that the past and future are impermanent, became weary concerning the present. Then, for them...

Knowing their underlying inclination—that those of the past and future as well would awaken when it is said that "the present is impermanent"—the Teacher delivered this teaching according to the disposition of the individuals. Ninth.
10–11. Commentary on the Suttas on Suffering in the Three Times, etc.

10–11. The tenth and eleventh [suttas] were spoken with precisely that same inclination toward persons (puggalajjhāsaya), having distinguished them by the terms "suffering" and "non-self. Thus end the tenth and eleventh.
The first chapter, the Nakulapituvagga.
2. The Aniccavagga.
1–10. Commentary on the *Anicca-sutta* and others. 12–21.

In the *Anicca-vagga*, the final sutta was taught in response to a question; the remaining suttas were taught according to the specific inclinations of those who were to be awakened by them. These are the first [suttas] and so forth.
The second chapter is the *Anicca-vagga*.
3. The Chapter on the Burden (Bhāravagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Burden (Bhārasuttavaṇṇanā) 22.
Regarding the first [discourse] of the Chapter on the Burden: "It should be said: 'The five aggregates of clinging,'" thus [it refers to] the five aggregates of clinging.
"Thus he should be addressed" means that it should be spoken in this way. "This, monks, is called the burden":
these five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) are what is called the burden. In what sense? In the sense of being a burden to be carried.
For their carrying—namely, having them placed, moved, seated, laid down, bathed, adorned, fed, and fed with food—is [the burden].
"Burden" is called "burden" in the sense of being heavy to carry. "Named thus" means having a name such as Tissa or Datta.
"Clan-named thus" means having a clan such as Kaṇhāyana or Vacchāyana. Thus, he shows the person—established merely by conventional usage—as the "bearer of the burden.
For the person, at the very moment of rebirth-linking, takes up the burden of the aggregates and [carries it] for ten years...
Even for two hundred years—that is, for as long as one lives—one carries this burden of the aggregates, nourishing it, feeding it, seating it on beds and chairs of soft touch, and laying it down;
yet at the moment of death, having cast it aside, one takes up another burden of the aggregates at the moment of rebirth.
Therefore, one is called the "bearer of the burden."
"Leading to renewed existence" means producing further becoming. "Accompanied by delight and lust" means having gone to a state of oneness with delight and lust;
for here, what is intended is that which is accompanied by the very presence of those [states].

"Rejoicing here and there" means having the habit of rejoicing in various places of rebirth or in various objects such as visible forms. Among craving for sensual pleasures and so forth, it refers to that consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure.

Lust is called craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*); lust for existence in the realms of form and formlessness, attachment to meditative absorption, and lust accompanied by the view of eternalism—this is called craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*);
lust accompanied by the view of annihilationism is called craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).

"Taking up the burden" means grasping the burden; for it is through craving that one takes up this burden. "The remainderless fading away and cessation," and so forth—all [this] refers to Nibbāna itself.
This is a synonym. For by relying upon it, craving is detached from without remainder, ceases, is relinquished, is renounced, and is liberated;
and herein there is neither clinging to sensual pleasures nor clinging to views—thus Nibbāna receives these names.
"Craving with its root": ignorance is called the root of craving. "Uprooted": by means of the path of Arahantship, that [craving] together with its root...
"Having pulled out. "One who is free from hunger is called one who has attained final Nibbāna (parinibbuto) because he is free from craving"—this may rightly be said. First. 2.
Commentary on the Pariññā Sutta (Sutta 23).

In the second [sutta], "that which is to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) means that which is to be thoroughly known, that which is to be transcended. "Full understanding" (*pariññā*) refers to ultimate full understanding (*accantapariññā*).

"Surmounting" is the meaning. "The destruction of lust," and so forth, is a name for Nibbāna; for that is indeed called ultimate full understanding (*accanta-pariññā*). This is the second [sutta]. 3. Commentary on the *Abhijāna-sutta* (Sutta 24).

In the third [sutta], "they directly know" means "one who directly knows. By this, full understanding as the known (*ñāta-pariññā*) is explained; by the second phrase, full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*); and by the third and fourth [phrases], full understanding as abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*). Thus, three kinds of full understanding are explained in this sutta. This is the third.
4–9. Commentary on the *Chandarāgasutta* and others (25–30).

The fourth and subsequent discourses are to be understood according to the same method explained in the *Dhātusaṃyutta*. However, in this sequence, the Four Noble Truths are discussed in the fifth, sixth, and seventh; in the eighth and ninth, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) are treated.
[End of] the fourth and subsequent discourses. 10. Commentary on the *Aghamūlasutta*.
31. In the tenth [verse], "aghanti" means suffering. Thus, here only the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*) has been explained.
This is the tenth. 11. Commentary on the *Pabhaṅgu-sutta*: 32.
In the eleventh [verse], "pabhaṅgu" means having the nature of breaking up. Thus, here only the characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇa*) has been explained. This is the eleventh.
The Third Chapter on Burdens.
4. The Chapter on What Does Not Belong to You. 1. Commentary on the Discourse on What Does Not Belong to You.
33. In the first section of the *Natumhāka-vagga*, regarding the phrase "abandon": abandon by means of abandoning desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*). Regarding "grass and so forth":

"grass" refers to things such as the palmyra palm and the coconut, which have pith within and bark without. "Wood" refers to things such as the acacia, the *sāla* tree, the *sāka* tree, and the breadfruit tree, which have bark within and pith without.
"Branches" refers to what has emerged from the tree like its arms. "Foliage" refers to the leaves of the palmyra palm, the coconut, and so forth. This is the first [section].
2. Commentary on the Second *Tumhāka-sutta* 34.
The second [sutta] was spoken with the intention of those who attain awakening without a simile. This is the second.
3. Commentary on the *Aññatara-bhikkhu-sutta*
35. "If, venerable sir, form underlies [the mind] (*anuseti*)," that is, if form underlies it;

"by that one comes to be designated" means that by whichever underlying tendency (*anusaya*) one underlies that form—among those such as sensual lust and so forth—one comes to receive the designation "lustful," "hated," or "deluded" by that very underlying tendency.
"One does not come to be designated by that" means that one does not [truly] come to be designated as "lustful," "hated," or... by that unreal underlying tendency.
"He does not go by the designation 'deluded. This is the third [sutta].
4. Commentary on the Second Sutta to a Certain Bhikkhu. 36.
In the fourth [sutta], "it is inferred from that" means that the material form (rūpa) which has been latent (anusayita) follows along with the dying latent tendency (anusaya).
For when the object is destroyed, those states that have that as their object do not persist.

"That which is inferred" means that form which one infers by means of a latent tendency (*anusaya*). "By that it is reckoned" means that by means of that latent tendency, one is reckoned as "lustful," "hateful," or "deluded.
Alternatively, *yaṃ* is an instrumental expression: by whichever latent tendency one is inferred, by that [one is so reckoned].
The meaning is that he comes to be reckoned as "lustful, hateful, and deluded.
This is the fourth [sutta]. 5–6. Commentary on the *Ānandasutta*, etc. (37–38). In the fifth [sutta], it is said:

"Change is perceived in what is stable" (*ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyati*). This means that aging is perceived in one who is enduring, one who is living. For "stability" (*ṭhiti*) is a name for the preservation known as the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), while "change" (*aññathatta*) refers to aging. Thus the ancients have said:
“Arising is declared to be birth, dissolution is called passing away, change is called aging, and stability is maintenance.

Thus, each aggregate has three characteristics consisting of arising, aging, and dissolution; it is with reference to these that it was said: “Bhikkhus, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.”

In this context, "the conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) refers to any formation (*saṅkhāra*) produced by conditions. Now, a formation is not the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), nor is the characteristic the formation;
yet it is impossible to define the characteristic without the formation, nor the formation without the characteristic.
However, through the characteristic, the formation becomes manifest. For just as the characteristic is not the cow itself, [so too with the formations and their characteristics].
The characteristic itself is not the cow, nor is it possible to define the characteristic apart from the cow, nor the cow apart from the characteristic;
rather, it is by means of the characteristic that the cow becomes manifest. This should be understood as being exactly like this.
In that context, at the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) of formations (*saṅkhārā*), both the formation and the characteristic of arising—known as time—and even its moment (*khaṇa*) [are present].
It is discerned. When it is said, "there is also arising," the formation, the characteristic of aging, the time reckoned as such, and its moment are all discerned.
At the moment of dissolution, the formation, that characteristic, the time reckoned as such, and its moment are also discerned.
However, others say: "The moment of aging for immaterial phenomena cannot be pointed out; [only] the Perfectly Enlightened One..."
And by saying, "In feeling, arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and change while standing is discerned," he demonstrates the three characteristics even for formless phenomena;
these are obtained with reference to the moment of existence. Having said this, he continued:
"The existence of all phenomena is what is called 'standing' (ṭhiti)."
"The breaking up of that very [existence] is death for all living beings at all times"—with this verse of the Teacher, they establish that meaning.
Alternatively, they say it should be understood as "abiding" (*ṭhiti*) in the sense of a continuous stream (*santati*).
However, since this distinction does not exist in the Sutta, one should not override the Sutta on account of the Teacher’s own opinion.
The Sutta itself must be taken as the authority. The sixth [sutta] is self-evident. [This concludes] the fifth and sixth.
7–10. Commentary on the *Anudhammasutta*, etc., 39–42.
Regarding the seventh, "one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammappaṭipanna*) means one who practices in conformity with the nine supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*).
"For one who has entered upon the preliminary practice": "this is the conformable dhamma" means this is the dhamma that accords with [the goal].
"Abounding in disenchantment": having become full of world-weariness. "Comprehends": he comprehends by means of the three kinds of full comprehension (*pariññā*). "Is liberated":

at the moment of the path, he is liberated by means of the full comprehension of abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*) which has arisen. Thus, in this sutta, it is the path itself that is explained; likewise...

In the three [sections] following this, however, the contemplation (*anupassanā*) is not specified here, whereas it is specified in those [three]. Therefore, even here, it must be specified by way of what was specified there;
for it is not possible to become disenchanted with or to fully understand [the aggregates] without one of the three types of contemplation.
The seventh section and so forth.
The Fourth Chapter: Natumhāka.
5. The Chapter on Being an Island unto Oneself. 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Being an Island Unto Oneself.

43. In the first section of the *Attadīpavagga*, "with oneself as an island" (*attadīpā*) means: "Dwell having made yourself the island, the refuge, the shelter, the destination, the final resort, and the foundation.
"With oneself as a refuge" (*attasaraṇā*) is a synonym for that very same thing. "With no other as a refuge" (*anaññasaraṇā*) is a statement negating another as a refuge;
for indeed, one person cannot be the refuge for another, nor can it be achieved through the effort of another.
Because it cannot be found in anything else; for this has also been said:
"The self is indeed its own protector;
for who else could be the protector?"
Therefore he said, “having no other refuge. But what here is meant by “self”? It is the mundane and supramundane Dhamma.
For this very reason he said, “having the Dhamma as their island, having the Dhamma as their refuge, having no other refuge.
*Yoni* means cause—as in such passages as, “For this, Bhūmija, is the source for the attainment of the fruit. *Kiṃpahotikā* means *kiṃpabhutikā*; the meaning is, from what do they originate?
"But as for form itself"—this was undertaken for the purpose of showing the abandonment of those very things, such as sorrow and so forth.

"He does not tremble" means he does not grasp or seize. "Extinguished in that factor" means extinguished in that factor because of the extinguishing of the defilements by that factor of insight (*vipassanā*).
In this sutta, only insight is discussed. First.
2. Commentary on the *Paṭipadāsutta* 44.

Regarding the second [sutta], "regarding the way leading to the origin of suffering": since personality (*sakkāya*) is suffering, the "way leading to its origin" refers to the viewing by means of wrong view, stated thus: "one regards form as self. Therefore...
“Contemplation leading to the origin of suffering”—this is the meaning here.
Regarding “contemplation leading to the cessation of suffering,” the knowledge of the four paths together with insight is what is called “contemplation.
Thus, in this sutta, the cycle of existence and its unraveling are explained. Second.
3. Commentary on the *Anicca-sutta* 45.
In the third [sutta], "to be seen with right wisdom" (*sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ*) means it is to be seen by means of the path-wisdom together with insight (*vipassanā*).

"It becomes dispassionate and is liberated" (*virajjati vimuccati*) means it becomes dispassionate at the moment of the path and is liberated at the moment of the fruit (*phala*). "Without clinging, through the taints" (*anupādāya āsavehi*) refers to cessation through non-arising.

With the taints ceased, not grasping [anything further], one is thus liberated. The passage beginning with "in the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu*) is stated for the purpose of demonstrating review-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇa*).
Some also say it is for the purpose of demonstrating review-knowledge together with its fruit. It is "established" (*ṭhita*) because there is no further duty to be performed.
Because it is established, it is "satisfied" (*santuṭṭha*), being content by virtue of having attained what was to be attained. "One attains final Nibbāna right here" (*paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyati*).
He attains final Nibbāna by himself. This is the third [sutta].
4. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Impermanence: 46.
Regarding the fourth [sutta], "speculations about the past" refers to the eighteen views that follow after the past.

"Views concerning the future" (*aparantānudiṭṭhiyo*) refers to the forty-four views that follow after the future; they do not exist [here]. "Gripping and misapprehension" (*thāmaso parāmāso*) refers to both the gripping of views (*diṭṭhithāmaso*) and the misapprehension of views (*diṭṭhiparāmāso*);
these do not exist [here]. Up to this point, the first path has been shown.

Now, in order to show the three paths and the fruits together with insight (*vipassanā*), the passage beginning with "In form" (*rūpasmiṃ*) is commenced. Alternatively, [it may be understood as follows:]
Views are indeed abandoned by insight alone; however, this [section] is undertaken to show the four paths together with insight that follow above. Fourth.
5. Commentary on the Sutta on Contemplation.
47. In the fifth [view], they regard the five aggregates of clinging, or one or another of them. By way of grasping them in their entirety, they regard the five aggregates;
by way of grasping them incompletely, they regard one or another of them.
Thus, this "regarding" (samanupassanā) is the regarding through views (*diṭṭhi-samanupassanā*). And for such a person, the thought "I am" has not yet disappeared. Regarding whom...
This "viewing" exists; in that state, the threefold proliferation (papañca)—consisting of craving, conceit, and views—expressed as "I am this," has not yet departed.
"There is the descent of the five faculties": when those defilements exist, there occurs the arising of the five faculties conditioned by karma and defilements.
“There is, monks, the mind”: this is said with reference to the kamma-mind. “Mental objects” refers to the object.
“The element of ignorance” refers to ignorance at the moment of impulsion (*javana*). “Born of contact with ignorance” means born from contact associated with ignorance.

Furthermore, “mind” refers to the resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*) at the moment of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) at the moment of adverting (*āvajjana*). “Mental objects,” etc. [refers to the remaining factors].
They are of the same kind as those already described. "The thought 'I am' occurs to him" means that, by way of craving, conceit, and views, the thought "I am" occurs to him in this manner.
In the following sections, the phrase "this I am" is stated by way of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*), having grasped some phenomenon among form and so forth, thinking "this I am.
"I shall be" is by way of the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). "I shall not be" is by way of the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). "Possessing form" (*rūpī*)...
"All [terms] beginning with 'will be' belong exclusively to eternalism. Now, "herein" means: while these faculties remain in that very same state.
"Ignorance is abandoned" means: ignorance, which consists of non-knowledge regarding the Four Truths, is abandoned.
"Knowledge arises" means: the knowledge of the path of Arhatship arises. Thus, herein, "I am" refers to craving, conceit, and views. Of karma...

Between the five faculties there is one junction; and by treating the resultant mind as belonging to the side of the five faculties, between the five faculties and the kamma there is another junction. Thus, there are three elaborations (*papañca*):
the past time, the present time consisting of the faculties and so forth, and therein the condition for the future is shown beginning with the kamma-mind. This is the fifth [section].
6. Commentary on the Khandha Sutta 48.
In the sixth [sutta], the aggregate of form belongs to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while the four [mental] aggregates belong to the four planes of existence.

"With taints" (*sāsava*) means being a condition by way of being an object for the taints (*āsava*). "Subject to clinging" (*upādāniya*) likewise means being a condition for the types of clinging (*upādāna*).
The meaning of the terms here is as follows: it is "with taints" (*sāsava*) because it proceeds together with the taints by making them its object.

It is "subject to clinging" (*upādāniya*) because it is to be clung to. Here too, the aggregate of form belongs to the sense sphere, while the remaining aggregates belong to the three planes and are mentioned by way of the practice of insight.
Thus, in this context, form is included among the aggregates in the sense of being a "heap," and among the aggregates subject to clinging in the sense of being a heap associated with taints.

Feeling and the other aggregates are both with taints (*sāsava*) and without taints (*anāsava*). All of them, in the sense of being a collection (*rāsa*), are included within the aggregates (*khandha*);
however, those belonging to the three planes, in the sense of being with taints, are included within the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*). This is the sixth [section].
7–8. Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta and others.
49–50. "I am better" means "I am distinguished, I am superior.
"What else could it be but the non-perception of things as they really are?"—what else could there be apart from the non-perception of things as they really are?

The meaning is that such non-perception would be nothing other than ignorance. Now, beginning the teaching on the "splitting of the diamond" by way of a reversal of this [view], he said: "What do you think, Soṇa? and so forth.
The eighth [sutta] is likewise self-evident. [This concludes] the seventh and eighth. 9–10.
Commentary on the *Nandikkhayasutta* and others. 51–52. Regarding the ninth and tenth:
"From the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust; from the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight"—this is what is meant by "delight" (*nandī*).

Or rather, it is stated that there is no difference in meaning between "disenchantment" (*nibbidā*) and "fading away" (*virāga*). By contemplating disenchantment, one who becomes disenchanted abandons delight (*nandi*); by contemplating fading away, one who becomes dispassionate abandons lust (*rāga*).

Having thus brought insight (*vipassanā*) to its conclusion, the path is shown here with the words, "With the destruction of lust comes the destruction of delight," and then: "With the destruction of delight and lust, the mind..."
"‘Liberated’—this shows the fruit. Thus end the ninth and tenth [suttas].
The fifth chapter, the Attadīpa-vagga, is finished.
The Mūlapaññāsaka is complete.
6. Upaya-vagga 1.
Commentary on the Upaya-sutta 53.
In the first [sutta] of the Upaya-vagga, "upaya" means one who has approached the five aggregates by way of craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi). "Viññāṇa" means...
Kamma-consciousness (*kammaviññāṇa*). "It would reach" means that, having impelled the kamma, it would reach growth and so forth by virtue of its capacity to draw on rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
The reason for not including the phrase "the resort of consciousness" has already been stated.

"The object is cut off" means that the object is cut off due to the absence of the capacity to draw on rebirth-linking. "A foothold for consciousness": [this refers to the state where consciousness is established].
There is no foundation for kamma-consciousness. "Not established therein" means it is not established.
"Liberated through non-conditioning" means liberated without having conditioned rebirth-linking. First.
2. Commentary on the Seed Sutta.
54. In the second [section], "seed-born" (*bījajāni*) means seeds. Root-seeds (*mūlabīja*) are such as *vaca*, *vacatta*, turmeric (*halidda*), ginger (*siṅgivera*), and so forth.
Stem-seeds (*khandhabīja*) are such as the *assattha* (pipal) tree, the *nigrodha* (banyan) tree, and so forth. Node-seeds (*phalubīja*) are such as sugarcane, bamboo, reed, and so forth.
Crown-seeds (*agga-bīja*) are such as the *ajjuka* and the *phaṇijjaka* plant, and so forth. Seed-seeds (*bījabīja*) are the early grains, such as *sāli* rice, *vīhi* rice, and so forth.
And other vegetables such as green gram and black gram. "Unbroken" means undivided. From the moment they are broken, a seed no longer serves the purpose of a seed.
"Unrotted" means not rotted by soaking in water; for a rotten seed does not serve the purpose of a seed.
"Not damaged by wind or sun" means not harmed by wind or sun, and thus not rendered sapless. For that which is sapless...
Chaff seed is not suitable for the purpose of seed. "Those that take up the essence" means those that have taken up the essence and established the essence;
for seed that lacks essence is not suitable for the purpose of seed. "Well-slain" means they have lain comfortably according to the rule of being placed in a granary for four months.
"Earth" refers to the earth below as the supporting base. "Water" refers to the moisture above. Four...
The "stations of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*) are the four aggregates—form and so forth—which serve as the objects of kamma-consciousness.
For they are like the earth element in that they provide a foundation by way of being objects. Delight-and-lust (*nandirāga*) is like the water element in the sense of its function of cohesion.

"Consciousness with its nutriment" (*sāhāraṃ viññāṇaṃ*) refers to kamma-consciousness together with its conditions; for, like a seed, it grows upon the "earth" of the object within the earth of the object. Second.
3. Udānasutta Commentary 55.
Regarding the third [sutta], "he uttered an udāna": he spoke an utterance (udāna) arising from intense joy.
On what basis did this arise for the Blessed One? It was on the basis of the fact that the Teaching leads to liberation (niyyānika). How so? It is said that this thought occurred to him:

“There are these three proximate causes: the proximate cause of giving, the proximate cause of virtue, and the proximate cause of development. Among these, the proximate causes of giving and virtue are weak, while the proximate cause of development is powerful.
For the proximate causes of giving and virtue lead one to the three paths and their fruits, whereas the proximate cause of development leads to Arahantship.
Thus, a bhikkhu established in a weak proximate cause, even while striving...
Striving, he severs the five lower fetters and realizes the three paths and fruits;
as he reflects, "Oh, how the Dispensation leads to liberation," this [insight] arose in him.
Therein, for the purpose of elucidating this meaning—that "standing upon a weak supporting condition, one who strives reaches the three paths and fruits"—[the following was said].

The story of the Elder Milaka should be understood: it is said that while he was a householder, making his living by the act of taking life, he set up a hundred snares and a hundred threshing-mills in the forest.
Then one day, having eaten meat roasted over coals and wandering among the places where the snares were set, overcome by thirst, he went to the monastery of a forest-dwelling elder. To that elder—
While walking back and forth, he opened a water jar standing nearby, but did not see even as much water as would fit in the hollow of his hand.
Becoming angry, he said: "Bhikkhu, bhikkhu! Having eaten and eaten what was given by householders, you sleep;
you do not leave even as much water as a handful in the water jar. This is not proper. The Elder [said]: "By me..."
"A water jar has been set out filled; what indeed is this?
Having gone there and looked, he saw that the jar was full and gave him a conch shell filled with water. After drinking from the conch shell until it was two-thirds full, he thought:
"Because of my own karma, even a jar filled to such an extent has become like a mere fragment of a bowl. What indeed will become of me in future existences?"

With a heart moved by spiritual urgency, he cast away his bow and said, “Venerable sir, grant me the going-forth. The Elder instructed him in the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *taca-pañcaka*) and ordained him.
As he was practicing the duty of a recluse, [he saw] the places where many deer and pigs had been killed, as well as snares and traps.
The place where it was applied appears [to him]. As he recollects that, a burning sensation arises in his body; like a wild bull, even the meditation subject does not enter its proper course.

Thinking, "What shall I do with this state of a monk?", and oppressed by dissatisfaction, he went to the Elder, paid homage, and said: "Venerable sir, I am unable to perform the duty of a recluse. Then—

The Elder said, "Perform manual labor. He replied, "Very well, venerable sir," and having cut down fresh trees such as *udumbara* and others, he made a great heap and asked, "What shall I do now? "Burn it," [the Elder] said.
Unable to burn it even after setting fire to it from the four directions, he said, "Venerable sir, I am not able. The Elder said, "In that case—"
"Get away! he said, and splitting the earth asunder, he drew forth from the Avīci hell a fire the size of a glowworm and cast him therein.
That [fire] instantly consumed that massive heap as if it were dry leaves.
Then the Elder, having shown him Avīci, stirred his sense of spiritual urgency by saying, "If you renounce the training, you will be roasted here. From the sight of Avīci, he...
From that time on, being greatly agitated, he asked, "Venerable sir, is the Buddha’s teaching leading to liberation? "Yes, friend," [the Venerable replied].
"Venerable sir, since the Buddha’s teaching is indeed leading to liberation, Milaka will achieve his own deliverance; do not worry.
From then on, he practiced the duties of a recluse with diligence, fulfilled his formal observances and reciprocal services, and [abandoned] sleep.
While tormenting him, he would place a bundle of straw on the novice’s head, step into the mud with his feet, and sit down.
One day, after straining drinking water and placing the jar on his thigh, he stood waiting for the water-jars to be refilled.
Then the Elder gave this recitation to the novice:
“For one who is industrious,
mindful, pure in action, acting with circumspection,
self-restrained, and living according to the Dhamma— ”
“The glory of the diligent increases.
He applied even this four-line stanza to himself alone: “One such as I must be diligent;
one such as I must also be mindful... and one such as I must also be heedful. Thus he applied that stanza.
Having brought [this realization] into himself and remaining right there at that very stage of the path, he severed the five lower fetters,
established himself in the fruit of non-returning,
and being joyful and elated, said: “Taking a bundle of green straw upon my head, I walked about;”
“I am one who has attained the third stage; of this I have no doubt.

Thus he spoke this verse of inspired utterance (*udāna*). Standing thus upon a weak supporting condition (*upanissaya*), striving and exerting himself, he severs the five lower fetters (*saṃyojana*) and realizes the three paths and fruits. Therefore the Blessed One said: “He would not exist...”
“‘May it not be mine; may it not come to be; may it not be for me’—resolving thus, a bhikkhu would cut off the lower fetters.
In this context, “may it not be mine, may it not come to be” means: “If I were not to exist, my requisites also would not exist.”
Or else, if there had been no past formation of kamma for me, this present pentad of aggregates would not exist.

Thinking, "It has not existed, and it shall not exist for me," I shall now exert myself in such a way that there will be no future formation of kamma productive of aggregates for me; when that is absent, there will be no future rebirth-linking.

“...so shall my name no longer be. “Resolving thus” means that a bhikkhu resolving in this way, while standing upon a weak supporting condition (*upanissaya*), may cut off the five lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*).
“When this was said” means when this *udāna* was spoken by the Blessed One, who was reflecting upon the liberating nature of the Teaching (*sāsana*). “Form will perish” means form will break up.

"By the dissolution of form" means by insight (vipassanā) together with the vision of dissolution. For the four paths, accompanied by insight, are indeed called "the vision of the dissolution of form and so forth.
It is with reference to this that it was said: "Venerable sir, a bhikkhu who resolves thus would cut off;
venerable sir, a bhikkhu who resolves thus would surely cut off the five lower fetters."
The fetters. Why will he not cut them?
Now, asking about the path and fruit that follow, he said, "But how, venerable sir," and so forth.

In that context, there are two kinds of immediate succession (*anantara*): the immediate succession of proximity and the immediate succession of distance. Insight (*vipassanā*) is the immediate succession of proximity to the path.
This refers to what is called "the distant interval from the fruit. With reference to this, he asks:
"But, venerable sir, for one who knows how and sees how does the fruit of arahantship—which is reckoned as 'the destruction of the taints'—occur immediately after insight?
"In a place where there is no trembling" means in a state where there is nothing to tremble at, nothing to fear. "He falls into those [fears]" means he encounters fear.
"Tāso" means fear. That weak insight which occurs in the form, "May I not be, and may nothing be mine," is called "fear" for the uninstructed worldling because it is unable to exhaust self-affection.
For he [thinks], "Now I shall be annihilated; now I shall be nothing at all," as if seeing himself falling down a precipice.
...as another brahmin saw [it]. It is said that beneath the Lohapāsāda, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga was reciting the Dhamma struck by the three characteristics.
Then, as a certain brahmin stood to one side listening to the Dhamma, the conditioned phenomena appeared to him as empty. He felt as if he were falling down a precipice, and through the open door—
Then, having fled and entered her home, she laid her son upon her breast and said, "Dear child, as I was reflecting on the Sakyaputta’s teaching, I have lost my mind.
For this bhikkhu is not afraid; such a powerful insight that has thus arisen does not constitute what is called "fear" for a learned noble disciple.
Indeed, it does not occur to him, "I shall be annihilated," nor does he think, "I shall perish."
“Or [one thinks], ‘I shall perish. But thus it is: ‘Only formations arise; only formations cease. This is the third [turning]. 4.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Turning of the Fourfold Cycle (Upādānaparivattasutta). 56.
In the fourth [turning], “fourfold cycle” refers to the manner of turning four times with respect to each aggregate. Form...
"I directly knew" means: "I directly knew that form is the truth of suffering. In this way, the meaning in all instances is to be understood by way of the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding "from the arising of nutriment": here, "nutriment" refers to physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) characterized by desire and lust.
"Practicing" means they are practicing from the stage of virtue up to the path of Arahatship. "Firmly established" means they are grounded. Up to this point...
Having spoken of the stage of the trainee (*sekkhabhūmi*), he now spoke the passage beginning with "But those, monks... while explaining the stage of the non-trainee (*asekkhabhūmi*).
"Well-liberated" means they are thoroughly liberated by the liberation of the fruit of Arhatship. "Perfect ones" (*kevalino*) means they are complete, having performed all that was to be done.
"There is no round for them to be designated" means that there is no remaining round of existence by which they could be designated.
There is no cycle to be pointed out. Alternatively, "cycle" refers to a cause; thus, there is no cause for pointing it out.
Up to this point, the section on the plane of the Asekhas has been explained. Fourth. 5.
Commentary on the Sutta of the Seven Bases.

57. In the fifth [verse], "skilled in the seven bases" (*sattaṭṭhānakusala*) means one who is proficient in the seven positions. "One who has lived" (*vusitavā*) means one whose dwelling has been completed.
"The supreme person" (*uttamapurisa*) means the most excellent person. The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated.

Furthermore, this sutta should be understood as both "exceedingly delightful" (*ussadanandiya*) and "enticing" (*palobhanīya*). For just as a king, having won a battle, [places] the warriors who were victorious in battle in high positions...
He pays them honor, setting them aside [from others]. For what reason?

Thinking, "Upon seeing this honor shown to them, the rest will also think themselves to be heroes," even so the Blessed One—having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for an immeasurable time, having achieved victory over the Māra of the defilements at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa), and having attained omniscience—sat in the great monastery of Jetavana in Sāvatthī and, while teaching this discourse, [acted thus].

Having exalted and praised those whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava), for what reason? [It was] so that the remaining persons in training (sekkha-puggala) might think, "The fruit of Arhatship is to be attained.
Thus, this sutta should be understood as "delightful through excellence" because it exalts and praises those whose taints are destroyed, and as "enticing" because it entices those in training.

"Thus, monks, a monk is skilled in the seven bases. Having thus concluded the teaching here by way of reviewing the path and the fruit, [the Buddha] further said: "And how, monks, is a monk a threefold investigator?
This refers to the fact that the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) dwells with constant abiding upon whatever object—whether a being or a person.
"It does not exist; rather, there is only the mere presence of the elements (dhātu), etc.

This was said to show both the constant abiding of one whose taints are exhausted, and the path by which he has come—namely, that "having performed the work within these phenomena, he has arrived here.
In this context, "he examines by way of the elements" means he sees and observes them according to their elemental nature. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. Fifth.
6. Commentary on the *Sammāsambuddhasutta* 58.

In the sixth [verse], what is the "additional application" (*adhippayāsa*)? It means what is the superior effort. Regarding the phrase "of the unarisen": for it was Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One who brought forth this Path;
no other Teacher in the interval was able to bring it forth. Thus, the Blessed One [spoke] regarding the unarisen Path.

One who causes [the path] to arise is called an "uppādetā. In the *Nagaropama-sutta*, where there was no road at places that were not yet cleared, it is called an "unarisen path" (*anuppannamagga*) in the sense of not having occurred;
"asañjāta" is a synonym for that same thing. "Anakkhāta" means "not spoken of. One who knows the path is "maggaññū";
one who has made the path known, understood, and manifest is "maggavidū. [He knows] both the path and what is not the path.
And "skilled" means skilled in the path. "Following the path" means following after the path.
"Attained afterwards" means: "I went first; the disciples attained it afterwards.
This is the sixth [sutta]. 7. Commentary on the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta*.
59. "To the group-of-five" means to the five persons, beginning with the Elder Koṇḍañña, who were his former attendants.

"Addressed them": starting from the day of the full moon of Āsāḷha, when they had gradually established themselves in the fruit of stream-entry following the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, [the Buddha] thought, "Now I shall teach the Dhamma for the destruction of their taints," and on the fifth day of the fortnight, he addressed them. "He said this."
