He spoke this *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta*, which proceeds in the manner beginning with, "Bhikkhus, this form is non-self," and so forth.
In that context, "non-self" means it is non-self for the four reasons previously stated. Why was the phrase, "What do you think, bhikkhus?
introduced? It is because up to this point only the characteristic of non-self has been explained, not the characteristics of impermanence and suffering.
It should be understood that this [treatise] has now been commenced in order to show, by way of illustration and synthesis, all three characteristics.
"Therefore" means: because these five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

The detailed explanation regarding "whatever form," and so forth, has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the development of wisdom, within the exposition of the aggregates. The remainder is the same everywhere.
This should be understood according to what has already been stated. However, in this sutta, only the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) is discussed. This concludes the seventh [sutta].
8. Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta:
In the eighth [sutta], such phrases as "exclusively suffering" and so forth follow the same method as explained in the Dhātusaṃyutta. This concludes the eighth [sutta].
9. Commentary on the Āditta Sutta (The Burning) 61.

In the ninth [sutta], "āditta" means burning and blazing with eleven fires. Thus, in both of these suttas, only the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) has been explained. The ninth is finished. 10.
Commentary on the Niruttipatha Sutta (The Path of Etymology)

62. *Niruttiyo* (linguistic expressions) are themselves *niruttipathā* (paths of linguistic expression). Alternatively, they are *niruttipathā* because they are both linguistic expressions (*niruttiyo*) and paths (*pathā*) for the meanings that are to be understood by means of those linguistic expressions.
The same method applies to the other two terms as well. It should be understood that all three of these are merely synonyms for one another.
*Asaṃkiṇṇā* (unmixed) means not abandoned; [one should not say], "What is the purpose of these? and so on.
"Abandoned": "Never previously discarded" means that even in the past they were never cast off.
"Are not being discarded" means that even now they are not abandoned with the thought, "What is the use of these? "Will not be discarded" means that even in the future they will not be cast off.
"Unreviled" means unopposed. "Past" means having transcended its own intrinsic nature or its very destruction. "Ceased" means without having moved to another location.
"Ceased right there" means stilled. "Altered" means having undergone change;
it is lost. "Unborn" means not yet arisen. "Unmanifested" means not become evident.
"Ukkalā" refers to the inhabitants of the Ukkala country. "Vassa and Bhañña": both of them were indeed proponents of root-heretical views.
Regarding the terms "proponents of causelessness" (*ahetukavāda*) and so forth: they are called "proponents of causelessness" because they hold that "there is no cause, there is no condition.

They are called "proponents of non-action" (*akiriyavāda*) because they hold that "evil is not done by one who acts. They are called "proponents of nihilism" (*natthikavāda*) because they hold such views as "there is nothing given," and so on.
In that context, these two persons possess three views; does each person have one and a half [views]? It is not so, as follows:
However, just as one bhikkhu produces all four jhānas in succession, it should be understood that in this case each [of the three types of persons] produces all three views.

For one who repeatedly adverts to, brings to mind, delights in, and relishes the thought, "There is no cause, there is no condition," it is as if he were seeing the path; thus he enters the fixed course of wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*).

...he enters; he is called "one who is entirely black. Just as in the case of the view of no-cause (*ahetuka-diṭṭhi*), so too in these instances—"no evil is done by one who acts," "there is no giving"—one enters the fixed course of falsehood (*micchattaniyāma*).
Regarding the phrase "they did not think it should be censured or rejected": here, "that which is called the past..."
When one says, "This is its past, or its future, or its present," one is called a reviler.
When one points out a fault therein and says, "What is the use of this which is reviled? one is called a rejecter.
Yet these proponents of views, who are utterly black, did not consider even these linguistic conventions as something to be reviled or rejected. [The past...]
However, they spoke of the past as only the past, the future as only the future, and the present as only the present.
"Fear of censure, reproach, malice, and attack" means: fear of censure from the presence of the wise, fear of reproach, fear of the attribution of fault, and fear of attack.
Thus, in this sutta, the designation of the aggregates belonging to the four planes is explained. The tenth [chapter].

63. In the first sutta of the *Arahantavagga*, "one who grasps" (*upādiyamāno*) means one who takes up [the aggregates] by way of craving, conceit, and views. "Bound by Māra" means bound by Māra’s snare. "Released from the Evil One" means released from the Evil One’s snare.

66–68. In the fourth [discourse], "desire" (*chanda*) means the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*). The same method applies to the fifth and sixth as well. These are the fourth and following. 7.

In the seventh, "what belongs to no self" (*anattaniya*) means that which does not belong to oneself; the meaning is that it is empty by way of being one's own requisite. This is the seventh.

In the eighth, "in the form of the seductive" (*rajanīyasaṇṭhita*) means established in the manner of something seductive; the meaning is that it stands as a condition for lust. 4. Commentary on the Arahantasutta 76.
Regarding the fourth [sutta]: "To whatever extent, monks, there are abodes of beings"—that is, monks, as many as there are so-called abodes of beings;

"to whatever extent, monks, there is the peak of existence"—that is, as much as there is that which is called the peak of existence. "These are the foremost, these are the best" means these have become supreme.

And they are indeed the most excellent. That is to say, "the Arahants," referring to those who are called Arahants. This sutta, too, should be understood as being both "exceedingly delightful" and "alluring" in the same manner as the previous one.
Then he spoke further with these verses, which elucidate that very meaning and elucidate its specific significance.

He spoke these words beginning with, "Happy indeed are the Arahants. In this context, "happy" means they are blissful through the happiness of jhāna, the happiness of the path, and the happiness of the fruit.
"Craving does not exist for them" means that craving which produces the suffering of the lower realms does not exist for them.
Thus, by the absence of even this craving-rooted [suffering], they are indeed happy. "The conceit 'I am' is utterly cut off."

The ninefold conceit (*asmimāna*) has been utterly eradicated by the path of Arhatship. "The net of delusion is rent asunder" means the web of ignorance (*avijjājāla*) has been torn apart by knowledge.

"Unshaken" refers to Arhatship, which is the abandonment of craving (*taṇhā*), here termed *ejā*. "Unsmeared" means untainted by the stains of craving and views. "Become sublime" means having become supreme.
"By thorough understanding" means having fully understood through the three types of thorough understanding (*pariññā*). "Having the seven true Dhammas as their domain."
Faith, moral shame, moral dread, erudition, exertion of energy, established mindfulness, and wisdom—these seven true qualities (saddhamma) are their range;
thus they are "those whose range consists of the seven true qualities.
"Endowed with the seven treasures" means being possessed of the seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). "They roam about" refers even to the people of the world.
They indeed continue to investigate. Here, however, the term "wandering without fear" (*nirāsaṅkacāra*) refers to those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
For this very reason, it is said: "those who have abandoned fear and terror. In that context, "fear" (*bhaya*) is simply fear, while "terror" (*bherava*) is intense fear.

"Endowed with ten factors" means possessed of the ten factors of one beyond training (*asekha*). "Great elephants" (*mahānāga*) are so called for four reasons. "Concentrated" (*samāhita*) means by way of access and absorption concentration (*upacārappanā*).
"Being concentrated, craving does not exist for them. Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "The world is deficient, unsatisfied, and a slave to craving.
Great King, even that craving which acts as a servant does not exist for them. By this, he shows the state of being a master for those whose taints are exhausted.
"Asekha-knowledge" is the knowledge of the fruit of Arhatship. "This is the final body" means this last physical existence.
"The essence of the holy life (*brahmacariya*)," he says, for "essence" means the fruit. "Not dependent on others regarding that" means that regarding that noble fruit, they do not rely on another;
having penetrated it through direct experience, they stand firm. "They do not waver amidst the various divisions" means they do not waver among the three types of conceit.
"The stage of the tamed" refers to *arahantship*. "The victors" refers to those who stand having conquered passion and the other defilements.
In the passage beginning with "Uddhaṃ," "above" refers to the top of the head; "below" refers to the soles of the feet; and "across" refers to the middle.
Alternatively, "above" refers to the past; "below" to the future; and "across" to the present. Or again, "above" refers to the world of the devas;
"below" to the world of the states of misery (apāya); and "across" to the world of human beings. "In these places delight is not found"—this is the summary of those points.
Or else, they have no craving for the aggregates of the past, future, or present. Herein, the absence of craving rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is shown.
They are called "Buddhas" because they have awakened to the Four Truths.
Furthermore, this is the lion’s roar made here: “We are happy with the happiness of liberation; craving, which produces suffering, does not exist for us.”
"The five aggregates have been abandoned, they have been fully understood; craving for being-a-servant and craving rooted in the round have been abandoned;

they are peerless in the unsurpassed state; because of their awakening to the Four Truths, they are Buddhas"—thus do those whose taints are destroyed, standing upon the back of existence, roar the lion's roar known as the "fearless cry. This is the fourth [discourse].
5. Commentary on the Second Arahat Sutta (Dutiya-arahanta-sutta). 77.
This fifth sutta was spoken with the intention of those who can understand when it is explained purely by itself, without verses. The fifth is finished. 6.
Commentary on the Siha Sutta.
78. Sixth: "Lion" refers to four kinds of lions—the grass lion, the black lion, the pale lion, and the maned lion.
Among these, the grass lion resembles a pigeon-colored goat and feeds on grass. The black lion resembles a black goat and likewise feeds on grass.
The pale lion resembles a goat the color of a withered leaf and feeds on flesh. The maned lion is as if prepared with lac-dye...
He was endowed with a face, a prominent nose, and four well-defined limbs.
From the top of his head down, three lines ran along the middle of his back as if drawn with a lacquer brush, curving to the right at the base of his spine;
and upon his shoulders rested a mane of hair like a woolen rug worth a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
The remainder of the area is pure, having the color of rice flour, powdered conch, and cotton.
Among these four types of lions, it is this maned lion that is intended here.
"King of beasts" means the king of the herd of beasts. "From his lair" means from his dwelling place, such as a golden cave, or a cave made of silver, jewels, crystal, or emerald.
Or it is said that he goes out. Furthermore, when going out, he does so for four reasons: either oppressed by darkness, for the sake of light;
or oppressed by the need to void excrement and urine, for the sake of their discharge; or oppressed by hunger, for the sake of food;
or oppressed by the urge to procreate, for the sake of engaging in unwholesome sexual intercourse. But in this case, it is for the sake of food.
"Has emerged" is what is intended.
"Stretches" means that, having placed both hind feet evenly upon one of the surfaces— whether of gold, silver, crystal, or emerald—
and having extended the forefeet forward, [he stretches] the rear part of his body.

Drawing forward the front part of its body, thrusting back its hindquarters, arching its neck, and making a sound like a clap of thunder, it stretches while striking its nostrils and shaking off the dust clinging to its body.
On the ground where it stretches, it runs back and forth like a young calf. As it runs, its body whirls about in the darkness.
It appears like a firebrand.

Why does he look back? Out of compassion for others. It is said that when he roars his lion’s roar, elephants, cattle, antelopes, and other creatures wandering in uneven places such as precipices and pits fall into those very precipices and pits; [he looks back] for their sake.
He surveys with compassion. But how can there be such a thing as compassion for one whose work is cruel and who eats the flesh of others?
Yes, there is. For instance, he thinks, "What is the use of killing many?
and thus he does not take even small creatures for his own food; in this way, he practices compassion. And this has been said: "May I not [kill] small..."
“When his life-force had reached its end, he brought about his own destruction.
He “roars a lion’s roar” means that he roars a fearless roar three times.

And as he stands upon the ground of his stretching and roars in this manner, his sound makes a single resonant cry throughout an area of three leagues on all sides; that is his resonant cry (*ninnāda*).
Upon hearing [the roar], the multitudes of bipeds and quadrupeds within a range of three *yojanas* are unable to remain in their respective places.
"He goes out for his range" means he goes for the sake of food. How so?

For standing on the ground where he stretches himself, as he springs up either to the right or to the left, he covers a space the measure of a bull (*usabha*); springing upwards, he covers four or even eight [of such measures].
It leaps over ox-lengths; leaping straight forward on level ground, it traverses a distance of sixteen or even twenty ox-lengths;
leaping from dry land or from mountains, it traverses a distance of sixty or even eighty ox-lengths;
and seeing a tree or a mountain along the way, it avoids it by turning to the left.
Or, having roared a third lion’s roar, it becomes visible at a distance of three *yojanas* together with that very sound.
Having gone three *yojanas*, it turns back and stands still, hearing the echo of its own roar.
Thus it proceeds with such swift speed.
"By and large" means for the most part. Fear, agitation, and terror—all these are merely names for mental trepidation.
For when they hear the sound of a lion, many beings are afraid, while few are not afraid. Who, then, are those who are not afraid?

They are the lion among men, the noble elephant, the noble horse, the noble bull, the noble man, and the one whose taints are destroyed (the *khīṇāsava*). But why do these not fear? Because the lion among men...

One does not fear thinking, "I am equal [to others] in terms of birth, clan, family, or heroism. Just as noble elephants and the like do not fear because of the strength of their own *sakkāyadiṭṭhi* (personality-belief), one who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) does not fear because of having abandoned *sakkāyadiṭṭhi*.
"Cave-dwellers" refers to those living in holes, such as snakes, mongooses, lizards, and so forth. "Water-dwellers" refers to those living in water, such as fish, turtles, and so forth.
“Forest-dwellers” refers to wild elephants, horses, oxen, deer, and so forth that live in the forest. “Enter” means they enter while looking along the path, thinking, “He will come now and seize me.

“With strong” means with firm ones. “With leather thongs” means with leather ropes. Regarding the passage beginning with “of great psychic power,” it refers to the ability to leap a distance of about twenty cubits by leaping from the right side and so on, or straight ahead for a distance of twenty cubits or more, while standing on the ground where one is displaying one’s powers.

His great psychic power (*mahiddhikatā*) is to be understood by his preeminence over all other deer; his great influence (*mahānubhāvatā*) is to be understood by the fact that when they hear his cry from as far as thirty *yojanas* around, they flee.
"In just this way," the Blessed One said, describing himself in various ways in those various suttas: "He is like a lion..."
“Monks, ‘Lion’ is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One”—in this sutta, he thus described himself as being like a lion.
“‘Physician, surgeon,’ Sunakkhatta, is a designation for the Tathāgata”—in this [sutta], he described himself as being like a physician.
“‘Brahmin,’ monks, is a designation for the Tathāgata.”
In this [passage], he is like a brahmin. In the passage, “‘A man skilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata,” he is like a man who points out the way.
In the passage, “I am a king, O Sela,” he is like a king.
But in this sutta, speaking of himself by comparing him to a lion, he said thus: “‘A lion,’ indeed, is a designation for the Tathāgata.”

In this regard, the similarity is as follows: just as a lion dwells in places such as golden caves, so too the Tathāgata—who had made his resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara and fulfilled the perfections for an immeasurable time—by both taking rebirth in his final existence and emerging from his mother’s womb, caused the ten-thousandfold world system to tremble; and as he grew up, [he attained] what was like divine excellence.
The period of his residence in the three palaces while experiencing prosperity is to be understood [as the equivalent]. Just as it was for Sīha when he emerged from the Golden Cave,
so too for the Tathāgata, in his twenty-ninth year, having mounted Kaṇḍaka through an open gate accompanied by Channa,
and having crossed over the three kingdoms, [he stood] on the bank of the river Anomā by the Brahmā’s...
Having donned the saffron robes given to him, on the seventh day after his going forth, he went to Rājagaha; there,
having wandered for alms and finished his meal at the Paṇḍava mountain cave, and having attained supreme enlightenment,
this is the period up until the time he gave his promise to the king to first visit the kingdom of Magadha.

The period beginning with the Tathāgata’s visit to Āḷāra Kālāma— having given his promise— and ending with the time he consumed forty-nine mouthfuls of milk-rice offered by Sujātā, should be understood as being like the lion’s stretching.
It was like the lion’s shaking of its mane when, at evening time, having taken eight handfuls of grass given by the grass-cutter, [he sat down].
While being praised by the deities of ten thousand world-systems and honored with perfumes and other offerings, he circumambulated the Bodhi tree three times,
ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), spread a layer of grass upon a spot fourteen cubits high,
and sat down having resolved upon fourfold energy; at that very moment, he scattered Māra’s army and, throughout the three watches of the night—

Having purified the three types of higher knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*), as he churned the great ocean of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—both forward and backward—with the churning-stick of the knowledge of the pairs, omniscience (*sarvajñatājñāna*) was penetrated;
it should be understood that by the power of that penetration, the ten-thousandfold world system shook.
Just as a lion surveys the four quarters, so did he who had penetrated omniscience remain at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) for seven weeks.
Having dwelt there and partaken of the offering of honey-rice balls, he accepted the invitation of Mahābrahmā for a teaching of the Dhamma at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree.

While dwelling there, on the eleventh day—at dawn, knowing that the full moon of Āsāḷha would occur the following day—he thought, "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma? [He then considered] the fact that Āḷāra and Udaka had passed away.
Having understood this, his surveying of the group of five monks should be seen as being for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.

It is like the time when a lion travels three *yojanas* for the sake of seeking food; it is the time of traveling the eighteen-*yojana* path after rising from the Goatherd’s Banyan tree following his midday meal, having taken up his own bowl and robe with the thought, "I shall set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma for the group of five."
The time for turning the Wheel of Dhamma was like the time of the Lion’s Roar: having traveled an eighteen-yojana path, the Tathāgata—
having exhorted the group of five monks and being seated upon the immovable seat (the Bodhi tree), surrounded by a host of deities gathered from ten thousand world-systems—
proclaimed in the manner beginning with, "Monks, these two extremes are not to be pursued by one who has gone forth."

It should be understood. And while this word was being taught, the lion-like Dhamma-voice of the Tathāgata pervaded the ten-thousandfold world-system, encompassing everything from the Avīci hell below to the peak of existence above.

Just as small creatures fall into a state of terror at the sound of a lion, so too, having illuminated the three characteristics of the Tathāgata, [he taught] the four truths by way of sixteen aspects.
The time for the arising of the knowledge and confidence of long-lived deities should be understood as occurring while he was expounding the Dhamma by analyzing it through sixty thousand methods.
"Yadā" means at which time. "Tathāgata": the Blessed One is called "Tathāgata" for eight reasons—namely, "tathā-āgato" (thus come).
A *tathāgata* is so called because he has gone thus (*tathā gata*); because he has come to the true nature (*tathalakkhaṇa*);
because he has perfectly awakened to the true dhammas as they really are (*yāthāvato*); because of his seeing thus; because of his speaking thus;
because of his acting thus; and in the sense of overcoming, he is a *tathāgata*. Their detailed exposition is also found in the commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
This has indeed been stated even in the *Mūlapariyāya-vaṇṇanā*. "In the world" means in the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*).

"Arises" means that it is said to arise from the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*) up until the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*) or the knowledge of the path of Arahantship; however, once the fruit of Arahantship is attained, it is said to have "arisen.
Terms such as "Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One," and so forth, are explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati-niddesa*).
"‘Such is form’: this is form, this much is form; there is no form beyond this.

To this extent—by way of intrinsic nature, by way of individual essence, by way of limit, by way of delimitation, and by way of defining—the four great elements and the derived form of the four great elements are all shown. ‘Such is the origin of form’ is this..."
This is called the arising of form (*rūpa-samudaya*). By this much, everything beginning with “the arising of nutriment is the arising of form” has been shown.

Thus, “the subsiding of form” (*rūpassa atthaṅgamo*) means this is the subsiding of form. By this also, everything beginning with “from the cessation of nutriment comes the cessation of form” has been shown.
This same method applies to “feeling” (*vedanā*) and so forth as well.

"Beautiful" means beautiful by virtue of the complexion of his body. "Having heard the teaching of the Dhamma" means having heard this teaching of the Dhamma by the Tathāgata, which is adorned with the fifty characteristics within the five aggregates. "For the most part"—whom does he exclude here?
Noble disciples and devas. For because their taints are destroyed, even fear of mental trepidation does not arise in them.
For one who is stirred by spiritual urgency, there arises the "spiritual urgency of knowledge" (ñāṇasaṃvega) due to having attained what is to be attained through systematic striving.

For the other deities, however, as they attend to impermanence with the thought, "This is a source of terror for monks," there arises both the fear and dread of mental agitation and the fear of knowledge at the time of powerful insight (balavavipassanā).
The address "Sir" is merely a form of polite address. "Included within personality" (sakkāyapariyāpannā) means included within the five aggregates.

Thus, while the Fully Enlightened One was teaching the Dhamma—having shown the fault of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) to them and having struck it with the three characteristics—the so-called "fear of knowledge" (*ñāṇabhaya*) descended upon them.
"Having known" (*abhiññāya*) means having understood.
"The Wheel of the Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*) refers both to the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*). As for the knowledge of penetration:
The knowledge called *nāma* is that knowledge by which, while seated at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*), he penetrated the Four Truths in sixteen aspects and sixty thousand methods.
The knowledge called *desanāñāṇa* is that knowledge by which he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*) with its three revolutions and twelve modes.
Both of these are indeed the "knowledge born on the breast" of the One Possessing Ten Powers (*dasabala*). Among them, it is here the *desanāñāṇa* [that is intended].

It should be understood that this [Dhamma] is set in motion until the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) arises for the Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās; once that has arisen, it is said to have been "set in motion.
"Appaṭipuggalo" means devoid of a peer. "Yasassino" means endowed with a retinue. "Tādino" means...
Of one who is exactly the same regarding gain, loss, and so forth. This is the sixth [sutta].
7. Commentary on the *Khajjanīya-sutta* (79).
In the seventh [sutta], the phrase "past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*) is not stated with reference to recollection by way of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), but rather by way of insight (*vipassanā*).
However, this was said with reference to ascetics and brahmins who recollect past lives. For that very reason it was said:

"They all recollect either the five aggregates of clinging or one or another of them. Indeed, for one who recollects by way of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), the object of focus is certainly the aggregates, the aggregates of clinging, the things connected with the aggregates, or even the designation (*paññatti*). It is form alone...
"He recollects" means that while recollecting in this way, he does not recollect any other being or person;

rather, he recollects only the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) that has ceased in the past. The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates. The section on emptiness (*suññatāpabba*) is finished.
Now, in order to show the characteristic of emptiness, he said: "And what, bhikkhus, do you call 'form'? and so forth. Just as...

For instance, a man searching for a lost ox, even if he sees a red or black bull wandering among a herd of cattle, cannot yet reach a definitive conclusion that "this is my ox" based on that alone. Why? Because there are others of that same appearance.
However, when he sees a mark such as a spear-wound or a thorn-piercing on a part of its body, [he knows]: "This is my ox."

Just as there is a definitive conclusion that "this is his property," even so, although emptiness (suññatā) has been mentioned, as long as the characteristic of emptiness is not explained, it remains as if unexplained;
but when the characteristic is explained, it is said to have been truly explained.
For emptiness is like an ox, and the characteristic of emptiness is like the characteristic of an ox. Just as when the characteristic of an ox is not observed...
Just as an ox is not properly recognized until it has been observed, and once it has been observed, it is said to be recognized;
even so, emptiness remains unexplained as long as its characteristic has not been stated, but once that has been stated, it is said to be explained.
Thus, in order to show the characteristic of emptiness, he said: "And what, bhikkhus, do you call 'form'? and so forth.
In this context, *kiñca* is a question regarding the cause; the meaning is: "For what reason do you call it 'form' (*rūpa*), for what reason is this called 'form'?
In the phrase *ruppatīti kho*, the word *iti* indicates the reason; the meaning is: "Because it is affected (*ruppati*), therefore it is called 'form'.
To be "affected" (*ruppati*) means to be disturbed, struck, oppressed, or broken; that is the meaning. Even by cold...

Regarding the phrase "it is afflicted" (*ruppati*) and so forth: first, affliction by cold is evident in the Lokantarika hell. Between every three world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), there is a specific Lokantarika hell measuring eight thousand yojanas.
There is no earth beneath it, nor is there the light of the moon, sun, fire, or jewels above; it is perpetually dark. For the beings born there...
Their bodies are three fathoms long; like bats, they cling to the mountain slopes with their long and broad claws and hang head-downwards.
When, crawling along, they come within arm’s reach of one another, they think, "We have found food!
and, busying themselves there, they turn over and fall into the water that sustains the world.
Even when struck by the wind, they break off like honeycomb fruits and fall into the water;

as soon as they have fallen, they dissolve with a crackling sound, like a lump of dough dropped into extremely alkaline water or into boiling oil. Thus, being "molded" (ruppana) by cold is evident in the Lokantarika hell.
It is likewise evident in regions such as the Mahimsaka country where snow falls and the air is cold.
For there, beings whose bodies are shattered by cold even reach the end of their lives.
The affliction by heat is evident in the Great Niraya of Avīci. The affliction by hunger is evident in the realm of Petas and during times of famine.
The affliction by thirst is evident among those such as the Kālakañjika Asuras. It is said that once, a certain Kālakañjika Asura...
Unable to endure his thirst, he entered the Great Gaṅgā River, which was a yojana deep and wide;
yet wherever he went, the water would part and smoke would rise, making it feel as if he were walking upon a heated stone slab.
As he wandered here and there, listening for the sound of water, the night passed away. Then, at dawn, [he set out] on his alms-round.
Seeing about thirty alms-collecting bhikkhus passing by, they asked, "Who are you, good man?
"I am a peta, venerable sirs," he replied. "What are you seeking? "Water, venerable sirs. "This Ganges is full; do you not see it?
"It is of no use to me, venerable sirs. "In that case, lie down on the bank of the Ganges and [place your mouth]—*mukhe*—"
“Let us pour water for him,” they said. He lay down on his back upon the sandy beach.
The bhikkhus brought out about thirty bowls, filled them with water, and poured it into his mouth. While they were doing so, the time for the alms-round drew near.
Then [the bhikkhus thought], “It is time for our alms-round, O good man; have you received at least some relief?”

They said: "The peta said, 'Venerable sirs, if even half a *pasata* of water poured from thirty bowls by thirty noble ladies of mine has reached my throat, let there be no liberation for me from this peta-existence. Thus, being afflicted by thirst is evident in the realm of petas.
Being afflicted by gadflies and the like is evident in places abounding with gadflies, flies, and so forth. And here, 'gadflies' refers to brown flies."
"Flies" means flies. "Winds" should be understood by way of abdominal wind, back wind, and so forth.
For when a wind-disease arises in the body, it breaks the hands, feet, back, and so on; it makes one blind, it makes one hunchbacked, and it makes one a cripple.
"Heat" means the heat of the sun; the resulting deformation caused by it is evident in places such as desert wastes. It is said that once there was a certain woman...
In a desert wilderness, having been separated from her caravan at night, she was unable to place her feet upon the sand that grew scorching hot as the sun rose during the day.

She lowered her basket from her head and stepped on it. Gradually, as the basket became heated by the heat and she could no longer stand upon it, she placed her upper garment over it and stepped on that. When that too became heated, she [stepped] with her own lap...
Having laid her son, who was clutching him, face down, she stepped on him while he was still crying;
together with him, she passed away at that very spot, consumed by the heat [of the fire].
"Reptiles" refers to any long-bodied creatures that move by crawling. By contact with them, there is affliction, as in the case of those bitten by venomous snakes and the like.

This is to be understood by way of [the distinction between] the universal and the individual. Thus, of the two characteristics of phenomena—the universal and the individual—which were taught by the Blessed One, the individual characteristic of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) has first been shown. For this belongs specifically to the aggregate of form and not to feeling and the others;
therefore, it is called the "individual characteristic. However, as for the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self—
This [characteristic] also applies to feeling and the others; therefore, it is called their "general characteristic" (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding such passages as, "And what, bhikkhus, do you call 'feeling'? and so forth, it should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
However, as for that which differs from the preceding, this is its explanation: one feels pleasure, thus [it is] "pleasure," referring to the object.
It feels and experiences. This same method applies to the two subsequent phrases as well.
But how is it that this object comes to be called "pleasant," "painful," or "neither-painful-nor-pleasant"? It is because of the conditions for pleasure and so forth.
And this very point has already been stated in the Mahāli Sutta: "But because, Mahāli, form is pleasant, followed by pleasure, and entered into by pleasure..."

Regarding the phrase "it feels" (*vedayati*): here it is feeling itself (*vedanā*) that feels, and not any other being (*satta*) or person (*puggala*). For feeling has the characteristic of being felt;
therefore, depending on a basis and an object, feeling itself feels. Thus, in this context, the Blessed One demonstrated by dividing out the individual characteristic of feeling as well.
"One perceives blue" means that, having performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*) upon a blue flower or a blue cloth, one attains access concentration (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*).
Or he perceives it as blue. For this so-called perception (saññā) includes both preliminary perception (parikamma-saññā), access perception (upacāra-saññā), and absorption perception (appanā-saññā);
even the perception that arises as "blue, blue" is certainly included. The same method applies to yellow and the other colors.
Here too, the Blessed One has demonstrated by dividing the individual characteristic of perception, which has the characteristic of perceiving.
"Forming form as form-ness by way of being conditioned (*saṅkhata*)" means:

just as one is said to "cook" *yāgu* as *yāgu*-ness and *pūva* as *pūva*-ness, so too, form—which has received the name "conditioned" because it is produced through the coming together of conditions—is formed for the state of being form, for the sake of its existence as form, just as that which is called "formed form" comes to be. Thus, it forms [it] for the purpose of its becoming form.
It means that it accumulates, aggregates, and brings to completion. The same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] as well. Here, however, is the summary:
it conditions—that is, produces—the material form (*rūpa*) arising together with itself, as well as the associated states such as feeling.
Here too, the Blessed One demonstrated the specific characteristic of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), which is defined by the act of intending (*cetayita*).
"It perceives sourness" means that it perceives sour things such as mangoes, ambāṭaka fruits, and mātuluṅga fruits as "sour. This same method applies to all the terms.
Furthermore, in this context, "bitter" refers to various kinds such as the nimba and paṭola; "pungent" refers to various kinds such as long pepper and black pepper;
"sweet" refers to various kinds such as ghee and molasses; and "astringent" refers to various kinds such as the vātiṅgaṇa fruit, coconut, the caturassa creeper, and young bamboo shoots.

"Akhārika" refers to various kinds of fruit or leaves mixed with *kāra* leaves and so forth. "Salty" refers to various types such as salted gruel, salted fish, salted rice, and so on. "Non-salty" refers to various types such as unsalted gruel, unsalted fish, unsalted rice, and so on.

Therefore it is called "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) because it cognizes this diversity of sourness and so forth by way of their mutually distinct qualities of sourness and so on; therefore it is called "consciousness."
It is said: "Thus here too, the Blessed One, having analyzed the individual characteristic of consciousness—which has the characteristic of cognizing—has demonstrated it.
However, because perception (saññā) is manifest through its grasping of the shape and configuration of an object, it is analyzed in the context of the eye-door.
Because consciousness (viññāṇa), even without [grasping] shape and configuration, functions by way of grasping the specific distinction of the object..."

It is evident; therefore, it is analyzed under the door of the tongue. Now, regarding these three—perception (*saññā*), consciousness (*viññāṇa*), and wisdom (*paññā*)—the distinctions between them should be understood here in the sense that they "perceive," "cognize," and "understand" for the purpose of discerning their own specific natures without confusion.

In this context, the distinction lies merely in the prefixes, while the verbal root *jānāti* (to know) itself is without distinction. Even within that [root], there is a distinction in the sense of knowing.
It should be understood as follows: perception (saññā) is merely the act of perceiving an object by way of its blue color and so forth;

it is not able to bring about the penetration of the characteristics (lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha) such as "impermanence," "suffering," and "non-self. Consciousness (viññāṇa), on the other hand, both knows the object by way of its blue color and so forth, and brings about the penetration of the characteristics such as impermanence and so forth;
however, even after striving, it is unable to bring about the manifestation of the Path (magga-pātubhāva).
It cannot [do so]. Wisdom knows the object by way of its blue color and so forth; it brings about the penetration of characteristics by way of impermanence and so forth;
and by striving, it brings about the manifestation of the path.
For just as when a pile of kahāpaṇa coins has been made upon a money-changer’s board, a village-dweller who has not yet developed intelligence thinks, "This is a great money-changer."
When the three men stood there looking on, the child Ajātabuddhi knew only the nature of the coins as being circular, variegated, square, and so forth;
he did not know that "this is what people consider to be a treasure for their use and enjoyment.
The village headman knew both their circular and other forms, as well as their status as treasures esteemed for human use and enjoyment, [thinking], "This..."

He does not know, "This is counterfeit, this is clever, this is base, this is smooth. However, a master goldsmith knows whether it is a mere semblance of mind (citta) and so forth, or whether it is a genuine jewel, or whether it is counterfeit and so on.
And knowing this, even after seeing the form, hearing the sound, smelling the odor, tasting the flavor, or even determining its weight with his hand, [he recognizes its true nature].

One knows, "It was made in such-and-such a village," or one knows, "It was made in such-and-such a market town, in such-and-such a city, in the shade of such-and-such a mountain, or on the bank of such-and-such a river," or one knows, "It was made by such-and-such a teacher.
In the same way, perception (saññā) knows only the mere object by way of its blue color and so forth, like a child whose intellect has not yet developed seeing a coin.
Consciousness (viññāṇa), however, is like a villager seeing that same coin.
Like [the sight of] a coin, wisdom knows the object by way of its blue color and so forth, and it brings about the penetration of characteristics by way of impermanence and so forth;
like the sight of a coin by a great money-changer, wisdom knows the object by way of its blue color and so forth,
brings about the penetration of characteristics by way of impermanence and so forth, and, having exerted itself, brings about the manifestation of the Path.
However, their distinction is difficult to penetrate. Therefore the Venerable Nāgasena said:
"It was a difficult task, Great King, performed by the Blessed One. "What, venerable Nāgasena, was this difficult task performed by the Blessed One?
"It was a difficult task, Great King, performed by the Blessed One: [to discern] these formless phenomena of mind and mental factors."
The differentiation of those [mental factors] occurring upon a single object has been declared thus: “This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness.
For just as these five—sesame oil, mustard oil, honey-tree oil, castor oil, and fat oil—are distinct, so too are these [factors].

Having placed these oils in a single vessel and stirred them together with a double-bladed churning-stick for a day, it would be difficult to extract each one separately, thinking, "This is sesame oil; this is mustard oil. But this is even more difficult than that.
For the Blessed One, however, because he has thoroughly penetrated omniscient knowledge, being the Lord of Dhamma and King of Dhamma, [he knows] these formless [states].
He made a distinction between the mental objects (dhammas) as they occurred upon a single object.

This point should also be understood by means of drawing out water individually from the place where five great rivers have entered the ocean, saying, "This is the water of the Gaṅgā; this is the water of the Yamunā."

Thus, having explained emptiness (*suññatā*) with the first section and the characteristic of emptiness (*suññatālakkhaṇa*) with the second—thereby teaching the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) through these two sections—he now spoke the passage beginning with "In this regard, monks," in order to show the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*).
Therein, "I am being devoured" does not mean that form devours him by tearing off flesh again and again like a dog; rather, it is as when one dressed in soiled clothes...
With reference to the distress arising from that cause, he says, "It eats me, O cloth!

In this way, it should be understood that even this [practice] is called "eating" because it produces such distress. "He is practicing" means he is practicing starting from virtue (sīla) up to the path of arahantship.
Furthermore, regarding the practitioner here who possesses powerful knowledge, keen intelligence, and superior wisdom, who exerts himself on the ground of striving—
If one is pierced by a stump or a thorn, or struck by a weapon, or seized and devoured by tigers and other such beasts, one sets aside that pain and,
contemplating the primary meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), attains Arahantship itself;
such a person is called "one practicing for the sake of disenchantment with feeling, for its fading away, for its cessation," just like the Elder Pītamalla.
Just like the Elder Mahātissa, son of a householder, who was one among thirty bhikkhus in the Vattaniya forest;
and like the bhikkhu who lay down before the mouth of a tiger; and like the elder who was pierced by a thorn.
It is said that while twelve bhikkhus were engaged in striving in the forest after striking the gong, one [bhikkhu] at sunrise...
As soon as the bell had ceased its ringing, he descended to the walking path and, while pacing back and forth, stepped upon a thorn hidden by grass.
The thorn pierced through the sole of his foot. A pain arose like that of being transfixed by a red-hot iron spike.
The Elder thought: "Shall I pull out this thorn, or shall I leave it as it is?"
“...pierced by a thorn that was already standing there? It occurred to him:
“Because I have been pierced by this thorn, there is no such thing as fear in the hells and other realms; it is merely a thorn that was naturally standing there, having pierced me.
Making that sensation negligible, he spent the entire night walking back and forth, and when the night had dawned, he gave notice to another. He came and asked, “What is it?”
“Venerable sir,” he asked. “I have been pierced by a thorn, friend. “At what time, venerable sir?
“This very evening, friend. “Why did you not summon us? We could have extracted the thorn and poured oil upon it.
“Friend, we were merely striving to extract the thorn that remained after it had already pierced its way in naturally. “Were you able?”
“Venerable sir, it has been extracted,” [he asked]. “It has been extracted by me, friend, only in part,” [the Blessed One replied].
The remaining sections have already been explained in detail in the *Satipaṭṭhāna-sutta-niddesa* within the commentaries on the *Dīgha Nikāya* and *Majjhima Nikāya*.
Why was it begun with the words, “What do you think, monks”? In this section, only the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) is discussed.
It is not the characteristic of impermanence. This [sutta] was begun in order to demonstrate that. It was also begun in order to demonstrate by bringing together the three characteristics.
"He dismantles, he does not build up" means he destroys the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); he does not accumulate it. "He abandons, he does not grasp" means he relinquishes that very thing;
he does not take it up. "He disperses, he does not collect" means he scatters it; he does not heap it together. He utterly shakes off.
"He does not blow upon it" means he extinguishes it, he does not cause it to blaze.
Why was this begun with the words, "Seeing thus, monks"? It was begun to show one who stands having destroyed the round of existence, the great one whose taints are exhausted.
Or rather, up to this point insight (vipassanā) has been explained; now, together with that insight—
This [section] was commenced in order to show the four paths. Alternatively, by means of this much [of the preceding] section, the first path has been explained;
now, this is commenced in order to show the [remaining] three paths together with insight (vipassanā). Or else, by means of this much section, the three paths have been explained;
now, this very same [section] is commenced in order to show the path of Arahantship together with insight as well.

"Along with their lords" means together with their lord, the king of the gods. "They pay homage from afar" means they pay homage even from a distance; they indeed pay homage even while standing far away, just as they did toward the Venerable Nīta Thera.
It is said that the Thera went forth after leaving a family that discarded flowers.

Having attained Arahantship at the very moment of shaving his head, he thought: "I have gone forth this very day; this very day my duty as one who has gone forth has reached its culmination, adorned by contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation."
“I shall fulfill the practice of the Great Noble Lineage. Having entered Sāvatthī for the sake of rag-robe material, he wandered about searching for cloth.
Then, a certain Great Brahmā, emerging from meditative absorption and surveying the human realm, saw the Elder and thought:
“Having gone forth this very day, and having attained Arahantship at the razor’s edge this very day, he shall fulfill the practice of the Great Noble Lineage.”
“...he is seeking a rag to fill his robe,” he said, and stood there with palms joined in reverence. Another Great Brahmā, seeing him, asked, “Whom are you paying homage to?
“I am paying homage to the Elder Nīta,” he replied. “For what reason?
“Because today itself, having gone forth, and today itself, having attained Arahantship at the razor’s edge, he is seeking a rag to fulfill the practice of the Great Noble Lineage.”
He too stood paying homage to him. Then another, and yet another—seven hundred great Brahmās stood paying homage.
Therefore it is said:
“Those seven hundred sublime deities...”
Brahmās, having emerged from their celestial mansions,
paid homage with serene minds to him who had been brought there, saying:
"One whose taints are exhausted takes up the rag-robe."
“Those seven hundred sublime deities,
having emerged from their celestial mansions,
paid homage with serene minds to him who had been led forth.”
“An arahant makes a rag-robe,” [it is said].
“An arahant washes a rag-robe”;
“An arahant dyes a rag-robe.”
‘The one whose taints are destroyed wears rag-robes.

Thus, in this sutta, the Blessed One turned away from the three realms of existence and reached the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred bhikkhus were established in Arahantship. This is the seventh [sutta].
8. Commentary on the Piṇḍolya Sutta.
80. "In some particular matter" means for some particular reason. "Having dismissed" means having sent away.

For on what occasion were these dismissed by the Blessed One? Indeed, during one rainy season, the Blessed One, having resided at Sāvatthī and having completed the rains retreat, performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony and departed from Sāvatthī accompanied by a great community of monks to wander through the countryside.
While traveling, he arrived at Kapilavatthu and entered the Nigrodha Monastery.
Upon hearing that "the Teacher has arrived," the Śākya kings had various permissible items—such as oil, honey, molasses, and other drinks—prepared after their meal.
Carrying these in hundreds of baskets, they went to the monastery, presented them to the Saṅgha, and after paying homage to the Teacher, stood to one side while exchanging friendly greetings.
They sat down. The Teacher sat there, delivering a sweet discourse on the Dhamma to them.
At that moment, some bhikkhus were attending to the lodgings, some were arranging the beds and benches, and the novices were clearing away the grass.
Among those present at the place where the distribution was to take place, there were both bhikkhus who had arrived and those who had not yet arrived. Those who had arrived...
Those who were taking the gains intended for those who had not yet arrived made a great clamor, saying, "Give to us! Give to our teacher! Give to our preceptor!
When the Teacher heard this, he asked the Elder, "Ānanda, what is that loud noise, that great clamor? It sounds like fishermen at a haul of fish. The Elder reported the matter to him. The Teacher—
Having heard this, he said, "Ānanda, the bhikkhus are making a great noise for the sake of material gain. "Yes, venerable sir," he replied.
"It is unbecoming, Ānanda, it is improper. For it was not for the sake of robes and such things that I fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons;
nor did these bhikkhus go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes and such things, but rather for the sake of arahantship."
"Having gone forth, they make what is harmful appear like what is beneficial, and what is essence-less appear like what has essence.
Go, Ānanda, and dismiss those bhikkhus. "At the time of the morning" means on the morning of the following day. "At the foot of a young beluva tree" means at the base of a young *beluva* tree.
"Pabāḷho" means expelled (*pabāhito*). There is also the reading "pavāḷho," which has the same meaning of "expelled" (*pavāhito*). Both terms refer simply to the state of having been removed.
It illuminates. "There might be a change" means there would be either a change in confidence (*pasāda*) or a change in state (*bhāva*).
How so? For those who cause their confidence to diminish by thinking, "We have been dismissed by the Perfectly Enlightened One for a trivial reason," there is what is called a change in confidence.
For those who depart for the sphere of other sects while still wearing the very same religious garb, there is what is called a change in state. "There might be a transformation" (*vipariṇāma*).

In this context, however, one should understand that "change" (*vipariṇāma*) refers to the renunciation of the training and returning to the lower life, [thinking]: "We went forth thinking we would be able to grasp the Teacher's intention; for those who cannot grasp it, what is the use of our going forth?
"Vaccha" means a calf that still drinks milk. "Alteration" (*aññathatta*) means the alteration of withering away. "Drinking milk" (*khīrūpaka*).
For indeed, Vaccha, by not seeing his mother and not receiving milk, he withers, trembles, and quivers.
"Change" (vipariṇāma) means death; for failing to receive milk, he withers from thirst for milk, falls down, and dies.
"Of young seeds" refers to those seeds that have sprouted and are to be nurtured by water. "Alteration" (aññathatta) is precisely the alteration consisting of withering.
For those [plants], not receiving water, wither. "Transformation" means destruction;
for they, not receiving water, having dried up, are destroyed and become mere straw. "Supported" means supported by both material support and Dhamma support.
"I would support" means I would support them with both of these supports. "Not long gone forth."
For indeed, when novices and young bhikkhus lack the requisites such as robes,
or when they are afflicted by illness, or when they are not supported by material assistance from the Teacher, teachers, or preceptors,
they become exhausted and are unable to perform recitation or mental attention; likewise, those not supported by spiritual assistance through formal instruction and exhortation.
Furthermore, those who are declining are unable to abandon unwholesome states and develop wholesome ones.
However, when supported by these two kinds of assistance, they proceed with recitation and mental attention without physical fatigue;
practicing according to the instructions, even if they do not receive that assistance later on, they possess the strength acquired through that previous support.
They are established in the Teaching; therefore, this reflection arose in the Blessed One.

"He appeared before the Blessed One" means that, having known the Teacher’s mind—thinking, "These bhikkhus have been sent away by the Blessed One, and now he intends to show them favor"—and realizing the reason for the Blessed One’s thought, [the deity] exerted himself in this matter.
“I shall know,” he said, and appeared clearly before him.

“There are monks here”—this was spoken by that Great Brahmā through his own proficiency, just as a skilled cook, having prepared with great care whatever flavors such as sourness the king prefers and making them even more delicious, presents them on the following day;
in the same way, by virtue of his own skill, he spoke exactly according to the simile brought forth by the Blessed One.
Having prepared [the request] with the words beginning with "Bhagavā," he speaks while entreating the Blessed One for the sake of favoring the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
In that context, "let him rejoice" means: "Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus come into my presence.
Thus, let him rejoice with sympathetic joy at their arrival. "Let him address them" means: let him address them by giving instruction and exhortation once they have arrived.
"Seclusion" (*paṭisallāna*) means being alone. "He performed a feat of supernormal power" (*iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsī*) means he exercised his psychic power.
"In groups of one or two" means having become either single or in pairs. "Appearing bashful" means having a nature characterized by modesty and fear.
But why did the Blessed One exercise his supernormal power for them to approach him in that manner? It was out of a desire for their welfare. For if they...

If they were to arrive in groups, they might even joke, saying, “The Blessed One dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and entered the forest, yet he was unable to stay there for even a single day; he has returned with great haste.
Consequently, they would neither manifest reverence for the Buddha nor be capable of receiving the teaching of the Dhamma.
However, thinking that those who were traveling with fear and trepidation would develop reverence for the Buddha upon their arrival after one or two days,
and would be able to receive the teaching of the Dhamma, he performed such a feat of psychic power (iddhi) out of a desire for their welfare.
"They sat down" means that as those men of lustful appearance were approaching, one bhikkhu thought, "The Teacher is looking at me alone;
he surely wishes to reprove me," and so he came slowly, paid homage, and sat down;
then another, and then another—in this way, five hundred bhikkhus sat down. When the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was thus seated, [the Buddha spoke] in the midst of them...

Seeing them as motionless as the great ocean when it is calm or as a lamp in a windless place, the Teacher thought, "What kind of Dhamma teaching is appropriate for these bhikkhus? Then it occurred to him:

"These men have been sent away because of food; a Dhamma teaching on alms-food (piṇḍiyālopaka) alone is suitable for them. Having shown that, I shall give a threefold-turning teaching at the conclusion."
“I shall teach them; at the conclusion of that teaching, they will all attain arahantship. Then, while delivering that Dhamma discourse to them, he said, “Bhikkhus, this is the end,” and so forth.
In this context, “the end” (anta) means the final, the wretched. “That is to say, the state of a beggar” (piṇḍolya) refers to that which results from such a search for alms.
...the life of one who maintains his livelihood [in this way]. Here, however, is the meaning of the words: he wanders for alms (*piṇḍa*) thus he is a *piṇḍola*;
the work of a *piṇḍola* is *piṇḍolya*, which means a life produced by the seeking of alms.
*Abhisāpa* means abuse. For when people are angry, they say of their adversary: "May he, having put on a robe and taken up an alms-bowl, wander for alms..."

They revile him, saying, "What is there that you have not already done, you who, though so powerful and endowed with energy, yet having abandoned shame and dread of blame, wander about like a wretched beggar with bowl in hand? Even thus they revile him.
And yet, even while being subject to such a curse, this state of mendicancy is [practiced] by sons of good family.

"They come seeking their own interests" means that in my teaching, sons of good family who are well-born and sons of good family who are well-conducted, being intent on their own interests and intent on their own purposes, come under the influence of those purposes.
Regarding the phrases "led by the king" and so forth:
those who, having consumed what belonged to the king, were imprisoned in a prison by the king, but then escaped;
They go forth; these are called "those led away by the king. For they are called "led away by the king" because they were led by the king into bondage.
But as for those who, having been captured by bandits in the wilderness, while some were being put to death, others say: "Master, we have been released by you;
without returning to our homes, we shall go forth. Therein, whatever merit we shall perform, such as worship of the Buddha and so forth..."
"Then we shall give you your share," they say; those who go forth having been thus released by them are called "those led away by bandits.
For they are indeed called "led away by bandits" because they have been led away by bandits to be executed.

However, those who, having incurred a debt and being unable to repay it, go forth after fleeing, are called "those oppressed by debt"; the meaning is that they are tormented by debt. The reading *iṇaṭṭhā* also occurs.
The meaning is "established in need. Those who go forth having been overcome and afflicted by any one of the dangers of kings, thieves, hunger, or disease are called "those driven by fear";
the meaning is "oppressed by fear. *Bhayaṭṭhā* is also a reading, meaning "standing in fear.
*Ājīvikāpakatā* means "afflicted and overcome by the struggle for livelihood," that is, those unable to support their wives and children.
"Otiṇṇāmhā" means we have entered within.
"And he is covetous" refers to the fact that although that clansman went forth having generated the thought, "I shall make an end of suffering," and so forth,
at a later time he was unable to make his renunciation conform to that ideal.
To demonstrate that, it is said: therein, "covetous" (*abhijjhālu*) means one who covets the goods of others; "of intense passion" (*tībhasārāga*) means one whose lust is thick;

"with a malevolent mind" (*byāpannacitta*) means one whose mind is ruined by putrefaction; "with corrupt mental intentions" (*paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappa*) means one with a wicked mind, like a bull with sharp horns;
"muddled in mindfulness" (*muṭṭhassati*) means one whose mindfulness is lost, like a crow that has dropped its food; [what was] done here...
"Here he perishes. "Lacking clear comprehension" means lacking wisdom; it means being devoid of the discernment of the aggregates and so forth.
"Unconcentrated" means not established through access or absorption concentration, like a boat tied in a violent current.

"With wandering mind" means having a restless mind, like a deer that has broken its bonds. "With unrestrained faculties" means having unrestrained sense-faculties, just as a householder looking at his sons and daughters has unrestrained faculties.
*Chavālātaṃ*: a firebrand in a place where corpses have been burned. *Ubhatopadittaṃ majjhe gūthagataṃ*: lit at both ends and smeared with excrement in the middle;
as for its size, it is merely eight finger-breadths long. *Neva gāme*:
for if it were possible to bring it into a village for the sake of yokes, ploughs, rafters, crossbeams, and so forth, it would be for the purpose of wood in the village.
He should spread it out. If it were possible to bring it into a field-hut for the purpose of making a wooden bed, a mat, or a couch, he should spread it out in the forest for the sake of wood.
But since it is not possible in either case, therefore this was said.
"And deprived of the enjoyments of a householder" refers to that wealth which would have been obtainable if the inheritance had been divided by householders living at home.

And from that he falls away. "The goal of recluseship" means the goal of recluseship to be attained by means of mastery of the scriptures and penetration [of their meaning], while remaining within the instruction of one's teachers and preceptors.
Furthermore, the Teacher did not bring forward this simile with reference to one who is immoral;
rather, he brought forward this simile with reference to a person of pure virtue who is nevertheless indolent and afflicted by defects such as covetousness.

Why was it begun with the words, "Monks, there are these three"? It was begun for the purpose of showing that this person's state, which is like a funeral pyre, was created neither by his mother and father nor by his teachers and preceptors, but rather by these evil thoughts.
Or, "signless concentration" refers to insight-concentration (*vipassanā-samādhi*); for that [concentration] arises through the total eradication of signs such as permanence.
It is called "signless. And here, the four foundations of mindfulness are mixed, while signless concentration is their preliminary stage.
Alternatively, it should be understood that signless concentration is mixed, while the foundations of mindfulness are its preliminary stage.
As for the statement, "Bhikkhus, there are these two views," this refers not only to the development of signless concentration itself, but to these [views] as well.
It is stated for the purpose of showing that this leads to the abandoning of the three great thoughts (*mahāvitakka*) and also effects the eradication of the views of eternalism and annihilationism.
"May I not be one who possesses faults" means "may I be faultless. The rest here is self-evident.
Thus, in this sutta as well, the Blessed One concluded his teaching with *arahantship*, having turned away from the three realms of existence.
At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
This is the eighth [chapter]. 9. Commentary on the Pālileyya Sutta: 81.
Regarding the phrase "he set out on a journey": at a time when a dispute had arisen among the bhikkhus of Kosambī, the Teacher one day—
Having brought forward the story of Dīghīti, the King of Kosala, he exhorted them with verses beginning, "For never in this world are enmities stilled by enmity.
On that very day, while they were still quarreling, the night turned to dawn.
On the second day as well, the Blessed One told that same story. And on that day too, while they were still quarreling, the night turned to dawn.
On the third day as well, the Blessed One spoke on that very same matter. Then a certain bhikkhu said to him:
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One dwell at ease, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life;
we shall be known by this quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute. The Teacher said: "Their minds and hearts are consumed..."
Thinking, "These foolish men cannot be persuaded," he reflected, "What have I to do with these?

I shall dwell in solitary wandering. Having attended to his physical needs early in the morning and walked for alms in Kosambī, he set out on his journey alone and without a companion, without taking leave of anyone at all.

"At whatever time, friends"—the Elder said this because today the Blessed One will set out with one bhikkhu, tomorrow with two, the day after with a hundred, the day after that with a thousand, and the day after that alone;
thus the entire pattern of the Blessed One’s movements was known, manifest, and evident to him. Therefore he spoke.
"Gradually" means that, desiring to see a bhikkhu who was living the life of a solitary wanderer while wandering for alms in succession through villages and market towns,

he went to the village of Bālakaloṇakāra. There, after explaining to the elder Bhagu the benefits of the life of a solitary wanderer for the entire afternoon and throughout the three watches of the night, on the following day, with him as his attendant, [he went] for alms.
Having practiced that [meditation] there, he turned back and went to the Eastern Bamboo Deer Park, thinking, "I shall see the three sons of good family living in harmony.
Having also explained to them the benefits of dwelling alone during the entire period after the meal and throughout the three watches of the night,
he turned them back right there and set out alone toward the city of Pārileyyaka.
Gradually he arrived at the city of Pālileyya. Thus it is said: "Wandering by stages on his journey, he came to where Pālileyyaka was.
At the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree:
this refers to a protected grove of forest not far from Pālileyya, where the inhabitants of Pālileyya had given a gift to the Blessed One.
There was a place called Bhaddasāla; having built a leaf-hut for the Blessed One there and obtained his promise, "Dwell here," they settled him.
Now, there was a certain beautiful and excellent *sāla* tree right there.
The Blessed One, depending on that city, dwelt at the foot of that tree near the leaf-hut in that grove. Therefore it is said, "at the foot of the Bhaddasāla."

While the Tathāgata was dwelling there in this manner, a certain great bull elephant—oppressed by the female elephants, the calves, and others during foraging, at river-crossings, and while plunging into water, and feeling weary of the herd—thought, "What use have I for these elephants?
Abandoning the herd, he went toward a human settlement; seeing the Blessed One in the Pālileyyaka forest grove, he approached with a thousand pots of water.
Having become extinguished like one whose fever has been quenched, he stood in the presence of the Teacher.

From that time forth, performing his duties for the Teacher, he provided water for washing the face, brought water for bathing, gave him tooth-sticks, swept the courtyard, and having brought sweet fruits from the forest, he offered them to the Teacher; the Teacher then partook of them.
One day, after walking for a time during the latter part of the night, the Teacher sat down on a stone slab.
An elephant stood nearby in a place not far away. The Teacher looked behind him and saw nothing; likewise he looked ahead and on both sides.
Then the thought arose in him: "How pleasant it would be for me to dwell apart from those who cause strife!"
The elephant, too, thinking, "There are no others who eat the branch I have bent down," and so forth, gave rise to the thought:
"How happy it is that I dwell all alone! I am able to perform the service for the Teacher.
The Teacher, observing his own mind and wondering, "If my mind is such as this, what must the elephant's be like? perceived that it was exactly the same for him as well.
Having seen this, he uttered this inspired exclamation:
“The mind of this elephant meets with the mind of that elephant, the tusker with the tusker, when one delights alone in the forest.”
Then, indeed, a number of bhikkhus— meaning that while the Tathāgata was dwelling there in this manner, five hundred bhikkhus who had completed the rains retreat in various directions,

thinking, "The Teacher, it is said, has dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and entered the forest," and being unable to go into the presence of the Teacher due to their own natural disposition, approached the Venerable Ānanda.
"Immediately after [the path], the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*)" refers to the fruit of arhatship following the path.

"By means of investigation" (*vicaya-sa*) means by means of investigation; the meaning is that it is delimited by knowledge capable of investigating the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of each respective phenomenon (*dhamma*).
"The Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the teaching. "The four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth, refers to those various sections delimited within which the Dhamma has been taught.

It was said for the purpose of explaining these. "Contemplation" (*samanupassanā*) means the contemplation of views (*diṭṭhi-samanupassanā*). "That formation" (*saṅkhāro so*) means that it is a formation consisting of views.
"Born from that" (*tatojo so saṅkhāro*) means that this formation is born from that craving (*taṇhā*).

This [craving] arises even in the four types of consciousness associated with craving. "And that craving" (*sāpi taṇhā*) refers to that craving which serves as the condition for the formation of views.
"That feeling" means that feeling which has become a condition for craving. "That contact" means that contact associated with ignorance which is the condition for feeling.
"That ignorance" means that ignorance associated with contact.
"May I not be, and may nothing be mine": if I were not to exist, my requisites would also not exist.
"But if I were not to exist, and it would not be for me: 'If I myself will not exist in the future, then my requisites too will not exist.
In these points, the Blessed One has come to cause that bhikkhu to relinquish the views he had grasped, both by means of the individual's disposition and by the elegance of his teaching.
"From that, there is this formation" refers to the consciousness associated with craving.
Since doubt itself does not exist [in those four types of consciousness], how can the volitional formation of doubt arise from craving?

It is because it has not been abandoned. For this statement was made with reference to that in whose case the volitional formation arises while craving has not yet been abandoned. This same principle applies to views as well;
for among the four types of consciousness, there is no such thing as a view associated with them. However, because of craving...
Because it has not been abandoned, that [defilement] arises; therefore, with reference to that, this meaning is also applicable there.
Thus, in this sutta, insight is explained as leading to Arahantship through twenty-three stages. The ninth [sutta].
10. Commentary on the Puṇṇama Sutta.
82. “On the tenth day, on that Uposatha,” and so forth, is already explained in detail in the Pavāraṇā Sutta.
Why did he say, “They teach only a little, for some reason; sit down on your own seats and ask whatever you wish”?
It is said that this bhikkhu was accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus. However, while the teacher remained standing, if those bhikkhus were to sit down as they asked questions...
If they stand up, respect is shown toward the Teacher, but disrespect toward the teacher;
if they rise, respect is shown toward the teacher, but disrespect toward the Teacher. Thus their minds will be distracted, and they will not be able to receive the teaching.
However, if they remain seated and ask questions, their minds will be one-pointed.
Knowing that they would be able to receive the teaching, the Blessed One spoke thus. Regarding the phrase "Venerable Sir, are these...":
this elder is the teacher of five hundred bhikkhus; it should not be said that he does not understand even the mere five aggregates.
However, by one who asks the question while knowing thus—"These are the five aggregates of clinging, and none other"—[the answer is given].
It is not fitting to ask as if one were already knowing; therefore, he asks as if he did not know.

Furthermore, his disciples will think, "Our teacher does not say 'I know,' but speaks only after comparing it with the knowledge of omniscience," and thus they will consider what he says worthy of being heard and believed; for these reasons as well, he asks as if he did not know.
"Rooted in desire" means rooted in the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*).
"Monk, clinging is not the same as those five aggregates of clinging"—this was said because mere desire and lust do not constitute the five aggregates.

However, since there is no clinging apart from the aggregates—whether by way of co-nascence or by way of being their object—it is also not the case that clinging exists elsewhere than in the five aggregates of clinging.
"Grasping" has been mentioned. For when a consciousness associated with craving is occurring, the matter produced by that consciousness is the aggregate of matter;
excluding that craving, the remaining immaterial phenomena are the four aggregates. Thus, even from the perspective of co-nascence, there is no grasping apart from the aggregates.
However, grasping takes one of the [aggregates], such as matter and so forth, as its object.
Apart from the five aggregates, there is no clinging, whether by way of arising or by way of object.

"A difference in desire and lust" means a diversity of desire and lust. "In this way, monks" means that because one does not take feeling or any other [aggregate] as the object for the desire and lust directed toward the object of form, there may be a difference in desire and lust. "A designation for the aggregates" means "aggregates."

This is the formal definition (*paññatti*). However, this connection (*anusandhi*) does not fit; yet, even though it does not fit, the question possesses its own connection, and the answer likewise possesses its own connection.

For this Elder asks according to the underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*) of those various monks, and the Teacher also answers according to their respective dispositions. The rest is clear everywhere. The tenth [chapter].
Furthermore, in each sutta of this chapter, five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship.
The eighth chapter, the Khajjanīya-vagga, is concluded.
9. The Theravagga.
1. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta 83.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the Chapter of Elders (*theravagga*): "Mantāṇiputta" means the son of the brahmin woman named Mantāṇī.

"Upādāya" means having come to, having begun with, having referred to, or depending upon. "Asmīti hoti" means that which occurs as "I am"—namely, the threefold proliferation (*papañca*) consisting of craving, conceit, and views.
“Hoti” means there is. “Daharo” means young. “Yuvā” means endowed with youth. “Maṇḍanakajātiko” means one whose nature is for adornment, one whose habit is for adornment.
“Mukhanimittaṃ” means the reflection of the face; for that is perceived in dependence upon a perfectly pure mirror-surface.
But when one looks at it, does one’s own face appear, or another’s face? If it is one’s own...

If it were one's own, it would appear [as such]; if it were another's, it would appear so after having turned away from oneself; and if it were different from oneself in terms of complexion and other qualities, it would appear as something dissimilar.
Therefore, they say that it belongs neither to oneself nor to another, but rather that what appears there is called a "reflected image" (*nibhāsarūpa*) based upon the mirror.
Now, for what reason does that which appears in water appear? It is because of the great elements (*mahābhūtāni*).
Because of its purity. "The Dhamma has been realized by me" means he declared: "By my knowledge, the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths has been fully understood;
I have become a stream-enterer. This is the first. 2.
Commentary on the Tissa Sutta.
84. "In the second [case], it is as if a sweet substance has formed": this means that, having become heavy, it is as if it has lost its functional capacity.
"'The directions do not appear to me either'": he says this to mean that even the directions—such as "this is the east" or "this is the south"—do not manifest to him;
they do not become clear. "'Even the teachings do not occur to me'": even the teachings of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) do not present themselves to him; what has been learned...
He says that what was recited is not seen. "Doubt" here refers to great doubt.
For in him, no such perplexity arises as "Is the Teaching leading to liberation, or is it not? Rather, he thinks:
