"Will I be able to perform the duties of a recluse, or shall I merely carry the bowl and robes?"

"This is a designation for sensual pleasures" means: just as there is a mere beauty to behold in a low-lying pool when one looks down upon it, yet whoever enters therein is dragged away by the presence of fierce fish and brought to ruin and disaster;
even so, there is a mere beauty in the objects of the five strands of sensual pleasure within the domains of the eye-door and the others, yet whoever [enters therein]...
In this context, those who fall into greed are dragged away and cast into the hells and other realms of suffering.

For sensual pleasures provide little gratification but much suffering and much despair; their danger is great. It is with reference to this fact that it is said: "This is a designation for sensual pleasures.
"I favor them" means that I favor them with the gifts of the Dhamma and material goods. "Delighting" means...

He accepted it. Not only did he rejoice, but having received this consolation from the Teacher, by striving and exerting himself, he established himself in Arahatship within a few days. This is the second [sutta].
3. Commentary on the Yamaka Sutta.

85. Regarding the third "wrong view" (*diṭṭhigata*): if it were to occur to him thus, "Formations (*saṅkhārā*) both arise and cease, and the occurrence of formations itself becomes non-occurrence," then it would not be called a wrong view;
it would be knowledge pertaining to the Dispensation (*sāsana*). However, because he held that "the being (*satto*) is annihilated and perishes," it is therefore a wrong view.
The name was born [from this]. "By the force of their views and by the misapprehension of their views" means:

just as when a border region is in revolt, royal officers unable to pacify it go into the presence of the commander-in-chief or the king, so too, when that Elder had become angry due to their adherence to wrong views...
Being unable to quell that [dispute], those bhikkhus approached the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma to the Dhamma King.

Unable to utter the words "It was explained thus" directly in the presence of the Elder—just as he had been unable to do in the presence of those bhikkhus—he spoke them with a sinking heart: "It was explained thus. [The Buddha asked: "What do you think, friend?"
Having heard these words of his, the Elder thought, "This man does not see the fault in his own tenets;
I shall make it clear to him through a teaching on the Dhamma. Thinking thus, he began to deliver a teaching consisting of three turnings.
"What do you think, friend Yamaka, 'Is form the Tathāgata'?"—for what reason was this begun? It was for the sake of the sequence of inquiry.
For the purpose of causing [the Elder] to give [the answer]. For at the conclusion of the teaching consisting of three rounds, the Elder became a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

Then, in order to cause him to undertake the practice of inquiry, the Blessed One said, "What do you think? and so forth. "Tathāgata" refers to a sentient being. He asks: "Do you regard these five aggregates—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—collectively as the 'Tathāgata'?"
And here, "you, friend," is the locative case used for the Elder’s inquiry. This is what is meant:
"And here, in these many instances, when beings are not apprehended as real or as stable even in this very life (diṭṭheva dhamme).
"If that is so, friend"—this he asks because he wishes to have him explain something else. "That which is suffering has ceased. That which...
The meaning is: "They would answer thus: 'Suffering has ceased; there is no other being called "one who ceases".
"For the sake of this very matter" means for the sake of this first path. "For the sake of further knowledge" means for the sake of exceeding measure of knowledge;
that is to say, for the sake of the manifestation of the three subsequent paths together with insight.
"Endowed with protection" means possessed of both internal and external protection. "Desiring security from bondage" means not desiring a state of safety from the four bonds (*yoga*).
"Having overcome" means having subdued or conquered. "Having intruded" means having entered within. Regarding "one who rises early" and so forth:
seeing [the teacher] coming even from afar, one rises from one's seat earlier than [he does]; thus, one is "one who rises early."
Having given him a seat, he falls down behind him once he is seated; thus he is "one who falls behind" (*pacchānipātī*).
Rising early in the morning, he says, "So many go to plow; so many go to sow," and he rises before everyone else;
thus he is "one who rises early" (*pubbuṭṭhāyī*). In the evening, when everyone has gone to their respective dwelling places, he provides protection all around the house.
Having prepared the doors and having closed them, he is one who lies down last even after everyone else has lain down;

thus, he is "one who lies down last" (*pacchānipātī*). "What shall I do, noble son? What shall I do, noble son?"—thus, looking at his face, he gives his assent to whatever is to be done; thus, he is "one who assents to what is to be done" (*kiṅkārapaṭissāvī*).
He conducts himself agreeably, thus he is "one of agreeable conduct" (*manāpacārī*). He speaks kindly, thus he is "one of kind speech" (*piyavādī*). One would trust him even as a friend.
"He will come as my friend"—one should believe this. "He would gain confidence" means that by sharing food, drink, and so forth, he would become trustworthy.
"Well-confided in" means thoroughly confident.
"In the same way" refers here to this application of the simile: for just like the son of a foolish householder when he was dependent on the cycle of existence...

The uninstructed worldling is like a murderer or an enemy; the five aggregates are weak and frail, like the murderer or enemy when he approaches with the thought, "I shall attend upon the foolish son of a householder.
At the moment of rebirth-linking, the five aggregates have approached him just as that murderer has approached.
For the worldling who clings to the cycle of existence, it is like the time when he does not realize, "This is not my friend; this is a murderer and an adversary."
The time when one does not grasp the five aggregates as "these are not mine," but instead grasps them as "form is mine, feeling is mine, perception is mine,
formations are mine, consciousness is mine"— this is like the time when one, having taken a murderous enemy as "this is my friend," shows him honor; it is the time when,
having grasped the five aggregates as "these are mine," one provides them with bathing, food, and so forth.
The time for showing honor is like the severing of the head with a sword while one is still being honored, even though one knows, "This person is overly trusting of me";
in the same way, the exhaustion of the life of a foolish worldling who is trusting should be understood as occurring through the breaking of his own aggregates by sharp [arrows].
*Upeti* means he approaches. *Upādiyati* means he grasps. *Adhiṭṭhāti* means he resolves. "*Attā me*" means this...

‘This is my self. But, friend, the learned noble disciple—just as a wise householder’s son, recognizing an approaching enemy as ‘this is my enemy,’ remains vigilant, performs his various duties, avoids harm, and achieves his welfare—likewise, the learned noble disciple [recognizes]: ‘Form is not my self.’
By means of the method beginning with the words, “He regards [them]...,” one does not grasp at the five aggregates as “I” or “mine.

Knowing, “These are my enemies,” and applying oneself to insight (vipassanā) by way of the sevenfold sets of form and the sevenfold sets of the formless, one avoids the suffering arising from that source and attains the supreme fruit of Arahantship. The rest here is self-evident. The third [section].
4. Commentary on the Anurādha Sutta 86.
In the fourth [sutta], "in a forest hut" means in a leaf-hut at the edge of that very monastery.
"The Tathāgata" refers to your Teacher, the Tathāgata; "that being, the Tathāgata. "Apart from these" means, it is said, that he [Anurādha] thought thus:
[He thought]: "These are adversaries and opponents of the Teaching; as they speak, so will the Teacher not prescribe it, but he will prescribe it otherwise.

Therefore he spoke thus. When this was said, those other sectarians—meaning when the Elder had spoken thus without knowing his own system and that of others, yet knowing the system of the Teaching in part—[replied to] the Elder...
Desiring to point out a fault in the debate, those wanderers of other sects said this to the Venerable Anurādha.
Having heard his words, the Teacher thought: "This monk does not recognize the fault in his own doctrine;
however, he is diligent and devoted to practice. I shall make him understand through a teaching on the Dhamma. He then said to him: "What do you think, Anurādha?"
Desiring to give a teaching consisting of three turnings, he said, "What do you think, Anurādha? and so forth.
Then, as the Venerable Anurādha had attained Arahatship through that teaching, [the Blessed One] applied the duty of questioning to him, saying, "What do you think, Anurādha? Is form the Tathāgata?
and so forth. He declared, "I proclaim both suffering and the cessation of suffering," meaning both the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*) and...
I proclaim the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra as nibbāna. By the word "suffering," the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) is grasped;
when that is grasped, the truth of the origin (samudayasacca) is necessarily grasped as well, because it is the root of that [suffering].

By the word "cessation," the truth of cessation (nirodhasacca) is grasped; when that is grasped, the truth of the path (maggasacca) is necessarily grasped as well, because it is the means to that [cessation].
Thus, Anurādha, he shows that both in the past and now, it is only the Four Noble Truths that I proclaim.
In this way, the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) alone are explained in this sutta. The Fourth. 5. Commentary on the Vakkali Sutta.

87. "In the potter's dwelling" means in the potter's workshop. It is said that after the Elder had completed his rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, he was coming to see the Blessed One.
A severe illness arose in him midway through the city, and his feet could no longer carry him.
Then they brought him to the potter's workshop on a litter-bier. And that workshop was their workroom, not—
A dwelling hall. It was with reference to this that it was said, "He dwells in the potter's dwelling.
"Very ill" means extremely sick. "He bowed all around" means he showed respect by way of prostration. It is said that this is the proper conduct:
even one who is very ill, upon seeing an elder, should show respect by way of rising. Therefore...
However, one should say, "Do not move, do not move. Regarding the phrase "These seats are ready":

during the Buddha’s time, at the dwelling place of even a single bhikkhu, a seat was always prepared with the thought, "If the Teacher should come, he will sit here"—be it even a mere wooden plank or a simple spread of leaves. "Is it endurable? Is it sustainable?"—how is it?
He asks whether one is able to endure suffering or to maintain one's posture. "Turning back" means they retreat. "Advancing" means they approach.

"Retreat is theirs" means retreat belongs to them. "He does not reproach [them] regarding virtue" means he does not reproach them on account of virtue or by way of their virtuous nature. "I have been long-familiar" means I am long-familiar; from long ago.
This is the meaning. "With this putrid body": the Blessed One spoke thus regarding his own gold-colored body in the sense that it is constantly oozing.
"But he who, Vakkali, sees the Dhamma..."—here the Blessed One demonstrates the nature of the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya), as stated in the passage: "The Tathāgata, Great King, is the Dhamma-body.
For the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is indeed called the "body" of the Tathāgata.
Now, beginning the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma in its three turnings, he said, "What do you think? and so forth.

"Kāḷasila" refers to the Kāḷasīla Monastery. "For the sake of liberation" means for the sake of the liberation of the Path. "Being well-liberated, he will be liberated" means that having been liberated by the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship, he will be liberated [further].
It is said that those deities [thought], "By whatever method this [Elder] has begun insight..."
Knowing that he would attain *arahantship* without obstacle, they spoke thus. "Not evil" means blameless. "He drew the knife":

it is said that the elder was conceited; not perceiving the manifestation of defilements—which had been suppressed by concentration and insight—he became convinced, "I am one whose taints are destroyed," and thought, "What is the use of this painful life for me?"
Thinking, “I shall die by drawing a weapon,” he cut his windpipe with a sharp blade.

Then, painful sensations arose within him. At that moment, realizing his own state as an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*), and because he had not neglected his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he quickly took up his primary meditation subject and, while contemplating it, attained *arahantship* and passed away. (The Reviewing)
And what was his discourse? For one whose taints are destroyed, not all nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge are necessarily obtained;
however, even while one's head is being cut off with a sharp sword, one or two knowledges necessarily arise.
"Vivattakkhandhaṃ" means with the shoulders turned over. "Semānaṃ" means lying down. It is said that the Elder was lying on his back.
He drew his sword. His body remained exactly as it had been; however, his head turned to the right side and remained so.
For noble disciples (ariyasāvaka) generally pass away on their right side.
Therefore, while his body remained exactly as it was, his head remained turned toward the right side. With reference to this:
They also say that one who has been born is called "one whose aggregates have turned back" (*vivattakkhandha*). "Fuming" (*dhūmāyitatta*) means the state of fuming.
"Misting" (*timirāyitatta*) means the state of misting; the meaning is like a cloud of smoke and like a cloud of mist.
This is the fifth [sutta]. 6. Commentary on the Assaji Sutta.
88. In the sixth [case], "in the Kassapa Monastery" means in the monastery built by the merchant chief Kassapa. "Bodily formations" refers to inhalation and exhalation.
For he dwelt having repeatedly stilled those [formations] through the fourth jhāna. "It occurs thus" means that now, for one who does not attain that concentration, it occurs thus:
"I am not falling away"—that is, "Could it be that I..."
"Am I falling away from the Teaching? It is said that due to the fault of his illness, his attainments (samāpatti) repeatedly slipped away;
therefore, he thought thus. "Those who hold concentration as the essence and concentration as the core" means they consider concentration alone to be both the essence and the core.
"But in my Teaching, this is not the essence; insight, the path, and the fruits are the essence. You, however, [rely] on concentration...
"Why did you think, 'I am falling away from the Dispensation'?
Having thus comforted the Elder, the Teacher now began his Dhamma teaching with its three turnings, saying, "What do you think? and so forth.
Then, showing the constant abiding of the Elder who had attained Arahantship at the conclusion of that teaching with its three turnings, he said, "If he feels a pleasant feeling," and so forth.
In this context, "he understands as not delighting": while there may be delight in a pleasant feeling, how can there be delight in a painful feeling?
Upon encountering pain, one longs for pleasure; to the very extent that one longs for pleasure, to that same extent one longs for pain.
For it is through the change of pleasure that pain inevitably arrives; thus, there is delight even in pain.
[These things] are to be understood. The remainder is exactly as explained previously.
This is the sixth [discourse]. 7. Commentary on the Khemaka Sutta 89.

In the seventh [discourse], "belonging to self" (*attaniya*) refers to the collection of requisites belonging to oneself. "The notion 'I am' has been attained" means that the notion "I am" occurs in such a manner.
Craving and conceit were overcome. "By running about" means by going back and forth again and again.
"He approached" means he went from the Badarika monastery to Ghosita’s monastery, a distance of one *gāvuta*.
But the Elder Dāsaka traveled that two-yojana distance on that very day by going back and forth four times. Why, then, did they send him? Because he was renowned...
“We shall listen to the Dhamma from the presence of the Dhamma-preacher. Why did they not go themselves?
Because the forest where the Elder resided was crowded and confined; there was no space there for as many as sixty elders to stand or sit.
And why did they not send word, saying, “Come here and preach the Dhamma to us”? [Because] of the Elder...
Because of his illness. But why did they send him again and again? [Thinking], "Having understood for himself, he will come to tell us.
And the Elder also went only after understanding their intention.
"I am not form, friends"—for he who says "I am form" alone [does not see] the other four aggregates.
They are renounced. When one speaks apart from form, by that very act form is renounced.
The same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well. However, because the Elder had attained the notion "I am" even regarding the five aggregates as a unified whole, he spoke thus.
"Hoteva" means "it certainly exists. "Anusahagata" means subtle. "Ūse" means in alkaline ash. "Khāre" means in alkaline salt. "Sammadditvā" means having moistened and soaked.
"Even so," it is said; here is the application of the simile: the mental conduct of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) is like the soiled cloth;

the three contemplations (*anupassanā*) are like the three alkaline substances; and the mental conduct of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), established after being rubbed by the teaching, is like the cloth washed with the three alkalines;
while the odors of salt-earth and so forth still remaining are like the defilements to be abandoned by the path of arahantship.

The defilements are like a basket of perfumes; just as the odors of salt and so forth that accompany it are completely eliminated upon reaching the perfume-basket, so too is there the destruction of all defilements by means of the path of arahantship.
And just as one who has put on cloth scented with perfume wanders through the streets on festival days smelling sweetly of that fragrance, such is the case for the one whose taints are destroyed.
For one who perfumes the ten directions with the fragrance of virtue and so forth, there is freedom of action according to one’s wish.
To "explain" (ācikkhitum) means to speak; to "teach" (desetum) means to reveal; to "make known" (paññāpetum) means to cause to understand;

to "establish" (paṭṭhapetum) means to cause to be firmly established; to "open up" (vivaritum) means to make open; to "analyze" (vibhajitum) means to make well-analyzed; to "clarify" (uttānīkātum) means...

To make it clear. Regarding "about sixty elder monks": it is said that at each point where the Elder spoke, they established insight (*vipassanā*) and, by reflecting further and further, attained *arahantship* at the conclusion of the teaching.
The Elder, too, did not speak by any other method but spoke with a mind accompanied by insight (*vipassanā-sahagata-citta*). Therefore, he also attained *arahantship*.
Therefore it was said: “The minds of sixty elder bhikkhus were liberated from the taints through non-clinging, as was the mind of the Venerable Khemaka. This is the seventh [sutta].
8. Commentary on the Channa Sutta.
90. In the eighth [case], the Venerable Channa was born on the same day as the Tathāgata.
Having gone forth together with him on the day of the Great Renunciation, he later went forth again in the presence of the Teacher.
Being thus both contemptuous and arrogant, thinking "The Buddha is ours; the Dhamma is ours," he harassed his fellow celibates with harsh speech.
The Elder was doing so. "Taking his key" means having taken his lock.
"Going from monastery to monastery" means having entered one monastery, then another, and then another; thus, having approached this or that monastery by way of various monasteries, he said this:
"May they exhort me. Why did he do so with such great enthusiasm here and there?
"Having gone, why did he say this? It was because of his arising sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
For when the Teacher had passed away, the Venerable Ānanda, dispatched by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, went to Kosambī and imposed the "divine penalty" (*brahmadaṇḍa*) upon him.
When the divine penalty had been imposed, he became consumed with fever, fell unconscious, and upon regaining consciousness and rising again, he went into the presence of a certain bhikkhu.
He did not say anything to him. He went to another, but he too did not speak with him.

Having wandered thus through the entire monastery, he became despondent; taking his bowl and robes, he went to Bārāṇasī, and being moved by a sense of spiritual urgency, he went here and there and spoke thus:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" means all conditioned phenomena of the three planes are impermanent. "All phenomena are non-self" means all phenomena of the four planes are non-self.

Thus, while instructing the Elder, all those monks spoke only of two characteristics—the characteristic of impermanence and the characteristic of non-self—and did not speak of the characteristic of suffering. Why was that?
Thus, it seems, they thought: "If this monk proclaims the characteristic of suffering, he might grasp at the notion that 'form is suffering...
consciousness is suffering; the path is suffering, the fruit is suffering—therefore you monks have fallen into suffering.
We shall speak so as to leave him entirely blameless, ensuring that he cannot grasp such a notion."
They spoke of two characteristics.
"Agitation arises as clinging" means that both agitation and clinging arise.
"The mind turns back, thinking, 'Now who indeed is my self? means: if even one among form and the other aggregates is not-self, then who indeed is my self?
Thus he turns back, thinking, "This is my mind. It is said that this elder established insight (vipassanā) without having secured the requisite conditions;

that weak insight, being unable to overcome his grasping at a self, became agitated by the view of annihilation—thinking, "I shall be cut off, I shall perish"—as conditioned phenomena appeared to him as empty.
And it became a condition for him. Seeing himself as if falling into a precipice, he said, "Agitation and clinging arise;
the mind turns back; so who, indeed, is my self? But this does not happen to one who sees the Dhamma;
that is to say, it does not happen to one who sees the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "To that extent there was negligence."
"How much confidence can there be? Having heard his words, "I am face-to-face with him," the Elder thought, "What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for him?
While reflecting thus, he examined the entire word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas and saw the Kaccāna Sutta.
He perceived that this sutta, having first untied the knots of views, then in the middle illustrated the power of the Buddha, and finally [explained] the subtle and delicate nature of conditions...
Thinking, "He has gone away while making [the Dhamma] clear; I shall teach this to him," he spoke the words beginning with "In my presence" (*sammukhā me tan*), demonstrating this.
The eighth [sutta]. 9–10. Commentary on the Rāhula Sutta and others:

The ninth and tenth [suttas] have their meaning already explained in the *Rāhula-saṃyutta*. They have been included here solely because they belong to this "Thera-vagga" (Chapter of Elders). The ninth and tenth [suttas].
The Ninth Chapter: The Chapter on Elders (Theravagga).
10. The Chapter on Flowers (Pupphavagga). 1. Explanation of the Discourse on the River (Nadīsuttavaṇṇanā).
93. In the first chapter of the *Pupphavagga*: "Mountain-born" (*pabbateyyā*) means flowing from a mountain.

"Carrying away" (*ohārinī*) means that it carries down grass, leaves, wood, and so forth, as they fall into its current. "Far-reaching" (*dūraṅgamā*) means that, starting from the place where it issues forth, it travels four or five hundred *yojanas*.

"Swift-flowing" (*sīghasotā*) means having a violent current. "Kāsa" and the others are all species of grass. "Trees" (*rukkhā*) refers to weak trees such as the castor-oil plant (*eraṇḍa*) and others.
“They would hang over him” means that even those trees growing on the bank would bend down and hang over him with their tips touching the water;
the meaning is that they would hang above him. “They would crumble away” means they would fall upon his head together with the root-clay.
Being overwhelmed by them, as the sand, clay, and water enter his mouth, he would meet with great destruction.
"Even so," it is said here: the foolish worldling dependent on the cycle of existence is to be seen like the man who fell into the stream;
the five weak aggregates are like the *kāsa* grass and the rest on both banks;

and the grasping of those aggregates by the foolish worldling—who, like that man, does not know, "These will not be able to carry me across even if they are seized"—thinking, "These aggregates are not my companions."
Just as a man meets with disaster because of the decay of things he has grasped when he takes them up with four grips without understanding, so too,
it should be understood that the foolish worldling meets with the disaster of sorrow and the like due to the transformation of the aggregates grasped by the four grips. First.
2. Commentary on the Puppha Sutta 94.

In the second [verse], "he disputes" means that he disputes with one who speaks according to reality, saying "it is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul," by saying "it is permanent, pleasant, self, and beautiful. "Worldly phenomena" refers to the five aggregates.
For that is called a "worldly phenomenon" (lokadhamma) because its very nature is to perish. "What shall I do? means "How shall I act?
He shows that while the mere explanation of the practice is my burden, the fulfillment of the practice is the burden of noble sons (kulaputta).
In this sutta, three worlds are mentioned. For in the passage, "I am not [in conflict] with the world, monks," the world of sentient beings (sattaloka) is mentioned.

In the passage, “Bhikkhus, there is in the world the worldly nature,” the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*) is intended; in the passage, “The Tathāgata was born in the world, grew up in the world,” the world as space (*okāsa-loka*) is spoken of. This is the second [point].
3. Commentary on the Phena-piṇḍa Sutta (The Simile of the Lump of Foam).

95. On the third occasion, on the bank of the river Gaṅgā, the inhabitants of Ayujjha, seeing the Tathāgata—who was wandering on tour with an immeasurable retinue of bhikkhus—arrive at their city, prepared a dwelling for the Teacher in a location adorned by a great forest grove at a place where the Gaṅgā turns back and gave it to him. The Blessed One resided there.
It was with reference to this that it was said, "on the bank of the river Gaṅgā. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

while dwelling in that monastery, the Blessed One emerged from the Gandhakuṭi in the evening and, sitting on the excellent Buddha-seat prepared on the bank of the Gaṅgā, saw a large mass of foam coming down the river Gaṅgā and [thought], "In my teaching, that which is based on the five aggregates..."
Thinking, “I shall teach one Dhamma,” he addressed the monks who were sitting there surrounding him.

“A great mass of foam”: starting from the size of a ripe jujube fruit, it gradually increased through successive stages as it moved downstream with the current until it became as large as a mountain peak, wherein many creatures such as water-snakes and others [dwell].
They dwell upon such a great mass of foam. “Would bring” means he would carry it away. Now, this mass of foam breaks up at the very place where it arises;

it may break after traveling a short distance, or after going far—by way of one or two leagues—and even if it does not break in between, it must inevitably break upon reaching the great ocean. “Would contemplate” means he would look upon it.
"One should examine it thoroughly" means one should examine it by way of reason.
"For what essence could there be in a lump of foam?"—monks, what indeed would be called an essence in a lump of foam? It would simply dissolve and fall apart.
"In the same way" means that just as a lump of foam is without essence, so too is form devoid of any permanent essence, any enduring essence, or any essence of a self.

It is indeed without core. And just as that [piece of wood] cannot be taken up with the thought, "I shall make a bowl or a saucer from this," and even if it were taken up, it would not serve that purpose but would simply break apart;
in the same way, form cannot be grasped as permanent, stable, as "I," or as "mine. Even if it is grasped, it does not remain as such; it is impermanent and suffering.
"It is non-self and indeed unattractive"—thus it is exactly like a mass of foam.

Or again, just as a mass of foam is perforated here and there, composed of many joints, and is a dwelling place for many creatures such as water-snakes, so too form is perforated here and there, composed of many joints;
herein, by way of its constituent parts, eighty families of worms dwell. That very same [form]...
For them, there is even a birth-chamber, a latrine, a sick-room, and a cemetery; they do not go elsewhere to perform the delivery of a child and so forth.
In this way too, it is like a lump of foam.
And just as a lump of foam, having initially been the size of a ripe jujube fruit, gradually becomes even the size of a mountain peak, [so too is the body].

Thus, even such a form as this, having initially been merely a *kalala*, gradually becomes the size of a fathom for cows, buffaloes, elephants, and so forth, or the size of a mountain peak for fish, turtles, and the like, or even hundreds of yojanas in measure;
and yet it is like a lump of foam. And just as a lump of foam breaks up immediately upon rising, or after traveling only a short distance, [so too is this body].
Even after traveling far and reaching the ocean, it inevitably breaks apart; in the same way, form also breaks apart at the stage of the *kalala*, and at the stages of the *abbuda* and so forth.
Even if it does not break in the interim, once it reaches the hundredth year for those with a lifespan of a hundred years, it inevitably breaks apart;
at the mouth of death, it becomes a mere powder and dust. Thus, too, it is like a mass of foam.

For what could be the essence of feeling, monks? In such passages as these, the similarity of feelings and the other aggregates to bubbles and the like should be understood. Just as a bubble is without essence, so too is feeling.
And just as it is weak, ungraspable, and impossible to take hold of it to make a raft or a seat—even when grasped, it simply breaks apart—so too is feeling.
"Ungraspable" means that it is not possible to grasp it as "permanent" or "stable";
even when grasped, it does not remain as such. Thus, although ungraspable, feeling is like a bubble.
Just as a bubble arises and breaks in each drop of water and does not endure for long, so too does feeling arise.
It breaks up and does not endure for long; having arisen within the duration of a single finger-snap, it ceases after numbering one hundred thousand times ten million moments.

And just as a bubble arises dependent upon four causes—the surface of the water, a drop of water, the froth of the water, and the gathering wind—so too does feeling arise dependent upon the physical basis and the object.
It arises dependent upon four causes: the mire of defilements and the impact of contact. Thus, feeling is like a bubble.
Perception, too, is like a mirage in its lack of substance; likewise, it is so in its ungraspability.
For it is not possible to take hold of it to drink from, bathe in, or fill a vessel with. Moreover, just as a mirage quivers, surging with waves...
Just as it appears [as water], so too perception— divided into the categories of blue-perception and so forth—
quivers and vibrates for the purpose of experiencing blue and the rest. And just as a mirage deceives the multitude, making them say, "It looks like a full pond,
it looks like a full river," so too perception deceives, making them say, "This is blue, beautiful, pleasant, and permanent."
The same method applies to the yellow and other colors as well. Thus, perception (saññā) is like a mirage because it deceives.

"Not grown crooked" means that no dense fibers have developed within. Formations (saṅkhārā) are also like the trunk of a plantain tree in their lack of core substance, and likewise in their being ungraspable.
For just as it is impossible to take anything from a plantain trunk to use for rafters and so forth—

Just as it is impossible to bring a plantain trunk to serve a purpose, and even when brought there, it does not remain so; in the same way, the aggregates of formations cannot be grasped as permanent and so forth, and even when grasped, they do not remain so.

And just as a plantain trunk is a collection of many layers of leaves, so too the aggregate of formations is a collection of many phenomena. And just as a plantain trunk possesses various characteristics.
For the color of the outer layer of a plantain trunk is one thing, and that of the successively inner layers is another;

even so, within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), the characteristic of contact is one thing, and that of volition and the rest is another, yet when taken together they are called the "aggregate of mental formations. Thus, too, the aggregate of mental formations is like the trunk of a plantain tree.
"A man with eyes" means one who possesses eyes by way of two types of vision: the fleshly eye and the wisdom-eye.
For his fleshly eye must be pure, free from cataracts and film; and his wisdom-eye must be capable of seeing the lack of essence.
Consciousness, too, is like an illusion in the sense of being without essence, and likewise in the sense of being ungraspable. And just as an illusion is transient...
Consciousness has quick manifestation; thus is consciousness. For it is even more fleeting and more quickly manifest than that [body].
Indeed, by that very mind, a person appears as if coming, as if going, as if standing, and as if sitting.
Furthermore, the mind at the time of coming is one thing, while at the times of going and so forth, it is another. In this way, too, consciousness is like an illusion. And the illusion—
He deceives the multitude by making them take up whatever he says is "gold, silver, or pearl. Consciousness also deceives the multitude;

for with that very same consciousness, it makes one appear as if coming, as if going, as if standing, or as if sitting, and causes one to take hold [of the object]. Furthermore, the consciousness at the time of coming is one thing, while the consciousnesses during going and so forth are another. Thus too...
Consciousness is like an illusion.
"By one of vast wisdom" means by one possessing both subtle wisdom and expansive, extensive wisdom. "Life-span" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
"Heat" refers to the fire-element born of karma. "Food for others" means having become food for various kinds of swarms of worms and so forth. Such is this [consciousness].
“Lineage” (santāna) means this succession which is struck down from the dead as far as the cemetery.
“This is a deception that deceives the foolish” means that this so-called aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) is called a deception that leads the foolish masses astray.

“The murderer” means that this [aggregate] termed the aggregates is a murderer for two reasons: both by way of mutual destruction among themselves, and because as long as the aggregates exist, there is death.
It is also evident as follows: for when the earth element breaks up, it breaks up only while taking the remaining elements along with it; likewise for the water element and the others.

And when the aggregate of material form breaks up, it breaks up only while taking the immaterial aggregates along with it; likewise, among the immaterial aggregates, feeling and the others [break up] while taking perception and the others along with them.
These four [aggregates] are also the "basis-form" (*vatthurūpa*); thus, there is here a mutual support.

The state of being a slayer is to be understood. Since killing, binding, cutting, and so forth are possible when the aggregates exist, the state of being a slayer is to be understood through the fact that these [aggregates] constitute the very nature of being slain.
"Every fetter" refers to all ten kinds of fetters. "The deathless state" is Nibbāna. This is the third [chapter].
4–6. Commentary on the *Gomayapiṇḍasutta*, etc. (96–98).
In the fourth [sutta], "eternal as the world" (*sassatisama*) means equal to those things that are eternal, such as Mount Sineru, the great earth, the moon, the sun, and so forth.
"A small ball of cow dung" (*parittaṃ gomayapiṇḍaṃ*) refers to a tiny fragment of cow dung, about the size of a *madhuka* flower. But from where did he get this?
"Obtained. According to some, this means "taken from what was brought for the purpose of making a border.

However, it should be understood as having been fashioned by supernormal power (*iddhi*) and placed upon the hand for the purpose of making the meaning known. "The acquisition of a personal existence" (*attabhāvapaṭilābho*) means a personal existence that has been acquired.
"This dwelling in the holy life would not be discerned" means that this so-called dwelling in the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariyavāsa*) would not be discerned.
For the Path arises turning away from the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) of the three planes.

And if this much of a personal existence (*attabhāva*) were permanent, then even after the Path had arisen, it would not be possible to turn away from the cycle of conditioned phenomena; thus, the living of the holy life (*brahmacariyavāsa*) would not be known.
Now, if any conditioned phenomenon were permanent, the prosperity experienced by me during the time of King Mahāsudassana—
In order to show that even that [city] would be impermanent, he said, "Bhikkhus, in the past I was a king," and so forth.
Therein, "headed by the royal capital Kusāvatī" means that the royal capital Kusāvatī was the foremost among those cities;
the sense is that it was the most excellent. "Made of heartwood" means made of the heartwood of red sandalwood. As for the cushions, however, they were all made of thread.
"Spread with *goṇaka* wool" means spread with black *ujjola* wool that is more than four finger-breadths thick, which they call "great back-wool.
"Spread with *paṭaka*" means spread with white woolen blankets (*kambala*) made of wool from both sides.
"Spread with *paṭalikā*" means spread with a thick, flower-like woolen covering. "Exquisite spreads of *kadalimiga* deer-skin" means made from the skin of the *kadalimiga* deer.
They were spread with excellent coverlets. It is said that those coverlets were made by spreading out a leopard skin over white cloth, then sewing it together.
"With upper-canopies" means together with an upper canopy, that is, together with a red awning tied above.
"With red pillows on both sides" means with a pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet.
The couches had red cushions at both ends. Regarding the phrase "headed by the Vejayanta chariot":

here, the Vejayanta is the name of that king’s chariot, whose wheel hubs were made of sapphire, whose spokes were made of the seven precious gems, whose rim was made of coral, whose axle was made of silver, whose interior framework was made of sapphire, and whose pole was made of silver. It was for them...
"Foremost of chariots" means the very best. "Dukūla-ropes" refers to mats spread with dukūla cloth. "Brass supports" refers to milking vessels made of silver.
"Thousands of kotis of garments" is said with reference to the garments brought forward at the time he stands after bathing, thinking, "He will use them as he pleases.
"An offering of food" refers to the food that is to be served.

"At that time, I dwell in Yamaka"—meaning, that place where I live is only a single city, while my sons, daughters, and so forth, as well as the male and female servants, lived in the remaining [cities].
The same principle applies to the palaces, gabled houses, and so on.
Among the couches and such, he himself uses only one, while the rest become the property for his sons and others. Among the women, only one attends upon him.
The rest are merely attendants. "Velāmikā" means those born from the womb of a Kṣatriya woman by a Brāhmaṇa, or a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Kṣatriya.

"I wear" indicates that he wears only one pair of garments himself, while the remaining ones belong to the sixteen hundred thousand men, plus eighty thousand more, who move about surrounding him. "I eat" [indicates...]

He shows that by the highest standard, I eat only a measure of cooked rice from a nāḷika-measure, while the remainder belongs to the eight hundred thousand and forty thousand men who wander about surrounding me.
For indeed, a single offering of alms-food (ekathālipāka) suffices for ten people.
Thus, having shown this prosperity during the time of Mahāsudassana, he now demonstrates its impermanence: "Thus..."

He said, "O monks," and so forth. Therein, "transformed" (*vipariṇatā*) means that by abandoning their original nature, they have reached a state of non-designation (*apaṇṇattika*), like an extinguished lamp.
Thus, "O monk, conditioned phenomena are indeed impermanent" means they are impermanent in the sense of not existing after having existed.
At this point, the Blessed One was as if a man who, having built a ladder against a *campaka* tree eighty cubits high and climbed up, [beheld its summit].
Just as one might take a *campaka* flower and descend while letting go of the ladder, even so, as if binding a ladder, he has ascended to the great fortune of Mahāsudassana—
which rises to the height of many hundreds of thousands of millions of years— and having taken hold of the characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇa*) standing at the summit of that fortune,
he has descended like one letting go of the ladder. Thus, "it is unstable" refers to things such as water bubbles and the like.
"Devoid of permanence" means lacking a fixed state. "Thus unreliable" means that, like water drunk in a dream or like sandalwood paste smeared on the body, they are devoid of any true consolation.
Thus, the characteristic of impermanence is explained in this sutta. In the fifth [sutta], everything is exactly according to the method already stated.
The sixth was spoken with reference to the inclination of one who understands in that way. As for the fourth and the others...
7. Commentary on the Gaddulabaddha Sutta 99.
Regarding the seventh [verse], "When the great ocean": at the time when the fifth sun has arisen, the great ocean dries up.
"The making of an end to suffering" refers to those very people who, without having penetrated the Four Truths, remain shrouded by ignorance.
"I do not say there is an end-making or a limit to the suffering of saṃsāra. "A dog tied with a leash" means a dog bound by a leash.
"A large stake" refers to a great stake driven into the earth. "A pillar" refers to a pillar set up after being buried [in the ground].
"In the same way" means here the fool who depends on the cycle of existence is like the dog; the view is like the leash; and self-identity is like the pillar.

Just as a dog tied to a post with a hemp rope revolves around that post, so too should it be understood that an ordinary person (puthujjana), bound to the personality-aggregate (sakkāya) by craving for views, revolves around that personality-aggregate. This is the seventh [sutta].
8. Commentary on the Second Gaddulabaddha Sutta.

100. In the eighth [verse], "therefore" (*tasmā*) means: because the foolish worldling, who depends on the round of existence and is tied to the pillar of individuality by the rope of craving which rests upon the rafters of views, proceeds in all postures supported solely by the five aggregates;
or, because this mind has been defiled for a long time by lust, hatred, and delusion—therefore, "[it is] the defilement of the mind. (*Cittasaṃkilesā*)
For even those beings who have bathed well become defiled by the defilement of the mind alone;
and even those whose bodies are covered in filth are purified through the cleansing of the mind. Thus said the ancients:
"When form is defiled, young men are defiled; when form is pure, they are purified."
"When form is pure, they are purified; this was not fully declared by the Great Seer.
When the mind is defiled, young men are defiled;
when the mind is pure, they are purified—thus it was said by the Great Seer."
“Caraṇa” means mind; it is the wandering mind. “Saṅkhā” refers to Brahmins and heretics;
having constructed a small booth, they have various kinds of success and failure—by way of happy and miserable destinies—inscribed there.
Showing that “by doing this deed one obtains this, by doing that deed one obtains that,” they wander about, seizing hold of that mind.
"By mind alone it is thought": because it is made by thinking through the act of mental fabrication (*cittakāra*), it is called "thought by mind.
"Mind itself is more subtle than mind": the mind that seeks the means for that [previous] mind is even more subtle than that mind.
"Animals are thought by mind alone": they are thought by the very mind of karma. And that mind of karma refers to these quails, partridges, and so forth.

There is no such thing as "exerting" with the thought, "We shall become thus-minded. Rather, it is karma that leads one to a particular mode of birth (yoni); their state of mind is rooted in that birth.
For beings who have entered a particular mode of birth possess minds similar to those belonging to that specific class of birth.
Thus, while the state of mind is established by birth, it should be understood that the mode of birth is established by karma.
Furthermore, this so-called "mind" (citta) should be understood as even more "minded" than the mind of an animal, by virtue of its being co-nascent with the co-nascent states of mind—

namely, through its nature as the plane of mind, the basis of mind, the door of mind, and the object of mind— and by virtue of its producing many kinds of mental states rooted in the diversity of kamma,
such as the diversity of gender, the diversity of perception, and the diversity of conventional expression.
Just as a dyer among clothers produces form through dye, yet an unskilled one produces an unattractive form while a skilled one produces one that is attractive and beautiful to behold—
in the same way, an ordinary person (puthujjana) produces an ugly form, devoid of excellence of the eyes and so forth, by means of an unwholesome mind or a wholesome mind dissociated from knowledge;
whereas [the noble one] produces one endowed with excellence of the eyes and so forth by means of a wholesome mind associated with knowledge.
Beautiful. The eighth [chapter].
9. Commentary on the Vāsijaṭa Sutta. 101.
In the ninth [sutta], "Just as, monks, a hen's eggs..."—these [verses] are according to the dark side and the bright side.
Two similes have been spoken. Of these, the simile on the dark side does not establish the meaning, while the other does.
The meaning of the simile on the bright side should be understood thus: *seyyathā* is a particle used in the sense of a comparison; *api* is used in the sense of possibility.
By both together, he shows: "Just as, monks. A hen [lays] eight or ten or twelve eggs.
Regarding this, although the eggs may be fewer or more than the number stated for a hen, it is expressed in this way for the sake of linguistic elegance;
for such is the elegant usage in the world. "Tānassu" means "tāni assu," which is to say, "they would be.
"Properly incubated by the hen" means that the mother hen has spread out her wings over them.

"Properly laid upon them" means she lay upon them correctly. "Properly incubated" means she caused them to receive warmth from time to time, so that they were thoroughly and completely warmed and heated all over.
"Properly developed" means she caused them to be well-developed all around from time to time; the meaning is that she caused them to take on the scent of a cock. Even though it was that hen...
If that hen, having practiced diligence through these three kinds of actions, were not to have such a desire arise [to hatch],
nevertheless those chicks would still be capable of emerging safely in the manner described.
For they [would be capable] because those eggs were treated by that hen in these three ways.
As they are being nourished, they do not rot; whatever moisture they have also comes to exhaustion.
The skull becomes thin, the tips of the toenails and the beak become rough, and their bodies themselves undergo transformation.
Because the skull has become thin, light from outside is perceived within; therefore, [they think]: "Alas, for a long time we have had our hands and feet cramped!"
Thinking, “We have been lying in a cramped space, yet this light is visible outside; now we shall dwell in comfort here,” they desire to go out.
They strike the skull with their feet and stretch out their necks, whereupon that skull breaks in two.
Then, flapping their wings and crying out according to the occasion, they indeed emerge.
And having emerged, they wander about, adorning the village precincts.
"In the same way" is the application of the simile. This should be understood by correlating it with the meaning as follows:
for just as that hen performs the threefold action upon her eggs, so too does this bhikkhu apply himself to spiritual development (*bhāvānuyoga*).

It is time for application; just as the eggs of a hen do not rot through the performance of the threefold action, so too there is no decline of insight-knowledge for a bhikkhu devoted to the practice of meditation through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation.

And just as the moisture of fresh eggs is exhausted by performing those three actions, so too is the moisture of craving that follows the three realms of existence exhausted for that bhikkhu through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation.
Just as the eggshell becomes thin, so too does the shell of ignorance become thin for that bhikkhu;
just as the claws, beaks, and mouths of chicklets become firm, hard, and sharp, so too does the insight-knowledge of the bhikkhu become sharp, harsh, clear, and courageous;
and just as it is the time for the chicklets to emerge from the egg, so too is it the time for the bhikkhu’s insight-knowledge to reach its culmination.

The time of growth is the time of conception; it is like the time when a chick, having split the eggshell with the tip of its claw or its beak and spread out its wings, emerges safely— so too for that bhikkhu who,
having been caused to conceive the womb of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and moving about, encounters a corresponding suitability of season or a suitability of food.
Or, having obtained what is conducive to a person or what is conducive to hearing the Dhamma, while sitting on the very same seat and increasing insight,

one should understand the time of reaching Arahantship in safety— having burst the shell of ignorance by means of the path to Arahantship attained through successive stages and having shattered the side of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). Just as [one knows] the state of maturity of chicks...
Just as a mother, knowing [the time has come], breaks the eggshell, so too the Teacher, knowing the ripening of the knowledge of such a bhikkhu, says:
"Cut off your own attachment, like an autumnal lotus with the hand;
cultivate only the path to peace, Nibbāna, as taught by the Sugata."
By this method, having pervaded [the world] with light, he strikes the eggshell of ignorance with the verse.
At the conclusion of the verse, having broken the eggshell of ignorance, he attains Arahantship.
From that time forth, just as those chicks roam about there, beautifying the village fields, so too does this one whose taints are utterly destroyed take Nibbāna as his object.
Having entered the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), he wanders about, adorning the monastery.
*Palagaṇḍassa* means of a carpenter. For he is called a *palagaṇḍa* because, holding a *pala*—which is to say a hanging block—he removes the swell (*gaṇḍa*) from the wood.
*Vāsijaṭe* refers to the place where the handle of the adze is grasped. "Indeed, this much... [is the extent].

“Today my taints are exhausted”: for one who has gone forth, the taints are constantly being exhausted through the summary of the going-forth, through recitation, through interrogation, through wise attention, and through the performance of duties.
However, as they are thus being exhausted, there is no such knowledge in him as, “So much was exhausted today, so much yesterday. This is the meaning.
By this simile, the benefit of insight (vipassanā) is illustrated. "In the winter" means during the winter season.
"Subside" means they diminish due to their becoming stable.
"In the same way" refers here to the Teaching (sāsana), which should be regarded as like the great ocean; the practitioner (yogāvacara) as like the ship; and the ship's...

A bhikkhu’s wandering in the presence of his preceptor and teacher during the time he has not yet completed five years of seniority is like the exhaustion [of the ship's provisions] in the great ocean;

the thinning of the fetters for a bhikkhu through the brief summary of the going-forth, as well as through recitation and interrogation, is like the loosening of the rigging of a ship being worn away by the waters of the great ocean. Of the ship—
The time when a monk who has been released from formal dependence takes up a meditation subject and dwells in the forest is like being lifted onto dry land;
the drying up of the moisture of craving by means of insight-knowledge is like being parched by the wind and heat during the day;
the moistening of the mind by the joy and gladness arising in dependence on the meditation subject is like being drenched by frost and water at night; [this occurs] day and night.

Just as the weakness of bonds that have been thoroughly dried by wind and heat and thoroughly moistened by cold water [is revealed when they are stressed], so too, on a certain day, having obtained favorable weather and other conditions, the fetters (saṃyojana) become exceedingly weak through the joy and gladness of the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa).
The knowledge of the path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) is like a rain-cloud; it is like the water from a cloud’s downpour upon the mooring-cable of a ship.

Just as a ship bound for a port of putridity might, after some time, reach its destination, so too for one who has begun insight and is increasing that insight by way of the "sevenfold set of materiality" and so forth—
while the meditation subject is being washed away and swept away— one day, having obtained favorable conditions such as a suitable climate,
attains the fruit of Arahantship while sitting in a single cross-legged posture; this is like the ship reaching its destination after some time.
The remaining of an Arahant who is supporting the great multitude for as long as his lifespan lasts,

and the attainment of the state of non-designation (apaṇṇattika-bhāva) by one whose taints are exhausted— having passed away through the element of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) upon the breaking up of the acquired aggregates (upādiṇṇakkhandha),
just as a boat bound with putrid materials gradually breaks apart and reaches the state of non-designation— by means of this simile [the destruction] of the fetters...

Commentary on the Discourse on the Perception of Impermanence (Aniccasaññāsutta): 102.
In the tenth [discourse], "perception of impermanence" refers to the perception that arises in one who develops [the contemplation] thus: "The impermanent is impermanent. "It consumes" means...
It causes to vanish. "All conceit of 'I am'" refers to the ninefold conceit of "I am. "Roots and continuities" means roots that remain by way of continuity.
For the perception of impermanence is like a great plough, while the defilements are like the small and minute roots and continuities;
just as a farmer, while ploughing, breaks them up with the plough, so too does the yogi [break up the defilements] with the perception of impermanence.
"By developing it, one shatters the defilements through the knowledge of the perception of impermanence"—this is the application of the simile here.

"Shakes off" (*odhunāti*) means he shakes them downward. "Shakes out thoroughly" (*niddhunāti*) means he winnows them away. "Throws off" (*nicchoṭeti*) means having winnowed them away, he discards them.
Here too, the defilements are like the chaff, and the knowledge of the perception of impermanence is like the shaking and throwing off; such is the meaning.
The simile should be connected as follows:
"With its stalk cut" means with its stalk cut by a sharp arrow-head. "They follow after it" means they follow that cluster of mangoes;
as that [cluster] falls, the mangoes fall to the ground. Here too, the defilements are like the cluster of mangoes.
The perception of impermanence is like a sharp arrowhead.

Just as when a mango cluster is cut by an arrowhead, all the mangoes fall to the ground, so too, when ignorance—the root of the defilements—is cut by the knowledge of the perception of impermanence, all defilements go to their destruction. This is the application of the simile.
"Going to the peak" (*kūṭaṅgamā*) means they go to the peak. "Sloping toward the peak" (*kūṭaninnā*) means they are inclined toward the peak by way of entering it.

"Converging at the peak" (*kūṭasamosaraṇā*) means they stand having converged at the peak. Here too, the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) is like the peak, and the wholesome states of the four planes are like the rafters.
Just as the peak is the foremost of all the rafters, so too is the perception of impermanence the foremost of wholesome states. But is it not [the case that...]?
The perception of impermanence is mundane; let it suffice as the foremost among mundane wholesome states. But how is it the foremost among supramundane states?

It should be understood as the foremost even for those [supramundane states] in the sense that it brings about their attainment. By this same method, the application of the similes should be understood in all cases.
Here, however, the function of the perception of impermanence is shown by the first three similes, while its power is shown by the latter ones. The tenth [chapter].

In the first [sutta] of the Rādha Saṃyutta: "Māro vā assa" means there might be death; "māretā vā" means one who is to be killed.
"Or else" (*vā*): "or whoever dies" (*yo vā pana mīyati*) means "or whoever passes away.

"For the sake of disenchantment" (*nibbidatthaṃ*) means for the sake of the knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*). "You have transcended" (*accayāsī*) means you have gone beyond. "Plunged into Nibbāna" (*nibbānogadhaṃ*):
this is called the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*); it is lived within the interior of Nibbāna, but it is not Nibbāna itself.
"Having transcended" is the meaning. "Nibbāna as its consummation" means that Nibbāna is its end, its fulfillment, or its finality; this is the meaning. First [section]. 2–10.

"Possessing" means they create a sense of ownership, thinking, "This is mine, this is mine," and do not even allow others to touch them.

They perform [these tasks]. In the third [verse], "the guide to existence" (*bhavanetti*) means the rope of existence (*bhavarajju*). The fourth is self-evident.
