1. The Chapter on Stream-Entry (Sotāpattivagga) 1. Commentary on the Vāta Sutta (The Wind Discourse) 206.
Regarding the passage in the Saṃyutta Nikāya beginning with "the winds do not blow," etc., it is said that their view was as follows: "Even these [things] such as tree branches..."
The winds blow breaking things apart, yet these are not winds; this is merely a "wind-portion," for the wind stands firm like a pillar of clay or like a mountain peak.
Likewise, as for these rivers that flow carrying grass, wood, and so forth, it is not water that flows here;
this is merely a "water-portion," for the water stands firm like a pillar of clay or like a mountain peak.
And it remains as if fixed. As for those who are called "pregnant women giving birth," although their bellies are withered, the fetus does not actually emerge;
this is merely a trace of a fetus, for the fetus itself remains like a pillar of wood or like a mountain peak.
And even these suns and moons that rise or set—neither of them rise [in the ultimate sense].
“They do not move; this is merely the radiance of the moon and sun, while the moon and sun themselves remain as steady as a pillar of iron or the peak of a mountain.
2–4. Commentary on the *Etam-mama-sutta* and others:
In the phrases beginning with “seen,” etc., the visible object-base (*rūpāyatana*) is what is seen. The sound-base (*saddāyatana*) is what is heard. The odor-base (*gandhāyatana*) is what is sensed.
The sense-base of taste and the sense-base of tangibles are called "sensed" (*muta*), because they are to be grasped upon being reached.
The remaining seven bases are called "cognized" (*viññāta*). "Reached" (*patta*) means reached either by seeking or without seeking.
"Sought" (*pariyesita*) means sought, whether it has been reached or not reached. "Mentally explored" (*anuvicaritaṃ manasā*) means mentally traversed. For in the world...
There is that which is obtained after searching, that which is not obtained after searching, that which is obtained without searching, and that which is not obtained without searching.
Among these, what is obtained after searching is called "obtained"; what is not obtained after searching is called "searched for.
What is obtained without searching and what is not obtained without searching are called "mentally traversed. Then...
Whether one has sought it out or not sought it out, whether it has been obtained or not obtained—in terms of its status as "obtained," it is called "obtained";
what has been sought out but not obtained is called "sought out"; and what has not been sought out and not obtained is called "mentally traversed.
Or rather, all of this is simply mentally traversed.
5. Commentary on the *Natthidinnasutta* 210.
Regarding the phrases "there is no gift" (*natthi dinna*) and so forth: they say "there is no gift" with reference to the absence of fruit for what has been given.
"Sacrifice" (*yiṭṭha*) refers to a great offering. "Oblation" (*huta*) is intended to mean hospitality consisting of food parcels. Both of these [also] lack any fruit whatsoever.
They reject [the teachings] by means of intentional ambiguity (*sandhāya*). "Of good and bad deeds" (*sukatadukkaṭānaṃ*) means of good and bad deeds;
the meaning is of wholesome and unwholesome [actions]. "There is no fruit, there is no result" (*phalaṃ vipāko*): they say that whatever is called "fruit" or "result" does not exist.
"This world does not exist": for one situated in the next world, this world does not exist. "The next world does not exist": even for one situated in this world [the next world does not exist].
They teach that there is no other world, and that all beings are annihilated right there and then.
They say there is no mother and no father, speaking thus because they maintain that there is no fruit for either right or wrong conduct toward them.
They say there are no spontaneously born beings, meaning they claim there are no beings who arise after passing away from one state. They say there are no recluses or brahmins in the world...
They say that in the world there are no ascetics or brahmins who have entered upon the right practice.
"Consisting of the four great elements" means made up of the four great elements. "Earth, the earth-body" refers to the internal earth element and the external earth element.
"Follows after" means it goes along with; "approaches" is a synonym for that, as is "follows."
The meaning is: they show that by both [means] one approaches and goes toward [it]. This same method applies to the words *āpādi* and so forth as well.
"Faculties" (*indriyāni*) refers to the faculties with the mind as the sixth. "Transmigrating" means they leap into space.
"With the couch as the fifth" means with the reclining bed as the fifth; the meaning is: the bed itself and the four men standing while holding the four legs of the bed. Up to...

“Āḷāhana” means as far as the cemetery. “Footprints” (padāni) refers to the words concerning virtues and faults that proceed in such a manner as: “This one was thus virtuous,” or “Thus he was immoral.
Alternatively, it is intended here that the body itself is what is meant by “footprints. “Kāpotaka” means pigeon-colored; the meaning is that they have the color of a dove’s wing.
“Bhassanta” means ending in ashes. Or rather, this is the very reading of the text: “āhutiyoti.”
Whatever gift has been given, whether in the form of presents, honors, and so forth, all of that ends with the ashes;
the meaning is that it does not continue beyond that to yield fruit. "Dattupaññattaṃ" means established by *dattu*-men, that is, foolish people.
This is what is meant: this gift was established by fools who lack wisdom, not by the wise.
They show that fools give and the wise take.
6. Commentary on the Sutta on Doing (Karoto-sutta) 211.
"Doing" means doing with one's own hand. "Causing to do" means causing another to do by command. "Cutting" refers to [cutting] others'.
"Of one who cuts off hands and so forth" means [of one] cutting them off. "Causing to cut" means causing others to cut them off. "Cooking" means oppressing with a stick.

"Causing to cook" means causing others to oppress with sticks and so forth. "Grieving and causing to grieve" means both personally causing grief to another by such acts as stealing their goods, and also causing others to do so.
"Fatiguing and causing to fatigue" means [by acts] such as depriving of food, imprisonment, and so forth.

"Whether causing oneself to suffer or causing others to suffer"; "while trembling or causing another to tremble" means while one is oneself trembling at the time of trembling, or while causing another who is trembling to tremble;
"while taking life or causing life to be taken" means while killing a living being or causing it to be killed.
Thus, in all instances, the meaning should be understood by way of both doing and causing to be done.
"Household junction" (*sandhi*) means the junction of a house. "Robbery" (*nillopa*) means a great plundering. "House-breaking" (*ekāgārika*) means plundering by surrounding a single house.
"Standing at the crossroads" (*paripantho tiṭṭhati*) means standing on the road for the purpose of seizing those who come along.
"Evil is not done by one who acts" (*karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ*) means that even if one acts with the perception, "I am doing some evil," no evil is actually committed; it does not exist.
It is evil. However, they demonstrate that beings possess the perception, "We are doing it. "With a razor-edge" means with a razor-rim, or with an edge resembling the blade of a razor.
"A single mass of flesh" means a single heap of flesh; "pile" is a synonym for that same thing.
"On that account" means on account of the making of that single mass of flesh.
“Dakkhiṇa” (the South) refers to the people on the southern bank, who are harsh and cruel; with reference to them, it is said, “he strikes,” and so forth.
“Uttara” (the North) refers to those on the northern bank, who possess faith and confidence, regarding the Buddha as their own, the Dhamma as their own, and the Saṅgha as their own;
with reference to them, it is said, “he gives,” and so forth. In this context, “sacrificing” means performing a great sacrifice. “By self-control” means by the control of the sense faculties.
By means of the Uposatha ceremony; by restraint, that is, by restraint through virtue (sīla); by the speaking of truth, that is, by truthful speech.
"Āgama" means coming, the sense being "occurrence. In every respect, they reject the very performance of evil and merit.
7. Commentary on the Hetusutta.
212. Regarding the statement "there is no cause, there is no condition": here, "condition" (*paccaya*) is indeed a synonym for "cause" (*hetu*).
By both terms, they deny that there exists a condition for defilement such as bodily misconduct, or a condition for purification such as bodily good conduct.
Regarding "there is no power": it is upon their own power that these beings are established, [attaining] even the state of a deva, a Māra, or a Brahmā.
They reject that power by which one attains the enlightenment of a disciple, the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha, or even omniscience.
All such statements as "there is no energy" and so forth are merely synonyms for one another.
However, these [denials] are taken separately by way of rejecting the speech that occurs in such forms as: "This was attained by our energy, this by human strength, and this by human exertion."
"All beings" (*sabbe sattā*) includes without exception camels, oxen, donkeys, and so forth.

"All living things" (*sabbe pāṇā*) refers to them by way of "one-facultied living things," "two-facultied living things," and so on. "All creatures" (*sabbe bhūtā*) is said with reference to those born from egg-shells or womb-sheaths.
"All souls" (*sabbe jīvā*) is said with reference to rice, barley, wheat, and so forth; for these [plants] exist by way of their capacity to grow.
"Perceiving a living soul. "Without mastery, without power, without vigor"—for them there exists neither mastery, nor power, nor vigor.

Regarding the phrase "transformed by destiny, chance, and inherent nature": here, *niyati* means necessity or fixedness. *Saṅgati* means the wandering from one place to another among the six classes of birth (*abhijāti*).
*Bhāva* means inherent nature itself. Thus, [they are so] by way of destiny, chance, and inherent nature.
And they have matured, having reached various states. They show that whatever is destined to become as it should, that indeed becomes so;
and whatever is not destined to become, that does not become. "In the six classes of birth alone" means that standing in these six classes of birth alone, they experience pleasure and pain;
they show that there is no other ground for pleasure and pain.
8–10. Commentary on the Mahādiṭṭhisutta, etc., §§213–215.
"Akata" means unmade. "Akatavidhā" means having no arrangement made; the meaning is that they have not even been caused to be made by anyone with the instruction, "Do it thus.
"Animmitā" means not fashioned even by means of psychic power (*iddhi*). "Animmātā" means not caused to be fashioned. It may also be read as "animmitabbā," meaning not to be fashioned.

The meaning is that they are not to be recited, nor are they to be constructed. "Barren" means fruitless and incapable of producing anything for anyone, like barren cattle, barren palm trees, and so forth.
"Fixed like a mountain peak" means standing like a peak. "Standing firm like a pillar" means standing as if having become like a pillar;
the meaning is that they stand just as a well-planted pillar of a pillar stands immovable. "They do not waver."
Because they stand like a pillar of glass, they do not waver. "They do not change" means they do not abandon their natural state (*pakati*).
"They do not obstruct one another" means they do not harm one another. "Not able" means they are not capable.

In the phrases "the earth-body" (*pathavīkāya*) and so forth, "earth-body" refers either to the earth itself or to a collection of earth. "Of these seven bodies alone" is as in the case of a heap of beans and so forth.
Just as a struck weapon enters only through the space between heaps of beans and so forth, so too does the weapon enter through the opening and gap between the seven bodily parts.
In that regard, they show that there is merely a mere perception [on the part of the killer], thinking, "I am depriving this person of life."
"Hundreds of thousands of principal wombs" refers to one hundred and fourteen thousand principal wombs—that is, the highest wombs—along with another six hundred and fifty, and five hundred actions;
thus, they propound a useless view based on mere reasoning alone. This is also the case in passages such as "five actions and three actions," and so forth.
The same method applies here. However, some say: "The 'five actions' are taken according to the five faculties, while the 'three' are taken according to bodily action and so forth.
Regarding the terms *kamma* and *aḍḍhakamma*, his view is that bodily and verbal actions constitute *kamma*, whereas mental action constitutes *upaḍḍhakamma* (half-action).
They say that "dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā" means sixty-two paths (*dvāsaṭṭhipaṭipadā*). [They also speak of] "dvaṭṭhantarakappā" (sixty-two intermediate aeons).
In one eon (*kappa*), there are sixty-four intermediate eons (*antarakappa*); however, not knowing the other two, he spoke thus.

Regarding the "six classes of birth" (*chaḷābhijātiyo*): they speak of these six classes of birth as the black class of birth, the blue class of birth, the red class of birth, the yellow class of birth, the white class of birth, and the supreme white class of birth.
Among them, [there are] the sheep-slaughterers, the pig-slaughterers, and the bird-catchers...
"Hunters, fishermen, thieves, executioners, prison wardens, and whoever else performs cruel deeds—these they call the black class of birth (*kaṇhābhijāti*).
They say that monks are the blue class of birth (*nīlābhijāti*);
for it is said that they consume the four requisites only after casting them into thorns, thinking, 'Monks live by thorns. This...
This is the canonical text itself. Alternatively, some say that there are indeed those who have gone forth who live like thorns.
They say that the Nigaṇṭhas, who belong to the blood-red caste, are the "one-clothed" ones. It is said that these are even more pure than the two preceding groups.

They say that the householders dressed in white, who are disciples of the Acelakas, belong to the turmeric caste. Thus, among the Nigaṇṭhas themselves, they are considered superior by their own providers of requisites.
The Ājīvakas and Ājīvikīs say: "This is one of the white-born class. It is said that they are whiter than the previous four.
They say: "Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla are of the supremely white-born class. It is said that they are whiter than all of them.

"There are eight stages of manhood": they say these are the stage of the infant, the stage of play, the stage of inquiry, the stage of rectitude, the stage of the trainee, the stage of the recluse, the stage of knowing, and the stage of wisdom.
Among these, for seven days from the day of birth, beings are dull and deluded because they have just emerged from the cramped place [the womb]; this is—
They call this the "Stage of Slowness. However, those who have come from an unhappy destination weep and cry out frequently;
those who have come from a happy destination smile as they repeatedly recollect that [past state]. This is called the "Stage of Play.
Taking hold of one's mother’s or father’s hand, foot, bed, or seat, and then placing the feet upon the ground, is the "Stage of Experimentation."

The time when one is capable of walking on foot is called the *ujugata-bhūmi* (the level of straightforwardness). The time of training in the various crafts is called the *sekha-bhūmi* (the level of training).

The time of going forth from the household life into homelessness is called the *samaṇa-bhūmi* (the level of the recluse). The time of learning by attending upon a teacher is called the *jānana-bhūmi* (the level of knowing).

Regarding the statement, "The bhikkhu is a victor who has laid down his burden and does not take up anything," they call such a recluse who has attained nothing the *pannabhūmi* (the level of having laid down the burden).
"Ninety-nine hundred Ājīvaka sects" means ninety-nine hundred modes of livelihood for the Ājīvakas. "A hundred wanderers" means a hundred types of wanderer’s renunciation.
"A hundred serpent-dwelling circles" means a hundred *nāga*-maṇḍalas. "Twenty hundred faculties" means twenty hundred faculties.
"Thirty hundred hells" means thirty hundred hells. "Dust-places" refers to places where dust is scattered, such as the backs of hands, the backs of feet, and so forth.

He speaks with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). "Seven wombs of the percipient" (*saññī-gabbha*)—he speaks with reference to the camel, the ox, the donkey, the goat, the sheep, the deer, and the buffalo.
"Seven wombs of the non-percipient" (*asaññī-gabbha*)—he speaks with reference to rice, barley, wheat, mung beans, *kaṅgu* grain, *varaka* grain, and *kudrūsa* grass.
"Wombs of the knotted" (*nigaṇṭhī-gabbha*)—he speaks with reference to those born from knots, such as sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and so forth. "Seven gods" (*deva*)...
He says that although there are many gods, they are but one being (*satta*). He says that although humans are infinite, they are but one being.

He says that although there are seven *pesācas*, these very large *pesācas* are but one being. Regarding "lakes" (*sara*), he refers to great lakes; taking the lakes of Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Siṅhapapāta, Chaddanta, Mucalinda, and Kuṇāla, he speaks of them as one.
"Knots" (*pavuṭā*) means tangles. "Precipices" (*papātā*) means great precipices. "Hundreds of precipices" means hundreds of small precipices. "Dreams" (*supinā*)...
"Great dreams. "Hundreds of dreams" means hundreds of minor dreams. "Great *kappas*" refers to great *kappas*.

Here, it is said that when one drops a single drop of water from a great lake with the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass every hundred years, and after doing so seven times that lake has become devoid of water, that constitutes one great *kappa*. There are eight million four hundred thousand such great *kappas*.
"Having exhausted both fools and wise alike, they bring about the end of suffering"—this is his tenet.
It is said that even the wise man cannot purify himself in the interval, and the fool does not go beyond that [point].
"By virtue" means by the practice of naked asceticism (*acelaka*) or by whatever other [practice]; "by conduct" means by such conduct as that; "by austerity" means...
By means of ascetic practice (*tapokamma*). One who thinks "I am wise" and purifies himself prematurely is said to "ripen what is unripe.
One who thinks "I am a fool" and proceeds after exceeding the time limit prescribed for him is said to "eliminate what is ripe by repeatedly touching it.
"It is not so" means it is not thus. This demonstrates that it is impossible to accomplish either of those two. "Measured by a *doṇa*" means by a *doṇa* measure.
"As measured" means like a measured amount. "Pleasure and pain" (*sukhadukkha*) refers to pleasure and pain. "With a limited duration" means having a limit set by the time already mentioned.
"There is no waning or waxing" means there are no instances of waning or waxing; the meaning is that for the wise man, *saṃsāra* does not diminish, nor does it increase for the fool.
"In excellence and deficiency" means excellence and deficiency; this is a term for waning and waxing itself.
This is a synonym. Now, in order to establish that meaning by means of a simile, he said, "Just as if," and so forth.

Therein, "a ball of thread" refers to a ball of thread made by winding it together. "It runs away even as it is being unwound" means that if it is thrown from atop a mountain or the top of a tree, it goes along only as it is being unwound to the length of the thread; when the thread is exhausted, it stops right there.

It does not go; in the very same way, both fools and the wise, being led away by the power of time, pass through pleasure and pain, transcending them according to the aforementioned time—thus it is shown.
11–18. Commentary on the Antavāsutta and others.
216–223. The view that "the world is finite" is a view arisen through either a grasping at the sign of expansion in one direction or through reasoning, taking the world to be so.
The view that "it is infinite" is a view arisen through either a grasping at the sign of immeasurable expansion in all directions or through reasoning, taking the world to be so.
The view that "the soul and the body are the same" is a view arisen from the notion that the soul and the body are one and the same. The rest is the same in all cases.
"Utterly obvious" means this. First, these eighteen explanations by way of the path of stream-entry constitute one section. 2.
Commentary on the Second Section on the Sections Beginning with the Second Journey (224–301).

The second journey is stated by way of suffering. Therein, there are likewise eighteen explanations; following those, there are eight explanations beginning with "The self is possessed of form. Together with those, that is called the second series.
In this context, "possessing form" (*rūpī*) is the view that grasps the object itself as "self. "Formless" (*arūpī*) is the view that grasps the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) as "self.

"Both possessing form and formless" (*rūpī ca arūpī ca*) is the view that grasps both the object and the absorption as "self. "Neither possessing form nor formless" (*neva rūpī nārūpī*) is a view grasped through mere reasoning.

"Exclusively happy" (*ekantasukhī*) is a view arisen in those who have attained gains, possess speculative reasoning, or are recollectors of past births; it also applies to those who have attained meditative absorption.
For this view arises in one who attends to a selfhood that was exclusively happy in the past.
It also arises in a reasoner (*takkin*) who thinks, "Just as I am exclusively happy now, so shall I be in the future.

It likewise arises in one who remembers past births (*jātissara*) and sees that he was happy in seven or eight previous existences. The same method applies to [the views] such as "exclusively suffering" and so forth.
The third series is stated by means of impermanence and suffering through those same twenty-six suttas; the fourth series is by means of the three turnings.
The commentary on the Saṃyutta on Views is finished.
4. The Connected Discourse on Entering.
1–10. Commentary on the *Cakkhusutta* and following suttas (302–311).
In the *Okkantasaṃyutta*, "resolves" (*adhimuccati*) means he acquires resolution through faith (*saddhādhimokkha*).

"One who has entered the certainty of rightness" (*okkanto sammattaniyāmaṃ*) means one who has entered the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). "And incapable of dying until then" indicates that while the Path has arisen, the Fruit [is yet to arise].
It illuminates the absence of obstruction. For when the path has arisen, there is no such thing as creating an obstacle to the fruit. Therefore it was said:
"Suppose this person were practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and it were the time for the world-system to be consumed by fire;
the world-system would not be consumed until this person has realized the fruit of stream-entry."
“This person is called one who maintains his world for an aeon. “They endure moderate reflection” means they endure looking [at things] with moderation.
The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the Okkanta Saṃyutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Uppādasaṃyutta (Connected Discourses on Arising) 312–321.
In the Uppādasaṃyutta, everything is already clear.
The commentary on the Uppādasaṃyutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Kilesa-saṃyutta* (322–331).
Regarding the statement, “This is an imperfection of the mind” (*cittassa eso upakkileso*) in the *Kilesa-saṃyutta*: of what kind of mind? Of a mind belonging to the four planes.
Let it be so for a mind of the three planes; but how can there be an imperfection of a supramundane (*lokuttara*) mind? Because it prevents its arising.

For it should be understood as an "impurity" (upakkilesa) because it prevents that [mind] from arising. "Inclined toward renunciation" (nekkhammaninna) means inclined toward the nine supramundane states (navalokuttaradhamma).

"Mind" (citta) refers to the mind of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā). "Regarding the states to be realized through direct knowledge" (abhiññā sacchikaraṇīyesu dhammesu) means regarding the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā), which are to be realized after having directly known them through reviewing-knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa);
or, if one takes it as referring to a single state, it is "renunciation."
It should be understood. The remainder is entirely clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Kilesa-saṃyutta* is finished.
7. The *Sāriputta-saṃyutta*.
1–9. Commentary on the *Vivekaja-sutta* and others (332–340).

In the first sutta of the *Sāriputta-saṃyutta*, the phrase "it does not occur thus" means that it does not occur thus because of the abandonment of the notions of "I-making" (*ahaṅkāra*) and "mine-making" (*mamaṅkāra*). The same method applies to the second and subsequent suttas as well. [The following are] the first and so forth.
10. Commentary on the *Sucimukhī-sutta*.

341. In the tenth [story], there was one named Sucimukhī. She approached [the Elder] because, having seen the Elder—who was handsome, pleasing to behold, golden-hued, and serene in every limb—she thought, "I shall engage in jesting with him.
Then, when her words were rejected by the Elder, thinking, "Now I shall refute his argument," she said: "In that case, ascetic..."
"He eats with his face turned upwards," he said. "Facing the quarters" means facing the four cardinal directions; the meaning is that he looks toward the four quarters.
"Facing the intermediate directions" means looking toward the four intermediate directions.
"In the low arts of geomancy" refers to the low art known as geomancy (*vatthuvijjā*). Geomancy...
It is the means for knowing the causes, the results, and the proper times regarding matters such as the *lābu* (gourd), *kumbhaṇḍa* (pumpkin), and *mūlaka* (radish) plots.

"They maintain their livelihood by wrong livelihood" means that they maintain their livelihood by that very wrong livelihood known as the science of sites (*vatthuvijjā*) and the science of animals (*tiracchānavijjā*),
consuming the requisites given by people who have been inspired by the successful cultivation of those plots.
The meaning is "they live. "With faces turned downwards" means they are called "eating with faces turned downwards" because they eat while looking down at the food.
In this way, the application [of the term] should be made in all instances. Furthermore, in this context, "astrology" (*nakkhattavijjā*) refers to the science of knowing:
"Today, one should travel under this constellation; under this [other] constellation, this and that should be done. "Messengership" (*dūteyya*)...
Messenger-work (*dūtakamma*) is traveling here and there after receiving various messages for those [people].
Sending-and-going (*pahiṇagamana*) is approaching another family on account of a message from a single family within the same village.

Science of limbs (*aṅgavijjā*) is the science of knowing that, having understood the excellence of the limbs by way of the characteristics of women and men, "By this excellence of limbs, such-and-such a thing is obtained."

"Facing the intermediate directions" (*vidisāmukhā*): since the science of limbs (*aṅgavijjā*) operates by taking various parts of the body as its object, it is said to operate in the intermediate directions;
therefore, those who make their living and eat by means of that science are said to "eat facing the intermediate directions. "He announced thus":
by saying "The recluses are righteous," and so forth, he spoke of the quality of the Dispensation's leading to liberation (*niyyānika*). And that [announcement was made] by the female wanderer...
"How did about five hundred families, upon hearing [this], enter the Teaching?
The commentary on the Sāriputta-saṃyutta is finished.
8. Nāga-saṃyutta.
1. Commentary on the Suddhika Sutta 342.
In the *Nāgasaṃyutta*, "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*) means born from an egg; "womb-born" (*jalābuja*) means born from the womb; "moisture-born" (*saṃsedaja*) means born from moisture;
and "spontaneously born" (*opapātika*) means born as if having arrived by way of spontaneous rebirth. Furthermore, this sutta was spoken on account of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
Indeed, a discussion arose among the bhikkhus: "How many, pray, are the nāga-births?
Then the Blessed One, for the sake of delivering individuals from the nāga-births, spoke this sutta while revealing those nāga-births.
2–50. Commentary on the Paṇītatarasutta and others.

343–391. Regarding the second and subsequent [verses]: "having abandoned the body" (*vossaṭṭhakāya*) means having cast off the body, not counting as [something beneficial] that which has been swallowed by a snake-charmer.
"Performing two kinds" (*dvayakārino*) means performing two types [of actions]; the meaning is "performing wholesome and unwholesome [actions]. "If today we" (*sacajja mayaṃ*) means "if today we.
"He is reborn into companionship" (*sahabyataṃ upapajjati*) means he attains a state of association. In that regard, his unwholesome [action] leads to rebirth.
It is a condition for the prosperity of those who have been reborn in a wholesome state. "Food" refers to hard foods and soft foods. "Drink" refers to any kind of beverage.
"Clothing" refers to undergarments and outer robes. "Conveyance" refers to anything that serves as a means of travel, beginning with parasols and sandals.
"Garland" refers to any kind of flower garland, such as jasmine and so forth. "Perfume" refers to any kind of fragrance, such as sandalwood and so forth.

"Ointment" means anything that serves to color or beautify the skin. "Beds, dwellings, and lamps" means he gives beds such as couches and stools, dwellings such as single-storied houses, and the requisites for lamps such as ghee and oil;
the meaning is that he gives these ten kinds of objects of giving after making a wish for their long life, beauty, and abundance of happiness.
Having given that gift, they are reborn there to enjoy that prosperity. The rest is clear everywhere.
The commentary on the *Nāga-saṃyutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Supaṇṇa-saṃyutta*.
392–437. In the *Supaṇṇasaṃyutta*, because of the beauty of their wings, the *garuḷas* are called *supaṇṇas*.
Here too, the first sutta is presented with its origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*) in the same manner as before. "They carry" means they lift up.

And when lifting them up, they are able to lift those who are inferior or equal to themselves, but not those who are superior to themselves. For there are seven kinds of nagas who cannot be lifted up.

There are indeed more excellent [beings] than the *kambalassatara*—namely, the *dhatarattha*, the inhabitants of the seven seas, those dwelling on the earth, those dwelling on mountains, and those dwelling in celestial mansions (*vimāna*).
Among these, the moisture-born (*jalābuja*) and so forth are more excellent than the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) and so forth; they cannot be carried off by the latter.
However, the *kambalassatara* are the Nāga generals; wherever one sees them, any *supaṇṇa* whatsoever is unable to carry them off.
He was unable [to lift them]. As for the Naga kings Dhatarattha and the others, no one was able to lift them either.
Furthermore, as for those who dwell in the great ocean within seven hundred yojanas, because it is impossible to cause any agitation anywhere there, no one was able to lift them.
However, since there is a place for the Earth-dwelling Nagas and others to hide, they too—
He is unable to lift them up. However, those who dwell upon the crests of the waves in the great ocean can be lifted up by any supaṇṇa, whether equal or superior.
The rest is exactly as stated in the Nāga-saṃyutta.
The commentary on the Supaṇṇa-saṃyutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Gandhabbakāyasaṃyutta* (438–549).
Regarding the phrase “dwelling in the root-fragrance” (*mūlagandhe adhivatthā*) in the *Gandhabbakāyasaṃyutta*:
it refers to those who have been reborn depending upon a tree that possesses fragrance at its root. For that entire tree serves as their support. The same applies to the remaining phrases.
The same method applies here. *Gandhagandhe* means "in the fragrance of fragrances," such as the scents of roots and so forth.

For whatever tree possesses the fragrance of all its parts, including the roots and so on, that is what is called "fragrance" (*gandha*) here. It is "in the fragrance of that fragrance," meaning dwelling within it.
Here, all the parts—roots and so forth—are beneficial for those very [beings]. "He is a giver of root-fragrances" refers to [trees] such as the *kāḷānusārika*.
"He is a giver of root-fragrances. In this way, the meaning is to be understood for all the following terms.
For it is in order to show that they make an aspiration by giving both similar gifts and dissimilar gifts that the tenfold basis of giving, beginning with "he gives food," has been stated.
The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Gandhabbakāya-saṃyutta* is concluded.
11. Commentary on the *Valāhaka-saṃyutta*, 550–606.
In the *Valāhaka-saṃyutta*, the term "those belonging to the host of clouds" (*valāhakakāyikā*) refers to sky-faring deities who have arisen within the divine host named "Clouds."
"Cold-clouds" (*sītavalāhakā*) means clouds that produce cold. The same principle applies to the remaining terms as well.

"In accordance with the mental aspiration" (*cetopaṇidhimanvāya*) means by way of the fixing of the mind. "It becomes cold": whatever cold occurs during the rainy season or the winter is produced solely by the season (*utusamuṭṭhāna*).
However, that which is excessively cold even when it is already cold, or the cold that arises during the summer, is produced through the power of the deities (*devatānubhāvena nibbattaṃ*).
"Cold" means this. Regarding "it becomes hot": that heat which occurs in the summer is simply natural, being produced by the season (*utusamuṭṭhānika*).
However, that heat which is excessively hot even during the summer, or the heat that arises during the cold season, is called "heat produced by the power of deities.
Regarding "there is a cloud": there is a canopy of clouds. Here too, as for the cloud that arises during the rainy season and the cool season—

That [cloud] which arises from the seasons is simply natural. However, that which is an excessive cloud—covering even the sun and moon for seven days and seven nights and creating total darkness—and that cloud which appears during the months of Cittā and Vesākha, is called "divine cloud" (devatānubhāvena uppannaṃ abbhaṃ).
"There is wind" refers to the natural wind of the north, south, and so forth, according to each respective season.

This is produced by the season alone. Furthermore, that which is called a "gale" which uproots tree trunks and so forth, as well as any other unseasonable wind, is said to be produced by the power of deities.
As for the rain that falls during the four months of the rainy season, that is produced by the season alone. However, that which is excessive rain even during the [proper] season—
And that rain which falls during the months of Vesākha and Phagguna is said to be produced through the power of deities.

Here is an account of this: it is said that a certain son of the rain-cloud deities, who dwelt at Talakūṭaka, went into the presence of an elder whose taints were destroyed, paid homage to him, and stood there. The elder asked, "Who are you? He replied, "Venerable sir, I am a son of the rain-cloud deities."
“Is it by your mind that the rain falls? “Yes, venerable sir. “We wish to see it.
“Then you will get wet, venerable sir. “Neither the cloud-head nor the thunder is visible;
how shall we get wet? “Venerable sir, the rain falls by our mind; you should enter the leaf-hut. “Very well, young gods,” he said.
Having washed his feet, he entered the leaf-hut. Just as he was entering, the son of the gods sang a single song and raised his hand;
an instant cloud formed over an area of three *yojanas* on all sides. The Elder entered the leaf-hut while still half-soaked.
Furthermore, this so-called "rain" falls for eight reasons: by the power of *nāgas*, by the power of *supaṇṇas*, and so forth.

[The clouds arise] through the power of a deity, through an act of truth (*saccakiriyā*), through temperature-born origination (*utusamuṭṭhāna*), through the provocation of Māra, through the power of psychic potency (*iddhibala*), and through a cloud of destruction.
The commentary on the *Valāhakasaṃyutta* is finished.
12. Commentary on the *Vacchagottasaṃyutta*.

607–661. In the *Vacchagottasaṃyutta*, [the term] "ignorance" (*aññāṇa*) is used in the sense of ignorance (*aññāṇena*). Thus, in all instances, the meaning should be understood through the instrumental case alone.

Furthermore, all these are merely synonyms for one another. And in this *Saṃyutta*, it should be understood that there are eleven discourses (*sutta*) and fifty-five detailed expositions (*veyyākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the Vacchagotta Saṃyutta is finished.
13. Jhāna Saṃyutta. 1.
Commentary on the Samādhimūlaka Samāpatti Sutta.
662. Regarding the first discourse in the *Jhānasaṃyutta*, "skilled in concentration" means being skilled in defining the factors: that the first jhāna has five factors and the second has three.
"Not skilled in attaining concentration" means one is unable to enter jhāna after having gladdened and made the mind fit. The remaining phrases should be understood in this same manner.
2–55. Commentary on the *Samādhimūlakaṭhitisutta* and others, §§663–716.
Regarding the second and subsequent [terms]: "Not skilled in stability in concentration" means one who is unskilled in maintaining meditative absorption (*jhāna*);

he is unable to maintain the absorption for even the duration of seven or eight finger-snap moments. "Not skilled in emerging from concentration" means one who is unskilled in emerging from meditative absorption.
He is unable to emerge according to the prescribed limit. He is unskilled in making the mind pliable for concentration;

that is, he is unskilled in gladdening the mind and making it serviceable. He is unskilled in the object for concentration; that is, he is unskilled regarding the kasiṇa objects. He is unskilled in the range for concentration;
that is, he is unskilled both in the range of the meditation subject and in the range of the alms-round. He is not...
"Skilled in directing toward concentration" means unskilled in directing the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"One who does not practice with care regarding concentration" means one who does not apply oneself carefully to entering *jhāna*.

"One who does not practice with persistence regarding concentration" means one who does not practice constantly for the attainment of *jhāna*, but practices only occasionally. "One who does not practice what is suitable regarding concentration" means...
One is unable to fulfill the factors conducive to and supportive of concentration.
Following that, tetrads are stated by connecting them with terms such as "attainment" (samāpatti) and so forth; their meaning should be understood in the same manner already explained.
Furthermore, the entire *Jhāna-saṃyutta* herein is spoken solely in terms of mundane jhāna.
The commentary on the *Jhāna-saṃyutta* is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Khandha-vagga* in the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta-nikāya*.
The Second Part of the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
